corrects him. Why did he deserve to be corrected by an angel? Because his suspicion was not malicious, but rather one of those that the Apostle says arise between brothers. Malicious suspicions are those of slanderers; the benevolent ones, those of the superiors. It is lawful to suspect evil of one's son, but it is not lawful to slander him. You suspect evil in him, but you want to find the good. He who suspects benevolently desires to be defeated, for he finds joy precisely when he discovers that what he suspected was false. Joseph was one of these with respect to his wife, to whom he had not united himself physically, although he had already done so through faith. Therefore, the virgin also fell under false suspicion. But in the same way that the spirit of Daniel was present on behalf of Susanna, so the angel also appeared to Joseph on behalf of Mary: Do not be afraid to welcome Mary as your wife, for what will be born from her is from the Holy Spirit. Suspicion was removed, since redemption was discovered. 4. Shortly before the wives were rejoicing with Susanna. Let the virgins rejoice with Mary. Let each other maintain chastity; the first, the conjugal one; the second, the virginal. Both forms of chastity have their merit before God. And, although the virginal is greater and the conjugal is lesser, both are pleasing to God, since they are a gift from God. They all lead to eternal life; but in it not all acquire the same honor, the same dignity, the same merit. Thus, eternal life and the kingdom of God will be, for example, like what we call heaven. All the stars are found in the sky; in the same way, in the kingdom Ab angelo corrigitur. Quare dignus fuet ab angelo corrected? Quia non in illo erat maliuola suspicio, quales apostolus dicit, maliuolas suspiciones nasci inter fratres (cf. 1 Tim 6:4). Maliuolae suspiciones sunt calumniantium, beniuolae suspiciones sunt gubernantium. Licet de filio male suspicari, sed filio non licet calumnian. Suspicaris malum, sed optos inuenire bonum. Qui beniuole suspicatur, uinci cupit: tune enim bene laetatur, quando falsum inuentum fuerit quod male suspicatur. Talis erat Ioseph circa coniugem suam, cui corpore non erat mixtus, sed tamen fide iam fuet copulatus. Venit ergo et uirgo in false suspicionem. Be sicut pro Susanna adfuit in Danihele spiritus, sic pro María adfuit Ioseph angelus: Noli timere accipere Mariam coniugem tuam. Quod enim de ea nascilur, de spirétu sancto est (Mt 1,18-20). Ablata suspicio est, quia ínuenta redemptio est. 4.

Gaudebant paulo ante coniugatae ad Susannam. Gaudeant uirgines ad Mariam. Utraeque teneant castitatem, illae coniugalem, illae uirginalem. Utraque enim castitas habet apud deum meritum. Et si [32] uirginalis maior est, coniugalis minor, tamen utraque grata est deo, quia donum est dei. Ad uitam aeternam omnes perueniunt, sed in uita aeterna non omnes eumdem honorem, eamdem dignitatem, idem meritum comparant. Sic erit uita aeterna et regnum dei, quomodo, similarityinis causa, quod dicimus caelum. In cáelo sunt omnia sidera; sic et in regno dei
Susana and José, models of chastity

of God all the good faithful will be present. Eternal life will be the same for everyone, since there no one will live longer than another, since we all have to live without end. This is the denarius that the workers are to receive, both those who worked in the vineyard and those who arrived at the eleventh hour: that denarius means eternal life, which is the same for all. But look at the sky; Remember the Apostle: The heavenly bodies are one way and the terrestrial bodies are another way; One is the splendor of the sun, another is that of the moon, and another is that of the stars, since one star differs from another in splendor. This is what will happen in the resurrection of the dead. Therefore, brothers, let each one strive in this world according to the gift he has received, to enjoy in the future. Are you married? It is an inferior way of life, an inferior reward is expected, but hope of reaching the eternal kingdom is not lost. You must comply with the marital precepts. What then? Just because you have a wife, shouldn't you recognize yourself as a pilgrim in this world? Must you not think that you must die and leave the bed of pleasure? In any case, look where you are headed: whether to miserable torment or eternal happiness. Think about it, then; keep what you received, carry your burden, which, if you love, is light, but heavy if you hate. It was not in vain that the Lord said—or was he referring only to the continents?—: Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you relief. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls—not for your flesh, but omnes erunt boni fideles. Vita aeterna par erit omnibus. Non enim ibi alius plus uiuit, alius minus, quando omnes sine fine uicturi sumus. Ipse est denarius, quem accepturi sunt operanii, siue qui uineam laborauerunt, siue qui ad horam undecimam uenerunt: denarius Ule uita aeterna est, quae omnibus par est (cf. Mt 20:9-10). Sed intuemini caelum, recordamini apostolum: Alia cor(1508)pora caelestia, et alia terrestria. Alia gloria solis, et alia gloria lunae, et alia gloria stellarum. Stella enim ab stella differt in gloria: sic et resurrectio mortuorum (1 Cor 15:40-42). Ergo unusquisque, fratres mei, pro dono quod accepit, certet in hoc saeculo, ut gaudeat in the future. Coniugatus is? Inferior uita est, inferius praemium speratur, aeternum tamen regnum non desesperatur. ÍPraecepta tibi coniugalia retinenda sunt. Quid enim?

Quia uxorem habes, don't you owe yourself agnoscere peregrinari in hoc mundo? (cf. 2 Cor 5:6). Moriturum non te deben cogitare, exiturum de lecto uoluptatis? Et uide quo uteumque pergas, ad tormentum calamitatis, an ad praemium aeternitatis. Cogita ergo, serua quod accepisti, perduc sarcinam tuam, quia leuis est, si diligis; grauis, yes hate. Non enim frustration dominus ait—aut uere, cum hoc ait, solis continentibus loquebatur?— Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam uos. Tollite iugum meum super uos, et discite a me quia mitis sum et bumilis corde, et inuenietis requiem animabus uestris —non carnibus uestris, sed animabus uestris— iugum enim
Susana and José, models of chastity

for your souls—; my yoke is easy and my burden is light; light for those who love, heavy for those who deny. Have you put the yoke of the Lord around your neck? It is soft, if you try to handle it well, and rough, if you resist. Married life is surrounded by temptations. Wasn't that Susanna tempted in her chastity by the fact that she had a husband? Are those who are married the only ones who do not suffer this kind of temptation? Behold, Susanna was another man's wife, she had her own husband, and yet she was tempted. It fluctuated in the storm. Anxiety, he said, surrounds me everywhere. He feared dying because of the action of false witnesses, but he feared dying more because of the sentence of the divine judge. The false witnesses would bring her a temporary death, the divine judge would punish her forever. He weighed both things and chose. He began fearing; then he weighed; He weighed and chose. It was a lesson for pious married women. He taught to resist temptation, to fight, to tire, to beg for help. 5. Scripture bears witness to the woman put to the test. Did he abandon the men? Did he allow them to lack an example to imitate? We have just seen Susana tempted by men who coveted her corruption. We just saw her in the fight. That reading was the amphitheater of our hearts; we were spectators of that athlete of God, that chaste spirit; We saw her fighting against the adversary. Let us triumph with the winner over the defeated. Pious wives have their example, they have something to imitate. feel indebted-

They keep what they keep before God, not before man, since they only keep it when they feel indebted to God for it. They keep it only if they feel indebted to those who see that they keep it, something that not even the husband sees. The husband is often absent, but God is always present. And it sometimes happens that the husband, as a man, suspects what is false. Then, the wife is to pray for the husband who suspects what is false. Pray for salvation, not damnation. False suspicion does not close the eyes of God. Your conscience is naked before the one who created it. He delivers the temporarily oppressed for eternity. But pray for your husband and strive not only to lead a holy life, but also to maintain a blameless reputation. Chastity itself frees a holy life from condemnation; On the other hand, a good reputation frees others from slipping due to false suspicion, and perhaps from falling into sin by judging what they do not see, as those judges of Susanna fell. The holy Daniel, or, better, the Lord through Daniel, more than Susanna, freed them from eternal death. He certainly freed her, but from being temporarily condemned; But he freed them so that, avoiding wrongly judging and condemning the innocent, they would not fall into the eternal damnation of that judge whom no one can corrupt and from whom no one can hide.

meum lene est, et sarcina mea leuis est (Mt 11,28-30), leuis amanti, grauís neganti. Iugum domíní ceruíce sumpsisti? Lene est, si bene conaris; asperum, si reluctaris. Circumstant temptationes coniugalem uitam. Numquid enim ist Susanna ideo non tentata est in ipsa pudicitia, quia marito erat coniuncta? Numquid [33] hae solae in hac parte non tentantur, quae uiris copulantur? Ecce Susanna uxor aliena erat, maritum habebat. Tamen tentata est. Fluctuauit in tempestate: Angustiae, inquit, mihi sunt undique (Dan 13,22). A falsis enim testibus timuit morí, sed a deo iudice uero timuit penitus morí. A falsis enim testibus ad tempus moreretur, a iudice deo in aeternum puniretur. Appendit, elegit. Prius timuit, et appendit. Appendit et elegit. Elegit et uicit. Docuit feminas religious coniugatas. Tentatori resistere docuit, struggle docuit, laborare docuit, adiutorium implorare docuit. 5. Si de femina tentata scriptura testis est, numquid uiros deseruit? Numquid eis exemplum imitationis deesse permisit? Intuebamur Susannam tentatam a viris concupiscentibus eius corruptionem. Intuebamur certantem. Lectio illa theatrum nostri cordis erat: athletam dei, pudicum spiritum, exspectabamus, certantem aduersarium uidebamus. De uicto cum uictrice triumphemus. Habent aedificium suum religiouse coniuges, habent quod imitatentur. Deo debenant quod seruant, non homini. Tune

6. Referring, then, to men, I said that they too have not been left without an example to imitate. Chaste men, men who fear God, men for whom their proenim seruant, si deo debenant, are enough. Tune seruant, si illi debenant, qui uidet quod seruant, quod etiam maritus non uidet. Saepe enim absens est maritus, semper est praesens deus. Et aliquando, quia homo est maritus, suspicatur falsum. Tune oret mulier pro marito suo suspicante falsum. Oret ut ille saluetur, non ut ille damnetur. False enim uiri suspicio non claudit oculos dei. Illius conscientia nuda est coram illo qui creat eam. Ipse enim ad tempus oppressam liberat in aeternum. Sed oret pro (1509) marito, et det operam, non solum habere bonam uitam, sed etiam illaesam famem. Bonam enim uitam ipsa pudicitia liberat, ne damnetur. Bona uero fame alios liberat, ne falsum suspicando labantur, et forte in peccatum decidant, dum quod non uident iudicant: sicuti isti ceciderunt, et Danihel sanctus, immo per Danihelem dominus, magis illos iudices quam Susannam ab interiore morte liberauit. Liberauit enim illam, ne ad tempus damnaretur. Liberauit autem illos, ne male judicando et innocentem damnando, in aeternum supplicium caderent eius iudicis, quem nemo potest corruptere, a quo nemo potest se abscondere. [34] 6. Dicebam ergo de uiris, quia nec ipsi sine exemplo dimissi sunt. Viri casti, uiri timentes deum, uiri quibus sufficiunt coniuges suae, uiri qui non uiolatis quod uobis uiolari non uultis, uiri qui fidem, quam
Susana and José, models of chastity

Dear women, men who do not violate the rights that you do not want to be violated, men who maintain the fidelity that you demand, you also contemplate, as I remember it, what your women contemplated when listening to the reading. The divine Scripture did not leave you without an example. They heard Susanna's story and rejoiced at winning. You set your sights on Joseph. Not in that Joseph to whom the virgin Mary had married, who begot Christ, because the temptation of suspicion came to him and he was healed instantly by the angel. Holy Scripture bears witness to another Joseph who was tempted by an impudent woman. She felt love towards the beautiful young man, but her mind was not chaste, but perverse; In it he had no eyes to see the spiritual and invisible beauty. He loved her beauty, but did not want her chastity. She loved a man who was not her own, she loved her husband's servant. But did he love the fidelity that he kept to his lord? What do you think: that she loved him or rather she loved herself? I didn't love him. If she loved him, why did she want to ruin him? See that I have shown you that I did not love him. The poison of passion burned, the flame of charity did not shine. But he knew how to see what she didn't know. He was more beautiful on the inside than on the outside, more beautiful in the light of his heart than in the skin of his flesh. He enjoyed his own beauty where that woman's eyes did not penetrate. Contemplating, then, the inner beauty of chastity, how could I allow it to be stained and violated by the temptation of that woman? She loved, but he loved too. But it was more exegistis, redditis, spectate et uos, me commemorante, quod spectabant uxores uestrae, lectore recitante. Nec uos sine exemplo scriptura diuina dimisit. Illae Susannam audiebant, et in ea uincendo gaudebant. Vos Ioseph attendite. Non illum Ioseph, cui desponsata fuet uirgo Maria, quae peperit Christum, nam ille suspicione tentatus est, et ab angelo mox sanatus est. Alium Ioseph sancta scriptura testatur, quem tentauit impudica. Amauit pulchrum non casta, et peruersa mente, ubi oculos non habebat, ubi uideretur spiritalis et inuisibilis pulchritudo. Quem amarat pulchrum, nolebat castum. Amauit alienum, amauit seruum uiri sui. Sed fidem seruantem domino suo amauit? An whores amauit illum potius se? Nec illum. If I loved, how will I lose uolebat? Ecce probaui quia non amarat. Veneno libidinis ardebat, non flamma caritatis luzbat.

Sed ille nouerat uidere, quod illa non nouerat. Pulchrior erat intus quam foris, pulchrior in cordis luz, quam in carnis cute. Quo illius feminae oculi non penetrabant, ibi ipse sua pulchritudine fruitatur. Intuens ergo interiorem pulchritudinem castitatis, quando illam maculari, quando uiolari illius feminae temptatione permitteret? Amabatilla. Sed amarat et ille.

that he loved more than what she loved, since he saw what she did not see. 7. If you want to see something of the spiritual beauty of chastity, if you have eyes, whatever they may be, capable of seeing it, I am going to propose something to you as an example. You love chastity in your wife. Don't hate in someone else's what you love in your own. What do you love in yours? chastity That chastity that you love in your wife, you hate in someone else's. You hate it in another's woman, whose chastity you want to ruin by lying with her. Do you want to kill in another's woman what you love in your own? Do you want to spoil in someone else's woman what you love in your own? How are you going to have the argument of mercy, you murderer of chastity! Safeguard, then, in another's woman what you want to see safeguarded in your own. Rather, he loves chastity itself. But perhaps you think you love your wife's flesh, not her chastity. Clearly sordid thought, but I won't leave you without giving you an example. I, in fact, think that you love chastity in your wife more than flesh. But to show you that you are absolutely a lover of chastity, I tell you that you love it in your daughter. What man is there who does not want his daughters to be chaste? What man does not enjoy the chastity of his daughters? Do you love their flesh too? Do you perhaps desire her beautiful body, which, if it is not chaste, causes you horror? See that I have shown that you are a lover of chastity. If, then, I have shown that you are a lover of chastity, what offense have you done to yourself not to also love it in yourself? Here Et plus erat quod amat ille, quam quod amat illa. Quia uidebat ille quod non uidebat illa. 7. Si uis uidere quomodocumque spiritalem pulchritudinem pudicitiae, si habes ad illam qualescumque oculos, exempli gratia aliquid tibi propono: ipsam amas in coniuge tua. Noli odisse in aliena quod [35] you love in tua. Who do you love in tua? Castitatem. Hanc odis in aliena quam amas in tua. Hoc odis in aliena, cum qua concumbendo eius uis will lose castitatem. Quod amas in tua, hoc uis interficiere in aliena? Quod amas in tua, hoc uis will I lose in aliena? Quomodo habebis rationem pietatis, homicidal castitatis? Serua ergo in aliena quod seruari cupis in tua. Ipsam castitatem potius dilige. Sed forte existimas te amatorem csse carnis uxoris tuae, (1510) non castitatis. Sórdida quidem cogitatio, sed non te dimitto sine example. Ego enim puto quod castitatem plus ames in coniuge tua, quam carnem. Sed ut te absolutissime ostendam umatorem castitatis: hanc amas in filia.

Quis hominum est, qui non filias suas castas uelit? Quis hominum, qui non filiarum suarum congaudeat aistitati? Numquid et ibi carnem amas? Numquid concupiscis corpus pulchrum, ubi exhorres incastum? Ecce probaui te amatorem castitatis. Si ergo amatorem castitatis ostendi te, quid te offendisti, ut non illam

You have a brief summary: love in yourself what you love in your daughter. Love it in another's wife, since your daughter will also be another's wife. Love, then, chastity in yourself too. If you come to love someone else's woman, you will not have her indefinitely; but, if you love chastity, you will have it instantly. Love, therefore, chastity to possess eternal happiness. 8. You may be tempted. An impudent woman can feel love for you. If he finds you alone, he will try to snatch your carnal embrace. If you refuse, he threatens you with the torment of defamation. This is what those false elders did with Susanna; That is what made Saint Joseph his master's wife. But set your sights on the one on whom both Susanna and Joseph set their sights. God does not cease to be present because there is no witness. Joseph did not want to offend his eyes, the eyes of his Lord, who was present. He did not want to give that impudent woman the consent to lie together. He rejected the lust of others and embraced his own chastity. She made good on her threat. She lied to her husband, and he believed her. For now, God tolerates it. Joseph is kept in prison as a criminal, he who did not offend God. But God was not absent there either, since he was not guilty. The Lord assisted Joseph in his patience. Not helping him immediately was a delay in increasing his reward. He gladdened with his own merits the one who exercised in torment. Because of his chastity, the holy Joseph also had to suffer something hard and bitter. If perhaps I had felt love for that loved one? Ecce habes compendium. Love in te quod love in filia. Ama hoc in uxore aliena, quia et filia tua uxor erit aliena. Ama ergo et in te castitatem. Si uxorem alienam amaueris, non continuo habebis. Si castitatem amaueris, mox habebis. Ama ergo castitatem, ut habeas aeternam felicitatem. [36] 8. Sed forte tentaberis. Amabit te mulier impudica. Inueniet te in solitude, conabitur extorquere complexum. Si renueris, minabitur infamando supplicium. Hoc seniores falsi Susannae fecerunt. Hoc uxor domini sui fecit sancto Ioseph. Sed attendite illum, quem attendit et Susanna et Ioseph. Non, quia nullus testis est, deus ibi non est. Eius oculos noluit offendere Ioseph, oculos domini sui praesentis. Noluit impudicae mulieri ad concubitum illicitum consentiré. Reppulit concupiscentiam alienam, amplexus est pudicitiam suam. Fecit tamen illa quod minata est. Mentita est uiro, credita est a suo marito. Adhuc patiens deus.

Sed Ioseph in prison custoditur tamquam reus, a quo non est offensus deus. Sed nec ibi defuit deus, quia ille non erat reus. Adfuit dominus Ioseph patíenter. Quod non cita subuenit, ad maiora praemia distulit. Laetificauit merit, quem exercuit supplicio. Debuit enim sanctus ipse Ioseph pro ipsa pudicitia aliquid etiam durum pati, hoc est amarum. Si ipsam impudicam mulierem forsitan amaret, pro illa paratus
Susana and José, models of chastity

impudent woman, I would have been willing to suffer any harshness for her. And she would not have considered the young man's love for her proven if she had not seen him willing to suffer such annoyances and fatigue for her and to return her love, or, better, not love, but perverse passion. In turn, she would be inflamed with love for him when she saw him burning with so much passion, to the point of not refusing to suffer any torture for her. If he had been willing to tolerate this for an impudent woman, how much more for chastity itself! Therefore, God does well to sometimes defer his help to test and exercise man, so that man may reveal himself. For nothing is hidden from God. 9. This, then, is my exhortation to you, brothers: put, above all, the beauty and beauty of wisdom above carnal lusts, worldly joys, vain and volatile pomp and the smoke of the present life; Put before them the sweetness and softness of wisdom, the beauty of purity, the beauty of chastity. All these things are hidden in the celestial treasure. These precious stones are naked in the eyes of God and shine very brightly. If you have eyes, you can see them. Put them before the various illicit pleasures. And if the temptation goes so far as to cause you to suffer discomfort, my brothers, who does not suffer it for his wallet? Who does not suffer them for their field, for a landmark at the edge of their plot? If you suffer for these things that you do not have in your power to retain them as much as you want or to leave them to whomever you want, but rather, esset dura perpeti. Et illa amorem suum erga se non proveet, nisi propter illam talia molesta uel dura spectaret, et caritati —immo non caritati, sed malae cupuditati— redderet uicem. Exardesceret illa in illum uicissim, quia uidebat eum mucho amore suo inardescere, ut propterea non recusaret quaecumque supplicia tolerare. Si hoc pro impudica, quanto magis pro ipsa pudicitia! Bene ergo aliquando deus differt adiutorium suum, ut probet hominem, ut exerceat hominem, ut ipse sibi homo innotescat. Yum deum nihil latet. 9. Hoc ergo monuerim caritatem uestram, fratres, ut ante omnia concupiscentiis carnalibus et gaudiis saecularibus et uanae pompae et uolaticae, uaporique uitae huius praesentis praeponatis decus et pulchritudinem sapientiae, praeponatis dulcedinem suauitatemque sapientiae, praeponatis decus pudicitiae, pulchri('í5íí)tudinem castitatis. Haec omnia abscondita sunt in thesauro caelesti.

Nudae coram oculis dei [37] moanme sunt istae pretiosae, multum lucent. If oculos habetis, uidetis. Diuersis ergo et illicitis delectationibus ista praeponite. Et si tentatio usque accesserit, ut etiam molestam patiamini, fratres mei, quis non patiatur_ propter sacculum suum? Quis non patiatur pro agro suo, pro uno lapide limitis agri sui? Si pro his rebus patiamini, quas non habetis in potestate, quamdiu uultis retiñere, et quibus uulti? resign, sed S.Ag. 26

We frequently lose them even in life, and not rarely, after our death, those we hate possess them; If for these goods—if we must call these things that do not make us good goods—men suffer so many evils with a serene spirit, why are they lazy in suffering them for the sake of faith? Why are they shy to suffer for the heavenly treasure, for those riches that not even shipwrecks can take from us? In fact, the righteous castaway, even if he comes out naked, comes out rich. 10. Holy Job was full of these riches. He had lost everything in one fell swoop, with nothing left in his house that had previously made him look rich. Suddenly he becomes a beggar, he sees himself among the manure, full of worms from head to toe. What is more miserable than this misery? What is happier than inner happiness? He had lost everything the Lord had given him, but he had the one who had given it all, God. Naked, he said, I came out of my mother's womb, naked I will return to the earth. The Lord gave it to me, the Lord took it from me. As it pleased the Lord, so it happened. Praise the name of the Lord. Is it true that he is poor? Is it true that you have nothing? If nothing remains, from what treasure do you draw these precious stones of praise to God? Then the tempter came to his flesh. After having taken everything from him, he left the woman to tempt him. He left Eve, but he was not Adam. And how was it found then? How did he respond to his wife, who suggested he blaspheme? You have spoken, he said, saepe amittuntur cum uiuimus, saepe post mortem nostram ab eis quos odimus possidentur; si pro his bonis —si tamen diganda sunt bona, quae non faciunt bonds— tanta mala homines aequo animo patiuntur, pro fide quare pigri sunt? pro thesauro caelesti quare timidi sunt, pro illis diuitiis, quas nec naufragia nobis possunt auferre? Iustus enim naufragus euadit diues et nudus. 10. His diuitiis plenus erat sanctus Iob. Omnia uno ictu perierant, nihil in domo eius remanserat, quibus paulo ante opulentus uidebatur. Súbito mendicus, in stercore a capite usque ad pedes uermibus scatens. What is misery miserius? Quid interiore congratulate yourself felicius? Perdiderat omnia illa quae dederat deus, sed habebat ipsum, qui dederat omnia, deum. Nudus, inquit, exiui de uterus matris meae, nudus reuertar in terram. Dominus dedit, dominus abstulit. Sicut domino placuit, ita factum est. Sit nomen domini benedictum (Iob 1,21). Certe pauper est? Certe nihil habet?

Si nihil remanet, de quo thesauro gemmae istae laudis dei proferebantur? Post usque ad carnem tentator second. Omnibus sublatis, tentatricem mulierem reliquit (cf. ib., 2,7.9). Euam resigned, sed Adam ille non Fuit. Et ibi qualis inventus est? How do I respond to uxori blasphemiam suggestive? Locuta is, inquit, tamquam an ex-insi-
Susana and José, models of chastity

like a foolish woman. If we have received good things from the hand of God, why should we not tolerate evil? Oh rotten and upright man, ugly and beautiful, wounded and healthy at the same time! O man sitting in the dung and reigning in heaven! If we love him, let us imitate him; To imitate him, let us strive, and if we fail in the task, let us implore help. He who instituted combat helps the combatant. In fact, God does not contemplate you, when you fight, in the same way that the people do the charioteer; The masses know how to shout, but not help. When you fight, God does not contemplate you as the instituter of the games to the athlete; He has the crown of hay ready, but he does not know nor can he help someone who is in trouble; In fact, he is a man, not God. And perhaps, as a spectator, he gets more tired sitting in the fray than the other. God, on the other hand, when he becomes a spectator of his combatants, if they invoke him, he calls them to himself. Love of God, love of the world
Theme: Love of God, love of the world. Location: Unknown. Date: Around the year 428.

1. In this life, every temptation is a struggle between two loves: the love of the world and the love of God; He who wins of the two draws to himself, as if by gravity, his lover. We come to God with affection, not with wings or feet. And, on the contrary, contrary affections tie us to the earth, with knots or some bodily chain. Christ came to transform love and make a lover of earth a lover of heavenly life; for us he became man who made us men; God assumed man to turn men into gods. This is the combat before us: the fight against the flesh, against the devil, against the world. But we have confidence, since the one who arranged the fight is a spectator who provides his help and exhorts us not to boast of our strength. In fact, whoever presumes about them, as a man, presumes about the strength of a man, and cursed is everyone who places his hope in man. The martyrs, inflamed in the flame of this pious and holy love, made the hay of their flesh burn with the oak of their mind, SERMO

Non enim pennis aut pedibus, sed affectibus venimus ad Deum. Et rursum non corporeis nodis et vinculis, sed contrariis affectibus terrae inhaeremus. Venit Christus mutare amorem, et de tierra faceré vitae caelestis amatorem: homo propter nos factus, qui nos nomines fecit; et assumens hominem Deus, ut nomines faceret déos. Hic propositus nobis agón, haec lucta cum carne, haec lucta cum diabolo, haec lucta cum saeculo. Sed fidamus, quoniam ille qui hoc certamen indixit, non sine adiutorio suo spectat, nec de viribus nostris ut praesumamus hortatur. Burning in this love, or, better, so that we burn in it, he says: Whoever loves his father or mother more than me, is not worthy of me, and whoever does not take up his cross and follow me, is not worthy of me. He has not eliminated love for parents, for wife, for children, but has placed it in its rightful place. He did not say: "Who loves", but: who loves more than me. This is what the Church says in the Song of Songs: He ordained love in me. Love your father, but not more than the Lord; love him who has begotten you, but no more than he who created you. Your father has begotten you, but it was not he who shaped you, because in doing so he did not know who or how you were going to be born. Your father fed you, but he did not bring out bread to satisfy you. Finally, whatever your father has in store for you on earth, he dies so that you may succeed him, and with his death he makes room for you in life. On the other hand, God is Father, and what he reserves, he reserves together with himself, so that you possess the inheritance together with the father himself and do not have to wait for him to die to succeed him, but, always remaining in him, you adhere to him who always remains. Love your father, then, but not above God; love your mother, but not above the Church, which gave birth to you for eternal life. But carnal affection gives way to his caresses and in a certain way human sensitivity is allowed to fall. Pick up the flow of the dress, gird yourself with courage. Does carnal love torment you? Take up your cross and follow the Lord. Also your own Savior, although God in the flesh, although God with flesh, let you see his human sensitivity when he said: Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. He knew that such a chalice could not pass, since he had come to drink it. He had to drink that chalice of his own free will, not out of necessity. He was omnipotent; If he had wanted it, it would certainly have happened, since it was God with the Father,

one God with God the Father. But in his form as a servant, in what he took from you for you, he let the voice of man be heard, the voice of the flesh. He deigned to personify you in himself so that in his person you could proclaim your weakness and gain strength. He showed you the will, subject in you to temptation, and immediately taught you which will you should put first and which. Father, he said, if it is possible, let this chalice pass from me. This is the human will; I am a man, I speak in the form of a servant: Father, if it is possible, pass this cup. It is the cry of the flesh, not of the spirit; the cry of weakness, not of divinity. If possible, pass this chalice. This is the will regarding which it is said even to Peter: But when you grow old, another will gird you, take you and take you where you do not want to go. Why, then, is it that the martyrs have also won? Because they put the will of the spirit before the will of the flesh. They loved this life and weighed it in the balance, and from there they deduced how much the eternal one had to be loved if this perishable one was loved so much. He who must die does not want to die, and yet he will necessarily die, even if he does not cease to refuse death. Although you do not want to die, you do nothing against it, you accomplish nothing, you achieve nothing: you have no power to eliminate the need to die. Even if you don't want it, what you fear will come; Even if you refuse it, what you differ will come. It is evident that you strive to defer death; perhaps to cancel it? Therefore, if lovers of this life take so much effort to postpone death, how much effort must be made to make it disappear!

If, then, love is not completely asleep in your heart, if a spark shines in the ashes of your flesh, if it has some strength in your heart, be careful so that not only does the wind of temptation not extinguish it, but, on the contrary, it ignites it more vividly; Do not burn like tow, which the slightest current of air extinguishes, but like oak, like coal, so that the wind fuels you. Consider the two kinds of death: one temporary, the first, and another eternal, the second. The first is available for everyone; the second only for the evil, the impious, the unfaithful, the blasphemers and anyone who opposes sound doctrine. Look, put these two deaths before your eyes. If possible, you certainly want to avoid either. I know that you love life, that you do not want to die, and that you would like to go from this life to the next not by resurrecting after death, but by changing in life to a better state. That's what you would want; This is how human sensitivity behaves; the same soul, I don't know in what way, wants it and desires it. Loving life, he hates death, and since he does not hate his flesh, he does not even want what he hates to happen to it. For no one has ever hated his flesh. This same sentiment is shown by the Apostle when he says: We have as a gift from God an eternal home in heaven, not

a house made by human hand. Here we groan, longing to clothe ourselves in our abode in heaven. We do not want, he says, to be stripped, but to be clothed, so that what is mortal is absorbed by life. You don't want to be bereft, but you will be. But it is better that you strive so that, when death strips you of the garment of flesh, you find yourself protected with the breastplate of faith. Thus he added below: In the case of being found dressed and not naked. The first death, in fact, has to strip you of the flesh, which you have to abandon for a period of time to recover it at the right moment. And this, whether you want it or not, because you are not going to be resurrected because you want it or not resurrected because you don't want to, nor are you going to stop being resurrected because you do not believe in the resurrection. Since you have to be resurrected, whether you want to or not, you must therefore behave in such a way that when you are resurrected you have what you want. The Lord Jesus himself said: The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, both the good and the bad; all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, and will be brought out of the hidden places. No creature will hold a dead person before the voice of the living creator. All, he says, those who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out. Saying all caused some confusion and mixing. But hear the distinction, hear the separation: Those who did good, he says, to the resurrection of life; who evil, for the resurrection of judgment. This judgment, to suffer which the wicked are resurrected, is called the second death.

Illos attendite, qui perdunt unde possunt • sempet vivere, ut concedatut eis paululum vivere. Quid est hoc? Fides

of faith, of piety, which are like the money with which eternal life is acquired. The terrifying enemy will come to you not from the front, but from the side; He will not say to you: "Give me your money, if you want to live," but: "Deny Christ, if you want to live." If you do this so you can live for a little, you lose what you could live with forever. Is this loving life, oh you who feared death? Good man, why did you fear death if not because you loved life? Christ is life. Why do you want the brief, until you lose the one that is sure? Or did you not lose faith, since you had nothing to lose? So have that which allows you to live always. Consider how much your neighbor does to live a little; Consider also how much evil he did who denied Christ for a few days of his life. And don't you want to despise those few days of your life so as to never die, to live in the everlasting day, to feel protected by your redeemer and to resemble the angels in the eternal kingdom? What have you loved? What have you lost? You have not taken up your cross to follow the Lord. 6. Look how wise he wanted you to be who told you: Take up your cross and follow me. Whoever finds his soul, he says, will lose it, and whoever loses it for me will find it. Whoever finds it will lose it, whoever loses it will find it. To lose it you must find it first, and once you have lost it, the last thing is to find it again. It is found, therefore, twice, and between each time there is a loss. No one can lose his soul vocatur, pietas vocatur: haec omnis tanquam pecunia est, qua vita aeterna acquititut. Veniet de transvetso inimicus tertitans, et non tibi dicet: Da mihi pecuniam tuam, ut vivas: sed dicet tibi: Nega Christum, ut vivas. Quod tu si fecetis, ut liceat tibi paululum vivete, petdes unde posses semper vivere. Hoc est amare vitam, qui timebas mortem? Homo bone, quare timebas mortem, nisi loving vitam? Christus is alive. Quare appetis parvam, ut perdas securam? An forte fidem non perdidisti, sed quod lose non habuisti? It dyes forever alive. Attende proximum tuum, quanta faciat ut modicum vivat. Attende et illum qui Christum negavit, quantum malum fecit propter paucos dies vitae. Et tu non vis ipsos paucos dies contemnere vitae, ut nullo die moriaris, et in sempiterno vivas die, a Redemptore tuo protegaris, in aeterno regno Angelis adaequeris? What did he knead? what did you lose? Ut sequeretis Dominum, cruze tuam non tulisti. 6.

I will lose animam, ut inveniatur anima.—Vide quam prudentem te velit, qui tibi dixit: Tolle cruze tuam, et sequere me. Qui invenerit, inquit, animam suam, perdet illam; et qui perdiderit eam propter me, inveniet eam (Mt 10,38.39). Qui invenerit, perdet eam; qui perdiderit, inveniet illam. Ut perdas, prius est ut invenías; et cum perdideris, dessertum est ut rursum invenías. Duae sunt inventiones: in medio est qua transit una perditio. Nemo potest animam suam I will lose propter
Love of God, love of the world

through Christ if he has not first found it, and no one can find his soul in Christ if he has not first lost it. Find it to lose it, lose it to find it. How do you have to find it the first time so you can lose it? When you think that you are partly mortal, when you think of the one who made you and with his breath created your soul, and you realize that you owe it to the one who gave it to you, that you must return it to the one who granted it to you, that the one who created it must guard it, you have found your soul by finding it in faith. If you have believed that, you have found your soul. In fact, before you believed you were lost. You found your soul: you were dead in disbelief, you revived in faith. It can be said of you: He had died, and is risen; He was lost, and has been found. Therefore, you found your soul in the faith of the truth if you revived from the death of infidelity. This means having found your soul. Lose it and may your soul become a seed for you. Well, the farmer also finds wheat in threshing and cleaning and loses it again in sowing. What was lost in the sowing is found in the threshing floor. What perishes in the sowing is what will be found in the harvest. Therefore, whoever finds his soul will lose it. He who labors to gather, why is he lazy to sow? 7. But be attentive to where you find it and why you lose it. Where could you find it if that light to which it is said: You will light my lamp, Lord? You already found it, then, thanks to the fact that he brought the lamp closer. look

Why do you lose it? We must not lose at every moment what was found with so much care. It does not say: "Whoever loses it will find it", but: Whoever loses it for me. If by chance you see the body of a shipwrecked merchant on the coast, tears of condolence fall in your eyes and you say: "Poor man! "He lost his soul because of gold." You just cry and feel sorry for yourself. Grant tears to those who do not help, because they could have lost their soul for gold, but they will not be able to find it in it. He was capable of bringing damage to his soul, but he was not capable of recovering it. You don't have to think about what you lost it, but rather why you lost it. If it was because of greed, look where the flesh lies; but where is the valuable? And yet, under the orders of greed, the soul was lost because of gold; On the other hand, through Christ the soul does not perish nor will it perish. Fool, don't hesitate! Listen to the creator's advice. He who made you, before you existed, capable of being wise, created you to be wise. Listen: don't hesitate to lose your soul for Christ. What you call losing is nothing other than entrusting it to the faithful creator. You, certainly, lose it, but he to whom nothing is lost receives it. If you love life, lose it to find it, because, once you have found it, you will no longer have anything to lose, because there will be no reason to lose it. Indeed, there is that life that is found in such a way that it can in no way be lost. Since Christ also, who by being born, dying and resurrecting gave you an example, risen from the dead, no longer dies and death no longer has dominion over him.

Christum, nisi eam prius invenerit; et nemo potest animam suam investé in Quisto, nisi eam prius perdiderit. Inveni, ut perdas; lose, you're wrong. Quomodo eam prius inventurus es, ut habeas quam perdas? Quando cogitas te ex parte mortalem, quando cogitas eum qui te fecit, et insuffiando animam tibi creavit, et videris eam illi debené, qui dedit; illi reddendam, qui commodavit; ab illo custodiendam, qui instituit; invenisti animam tuam, inveniens eam in fide. Credidisti enim hoc, et invenisti animam tuam. Nam perditus eras, antequam crederes. Invenisti animam tuam: mortuus quippe fues in infidelitate, revixisti in fide. Talis is, de quo dici possit: Mortuus erat, et revixit; perierat, et inventus est (Luke 15:32). Ergo invenisti animam tuam in fide veritatis, si a morte infidelitatis revixisti. Hoc est, animam tuam invenisti. Perde eam, et anima tua semen tibi sit. Nam et agricultural crushing et ventilando invenit triticum, et rursus seminando perdit triticum. Invenitur in area, quod perierat in sementé. Perit in sementé quod inveniatur in messe. Qui ergo invenerit animam suam, perdet eam (Mt 10:38). Who laborat colligere, quare piger est seminare? 7. Animam cuius gratia will lose iubemur.—Vide tamen ubi invenías, et quare perdas. Unde enim inve[1517]nires, nisi lumen tibi accenderet ille cuí dicitur: Tu illuminabh luzernam meam, Domine? (Ps 17:29). Iam ergo invenisti, illo tibi accendente Lucernam. Vide quare perdas.

Non enim passim perdendum est, quod tam diligenter inventum est. Non ait: Qui perdiderit eam, inveniet eam; thirst: Qui perdiderit eam propter me (Mt 10,39). Naufragi forte negotiatoris corpus cum in littore inspexeris, reddis lacrimas miseratus, et dicis: Vae huic homini! propter aurum perdidit animam suam. Bene plangis, bene miseraris. Redde illi fletum, cui non praestas et auxilium. Propter aurum enim will lose animam suam potuerit, propter aurum invenire non poterit. Ad damnum animae suae idoneus Fuit, ad eam lucrandam minus idoneus exstitit. Non enim cogitandum est quod perdidit, sed quare perdidit. Si propter avaritiam, ecce ubi iacet caro, ubi est quod erat carum? Et tamen iussit avaritia, et propter aurum perdita est anima, et propter Christum non perit anima, ñeque pereat. Stulte, noli dubitare: audi consilium Creatoris. Ipse te instituit ut sapias, qui te fecit antequam esses qui sapias. Audi, noli dubitare pro Christo animam I will lose. Fideli Creatori commendas quod diceris I will lose. You quidem perdes: sed ille suscipit, cui nihil perit. If you love vitam, perde ut invenías: quia cum inveneris, iam non erit quod perdas, non erit quare perdas. Ea quippe invenitur vita, quae invenitur ut omnino perire non possit. Quia et Christus, qui tibi nascendo, moriendo et resurgendo dedit exemplum, arises a mortuis iam non moritur, et mors ei ultra non dominabitur (Rom 6,9).
The contempt of the world SERMON
Topic: The contempt of the world. Place: Carthage. Date: The year 411 or, according to others, from the year 41.6 to 428.

1. Both the solemnity of the martyrs and the fact that it is the Lord's Day are inviting me to speak to your charity about what concerns the contempt of the present world and the hope of the future. If you ask what you have to despise, every holy and pious martyr despised even... even the present life. If you ask about what you have to wait for today, the Lord has risen. If you waver in reality, be strong in hope; If the task overwhelms you, raise the reward. The first reading of the Apostle, taken from the letter to Timothy, exhorts us to also fulfill what he commanded him when he said: Command the rich of this world not to behave proudly and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us everything in abundance to enjoy. Be rich in good works, give easily, distribute, lay up a good foundation for the future, in order to achieve true life. And do not think that this reading is not appropriate to the solemnity of the blessed martyrs, since it includes in SERMO
[MA 1,201] (PL 39,1517-1522: textum mutatum; PL 46,971-9980) TRACTATUS SANCTI AUGUSTINI DE CONTEMPTORIBUS TEMPORALIUM RERUM: HABITS IN NATALE MARTYRUM TUBURBITANARUM

1. Admonet nos et sollemnitas martyrum, et dominicus dies, hoc loqui caritati vestrae, quod pertineat ad contemptum praesentis saeculi, et ad spem futuri. Si quid contemnas quaeris, omnis sanctus et pius martyr etiam vitam praesentem contempsit. Si quid speres quaeris, hodie dominus resurrexit. If you hesitate in re, this fortis in spe; si te opus turbat, [202] erigat merces. Prima apostolica lectio, in epistle quam scribit ad Timotheum, nos quoque admonet quod ei praecepit dice: praecipe divitibus mundi huius, non superbe sapere, ñeque sperare in incerto divitiarum, sed in deo vivo, qui praestat nobis omnia abundantr ad fruendum. Divites sint in operibus bonis, facile tnbuant, communicent, thesaurizent sibi fundamentum bonum in futurum, ut apprehendant veram vitam (1 Tim 6,17-19). Et ista lectio non nobis videoatur minus congrua sollemnitati martyrum beatorum: habet enim contemptum saecu-

yes the contempt of the world. Indeed, if the rich are commanded to lay up a good foundation for the future and attain true life, this life is false. And this must be heard, above all, by the rich, because when the poor see them, they murmur about them, they lament, they praise them, they envy them, they wish to be equal to them, they are saddened at being unequal, and among the praises that are directed at them one frequently hears this: “They are the only ones; "They are the only ones who live." With an eye on these words with which weak men flatter the rich, telling them that they are the ones who live, the only ones who live, so that they do not think, inflated by the words of those flatterers, that they live in truth, he said: Command the rich of this world not to behave proudly and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives us everything in abundance to enjoy. Be rich; but in what? In good works; give easily, since you do not lose what you give; share with those who do not have. And what are they to do with this? Lay up a good foundation for the future, in order to attain true life, not assenting to the words of flatterers, who tell you that you live and that you are the only ones who live. This life is a dream; These riches slip away like in dreams. Listen to the psalm, oh extremely poor rich man!: They slept their sleep, and all the rich men found nothing in their hands. Sometimes even the beggar who lies on the ground, shivering with cold, overcome by sleep, dreams of treasures, and in his dream he is lied. Nam cum divitibus praecipitur, ut thesaurizent sibi fundamentum bonum in futurum, et apprehendant veram vitam, sine dubio ista false vita est. Et máxime hoc divites audire debent, quos quando pauperes intuentur, murmurant, gemunt, laudant, invident, aequari optant, odd se esse dolent, et Inter laudes divitum hoc plerumque dicunt: Soli sunt isti, isti soli vivunt. Propter haec ergo verba, quibus homines tenues ditivibus adulantur quia ipsi vivunt, et soli vivunt, ne bis adulan tium inflati verbis putent se vivere. Praecipe, inquit, divitibus huius mundi non superbe sapere, ñeque sperare in incerto divitiarum, sed in deo vivo, qui praestat nobis omnia abundantr ad fruendum. Divites sint: sed ubi? in operibus bonis; facile tribuant, quia non perdunt quod tribuunt; communicent cum eis qui non habent. Et quid ex hoc?

Thesaurizent sibi fundamentum bonum in futurum, ut apprehendant veram vitam; non assentientes adulantibus, who eos dicunt will live, and will live alone. Vita ista somnium est; divitiae istae velut in somnis fluunt. Audi psalmum, o dives pauperrime: dormierunt somnum suum, et nihil invenerunt omnes viri divitiarum in manibus suis (Ps 75,6). Aliquando et mendicus in terra iacens, frigore tremens, occupatus tamen somno, thesauros somniat, et gaudet et superbit in somnis, et patrem

He enjoys and is proud until he does not deign to recognize his ragged father. Until he wakes up he is rich. While he sleeps he enjoys, although falsely; When you wake up you will find true pain. Thus, then, the rich man, at the hour of death, is similar to the poor man when he wakes up after having dreamed of treasures. In fact, a certain rich man whose name is neither known nor deserves to be known, who despised the poor man who lay at his door, was also dressed in purple and finest linen; According to the testimony of the Gospel, he dressed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day. He died, he was buried; He woke up and found himself engulfed in flames. So he slept his dream, and that rich man found himself with empty hands, since he did nothing with them. 2. Riches are sought with an eye toward life, not life with an eye toward riches. How many have made pacts with their enemies, even if they took everything from them, as long as they left their lives! They bought their lives at the price of everything they had. How much must be given for eternal life if perishable life is so valuable! Give something to Christ to live happily, you who give everything to the enemy to live in begging. For your temporal life, which you redeem at such a high price, value how much eternal life is worth, which you neglect to live a few days, even if you reach old age. Few are the days of man from his childhood to old age; and, even if Adam himself had died today, he would have lived only a few days, since they were limited. Do you pay, then, a ransom for suum pannosum non digntur agnoscere, et doñee evigilet dives est. Cum ergo dormierit, invenit quod falsum gaudeat; cum evigilaverit, invenit quod verum doleat. Dives ergo moriens similis est pauperi vigilanti, qui thesauros videbat in somnis. Nam et ille induebatur purpura et bysso, quidam dives nec nominatus nec nominandus, with[203]temptor pauperis iacentis ante ianuam suam; induebatur purpura et bysso, sicut evangelicum testimonium est, et epulabatur cotidie splendide. Mortuus est, sepultus est: evigilavit, et se in flammis invenit. Dormivit ergo somnum suum, et nihil invenit ille vir divitiarum in manibus suis, quia nihil boni egit manibus suis. 2. Propter vitam ergo quaeruntur divitiae, non vita propter divitias. Quam multi cum suis hostibus pacti sunt, ut totum toUerent, et vitam relinquerent! Quantumcumque habuerunt, tanti vitam emerunt. How precious is this vita aeterna, if this vita peritura is also precious?

Da Christo aliquid, ut vivas beatus, si totum das hosti, ut vivas mendicus. Vita tua temporali, quam mucho pretio redimís, appende quanti valeat aeterna, quam neglegis, ut vivas diebus paucis, etsi ad senectutem perventurus sis. Omnes enim dies hominis ab infantia usque ad senectam pauci dies sunt: ​​et si ipse Adam hodie moreretur, paucos dies vixerat, quia omnes finierat. Paucos ergo dies, et hos laboriosos, in tanta
The contempt of the world

these few days lived in fatigue, in so much misery and temptation? How much do you pay? You are willing to be left with nothing in order to stay with yourself. Do you want to know how much eternal life is worth? Add yourself to everything else. Behold, the enemy who had held you captive said to you: "Give me all you have if you want to live"; and you, in order to live, gave everything to him; you, who today have seen yourself liberated, but who perhaps will die tomorrow; freed from one and tomorrow perhaps beheaded by another. These dangers, my brothers, must teach us. How is it possible to be so ignorant in the midst of God's words and human experience? Behold, you gave everything and left rejoicing, because you still live; Although poor, needy, naked, beggar, you feel joyful, because you live and feel the sweetness of the light. Christ be present; make a deal with him; he, who did not captivate you, but was taken captive by you; who does not seek to kill you, but deigned to die for you. He who gave himself for you—what a great price!—he who made you, says to you: “Come to a covenant with me. Do you want to have yourself at the cost of losing yourself? If you want to have yourself, you must have me; May you hate yourself to possess me, and, losing your life, find it, so as not to lose it by possessing it. I have already given you healthy advice regarding those riches that you possess with love, and that, however, you are willing to give up for your present life. If you love them, don't lose them; but where you love them, there they must perish with you. I also give you some advice regarding them. Do you love them? Send them where you have to go later, lest, loving them on earth, you either lose them in life or have to leave them a hopeless, in such temptation you redeem? Quantity? Nihil habere vis, ut habeas te. Vis nosse quanti valeat vita aeterna? Adde et te. Ecce inimicus, qui te captivaverat, dixit tibi: Si vis vivere, quidquid habes da mihi; et ut provisions, dedisti totum: hodie redemptus, eras forte moríturus: ab isto dimíssus, forte ab illo trudendus. Erudiónt nos pericula, fratres mei. Quid tam indocti, et inter dei verba, et inter humano experiences? Ecce totum dedisti, et abisti gaudens, quia vivís: etsi pauper, etsi egens, etsi nudus, etsi mendicus, gaudes tamen, quia vivís, et dulcís est lux. Appareat Christus: paciscatur et ipse, non qui te captivavit, sed qui pro te captivas est; Non qui te quaerít occidere, sed qui pro te occidi dignitus_ est.

Qui dedit se pro te — quantum pretium! — qui te fecit, djeit tibi: Mecum paciscere. Te vis habere, et totum will I lose? If I had seen you, I would have supported myself; ut oderis te, ut diligas me, et vitam tuam perdendo invenías, ne tenerdos perdas. De divitiis istis tuis, quas amas possidere, et quas tamen pro vita tua praesente paratas es daré, iam dedi salubre consilium. If you love et ipsas, noli et illas I will lose: sed ubi eas amas, tecum peritarae sunt. Consilium et de ipsis do. Do you love you? Mitte eas, quo sequaris eas; ne cum eas amas in terra, aut vivus amittas, aut
The contempt of the world

once dead. I have also given you advice in this regard. I didn't say: 'Lose them', but: 'Keep them.' Do you want to treasure? I'm not telling you not to do it, but rather I'm telling you where. Welcome me as someone who gives you advice, not as someone who forbids it. Where, then, do I tell you that you should store up? Store up your treasure in heaven, where no thief enters and where neither moth nor rust spoils it. 3. "But I do not see, you say, what I deposit in heaven." Do you see, in fact, what you hide in the earth? You feel safe hiding it in the earth, and do you have any qualms about giving it to the one who made heaven and earth? Save it wherever you want; entrust it to a guardian, if you find someone better than Christ. "I entrust it, you say, to my servant." How much better is he than your Lord? The servant may take it from you and run away; and among so many evils that have already been a reality, the most desirable thing would be for the servant to remove it and flee rather than lead the enemies to his master's house. Many servants suddenly became enemies of their masters and treacherously handed them over to them with everything they had. Who then do you entrust it to? — For now, you say, I entrust my gold to my servant. - I keep your gold; Who do you trust your soul to? —My soul, you say, I entrust to God. How much better would you be if you also entrusted your gold to the same person to whom you entrusted your soul! Or is he faithful to guard your soul and not to guard your money? Does not the one who keeps you keep it for you? Have confidence, then, in him. The servant may not steal it; but can it, perhaps, avoid

to lose it? The most you can trust him is not to steal from you; you look at his faithfulness; but why do you not consider his weakness? He deposited it, but could not hide it; Another came and stole it. Is there anyone who can do such a thing to Christ? Shake off your laziness, accept my advice: store up in heaven. Why did I say, “Shake off your laziness”? As if it were tiring to store up in heaven! But even if it were, it would have to be done; We would have to accept that fatigue and place what we consider of great value in a safe place, where no one can take it away. Christ does not tell you: «Treasure up in heaven; look for some stairs, put on some wings", but: "Give it to me on earth, and I will keep it for you there. Give it to me, he says, on earth; That's why I came to be poor here: so that you can be rich there. Make the transfer» '. Are you afraid of losing it in the hands of a scammer? Are you looking for someone to take it to the place where you are going? Christ assists you in both cases: he does not deceive you and transports it to you. 4. «But, you will say, where do I find Christ? My faith, which I heard in the Church, teaches me, and so I believe and I am imbued with this mystery, that he was buried, rose again on the third day, after forty days ascended to heaven in the presence of his disciples, is seated at the right hand of the Father and that at the end of time he will return. When can I find it here? To whom will I give my wealth? Don't worry; listen to everything; or, if you heard it all, say it all. I know you were taught this: Christ was hung on the cross, taken down from the tree, placed in the tomb, resurrected and ascended to heaven. But you also read that, when per-

mortuus dimittas. Et hinc, inquit, consilium dedi. Non dixi: Lose, thirst: Serva. [204] Thesaurizare vis? Non dico: Noli, sed dico: Ubi. Consultorem accipe, non prohibitorem. Ubi ergo dico thesaurizare? Thesaurizate vobis thesaurum in cáelo, quo fur non accessit, nec tinea, nec rubigo exterminat (Mt 6,20). 3. Sed non video, inquis, quod pono in cáelo. Vines enim quod obruis in terra. Securus is obruendo in terra: et sollicitus is ei dar, qui fecit caelum et terram? Serva ubi vis: si inveneris meliorem Christo, custodi commenda. Commendo, inquis, servo meo. How much melius domino tuo? Servus fortassis aufert, atque fugit; et inter tanta mala, quae íam accíderunt, hoc optandum Fuit, ut servus auferret, et fugeret, non ad dominum suum hostes duceret. Multi servi dominis suis suddenly inimici extiterunt, et eos, cum illo quod habebant, hostibus prodiderunt. Cui ergo commendas? Interim, inquis, servo meo commendo aurum meum. Aurum tuum servo: animam tuam cui? Commendo, inquis, deo ánímam meam. Quanto melius illi et aurum tuum, cui et animam tuam? An forte fidelis est in custodiendo animam tuam, et infidelis est in custodiendo pecuniam tuam? Non servat tibi, qui servat te? Fac ergo fidem. Servus agit ne tollat: numquid agit ne perdat? Tota fides eius

est, ne te fraudt: fidem eius attendis, et infirmitatem non attendis? Posuit, non latuit; venit alius, abstulit. Numquid hoc Christo quisquam facturus est? Pigritiam excute, consilium accipe: thesauriza in cáelo. Et quid dixi, pigritiam excute? Quasi labor sit in cáelo thesaurizare. Etsi labor esset, faciendum erat, et suscipiendus labor erat, et reponenda ea, quae pro magno habemus, in loco munito, unde ea nenio posset auferre. Non tamen dicit tibi Christus: In cáelo thesauriza, scalas quaere, pennas apta; sed: Mihi in terra da, et ibi servabo. In terra, inquit, mihi da: ideo veni pauper hic esse, ut tu ibi dives sis. Fac traiecticium. Times fraudatorem, ne perdas? Quaeris who portet quo migras? Christus tibi in utroque adest: non facit imposturam, sed facit laturam. 4. Sed Christum, inquies, ubi invenio? Cum habeat fides mea, quod audivi in ​​ecclesia, hoc didici, sic credidi, hoc sacramento imbutus sum: sepultus est, resurrexit tertia die, post quadraginta dies ascendit in caelum coram oculis discipulorum suorum, sedet in dextera Patris, [205] in fine venturus est. When did I make an invention? cui dabo? Noli satagere, totum audi; aut si totum audisti, totum dic. Scio quia hoc accepisti: suspensus est Christus in intersection, depositus est de ligno, positus
He has already spoken about the same thing in sermons 38,9; 42.2; 86.11.
The contempt of the world

Paul followed his Church, full of pride, cruel, longing for deaths and thirsting for the blood of Christians; when he tormented and persecuted her, taking letters to Damascus to lead prisoners to punishment as many men and women as he found followers of such a lifestyle... did you hear what the one who you confess to be sitting in heaven shouted at her? Remember, then, what he said, what you heard and read: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? Paul neither saw him nor touched him, and yet he said to him: Why are you persecuting me? 1. Remember with me, dear brothers, that the Lord said: While we live in the body we are pilgrims far from the Lord, for we walk in faith, not in vision. Jesus Christ our Lord, who said: I am the way, and the truth, and the life, wanted us to walk not only in him, but towards him. Where do we walk if not along the path? And where do we walk if not to truth and life, that is, to eternal life, the only one that deserves to be called life? In fact, this mortal life in which we find ourselves, compared to that, appears to be, rather, a death, since it changes with such great mutability and ends in a very short space of time. That is why the Lord, to the rich man who had said to him: Good Teacher, what must I do to obtain eternal life?, answered him: If you want to obtain life, keep the commandments. He was, therefore, in some other life, since he was not speaking to a corpse or to a man lacking one. But when he asked him about the attainment of eternal life, the Lord did not answer him: "If you want to reach eternal life," but rather: If you want to reach life, meaning that life WILL BE

That which is not eternal does not deserve to be called life, since true life is no more true than eternal life. Hence also the Apostle, advising the rich to give alms, said: Be rich in good works, give easily, distribute, lay up for yourselves a good foundation for the future, in order to attain true life. What do you call true life but eternal life, the only one that deserves to be called life, because it is the only one that is happy? In fact, those rich people whom the Apostle said had to be ordered to attain true life, lived this life in the midst of abundant riches; but, if the Apostle had considered it as true life, he would not have said: Lay up a good foundation for the future, in order to attain true life, indicating nothing other than that the life of the rich is not true life; life that fools not only consider true, but even happy. But how can it be a happy life if it is not true? We should not call a happy life anything other than the true one; nor is it true life but eternal life, a life that the rich realize they do not yet have, whatever the pleasures they have; which is why they are exhorted to attain it through alms so that they may hear at the end: Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you since the beginning of the world; for I was hungry, and you gave me food. How the same kingdom is eternal life was logically shown by the Lord himself shortly after when he said: Those will go to eternal fire; the righteous, however, to eternal life. gi volens, quoniam quae vita aeterna non est, nec vita diganda est; quia vera vita nonnisi aeterna est. They had already believed, because the evangelist expressed himself like this: Jesus said to those who had already believed in him: "If you continue in my word, you will truly be my disciples, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free." Thus, they had already believed and had begun to walk in Christ as the way. He exhorts them, therefore, that, abiding in him, they may arrive. Where but to what it says: The truth will set you free? What liberation is it if not liberation from all the mutability of vanity, from all corruption of mortality? Consequently, that is true life, eternal life, which we have not yet achieved while our pilgrimage away from the Lord lasts; but we will achieve it, because, through faith, we walk in the same Lord, if we remain with all perseverance in his word. For with what he says: I am the way, this other thing corresponds: If you continue in my word, you will truly be my disciples. Already these words: And truth and life correspond to these others: And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free. Therefore, in this pilgrimage and in this life, that is, in faith, with what can I exhort you except with the words of the Apostle, who says: Having these promises, dearly beloved, let us purify ourselves from every stain of the flesh and of the spirit, bringing sanctification to perfection in the fear of the Lord. For those who wish to be granted, before believing, that light of the most pure and immutable truth, since they cannot contemplate it except through faith, once the

heart—blessed are the pure of heart, for they will see God—are like blind men, who desire to first see the corporeal light of this sun in order to be cured of blindness, whereas they cannot see it unless they are first healed.

No one is allowed to stay here; The fickleness of time forces those who come into this life not to stop. There is no room for laziness; Walk, don't let yourself be dragged. Walking along the road, at a crossroads a man came out to meet us; not just a man, but God made man by men. He told us: «Do not go to the left; That path certainly seems easy, smooth and delicious, trodden by many and spacious, but its end is death. Let us review past times and the Holy Scriptures. Isn't that man the Word of God? Didn't that same Word become flesh and dwell among us? Before He became flesh and dwelt among us, did He not speak that same Word through the prophets? In truth, God spoke to Abraham with his Word, indicating that he was going to have a wandering descendant, despite the fact that the one to whom he announced it was old, and Sarah was old and barren. He believed it and it was fulfilled. He announced to him that his own descendants, that is, the people who would be born of him according to the flesh, would be slaves in Egypt for four hundred years: so it happened; that he was to be freed from that slavery: he was freed; who was to receive the land of promise: he received it. Things very distant in time and others closer were announced, and they were fulfilled and continue to be fulfilled. He spoke the Word of the Lord through the prophets, announcing that that people would sin and be delivered into the hands of their enemies for having offended their God: everything was fulfilled; that he would go captive to Babylon: it was fulfilled; that Christ, the king, would come out of him: Christ came, Christ was born, because he himself was the Word that proclaimed his future coming. It was also said that the Jews were going to crucify him, and they crucified him; it was predicted that

He would rise again and be glorified, and it was fulfilled: He rose again and ascended to heaven; It was predicted that all the earth would believe in his name and that kings would persecute his Church: both things came true; It was predicted that kings would believe in him: we are already seeing the faith of kings, and do we doubt the fidelity of Christ? The divisions caused by heretics were predicted: are we not also seeing them and groaning in the midst of the heresies that are being felt everywhere? It was predicted that the idols were going to be destroyed by the work of the Church and the name of Christ: we also see this come true; Scandals were predicted in the Church itself, tares and chaff were predicted, all things that we not only see with our own eyes, but that we tolerate with all the strength the Lord has given us. How did he deceive you who told you: "March this way"? Speak with confidence, if you are faithful, having such experience of the one who speaks to you: «I test him with these things, since he deigned to test himself in this way; If he tells the absolute truth, he does not deceive me; You know the truth of everything he has said, he has lied about nothing; "That's how I know him." It is the Word of God; He spoke by the mouth of his servants, and did not deceive; Can he deceive what he says through his own mouth? He to whom it is not yet known, he who doubts Christ, let him also say: "I will walk here, just in case he whom the whole world has already believed speaks the truth." 3. multitude in the time of Noah: none were saved except those who entered the ark. If they reflected and changed their ways away from impiety and converted to our Lord, they would make satisfaction for their sins and, turning to his mercy with tears, they would certainly not perish. Nor did God fail to show mercy towards Nineveh, who merited salvation in three days. Is there anything shorter than a three-day period? But they, despite the pressure of time, did not stop waiting for God's mercy to subdue his clemency. If such a large city had three days to conquer the mercy of God, was there not time in the space of one hundred, two hundred, three hundred years that the construction of the ark lasted? Since Christ began to cut down the incorruptible woods in the jungle of the Gentiles, that is, of the Church, if those men had changed their ways and customs, if in order to favor God they had offered him the sacrifice of a troubled heart, without a doubt they would have emerged unscathed. Let men therefore fear being found thus on that last day. We, brothers, let us behave in such a way that we change our ways away from impiety and amend our customs while we have time, so that that day finds us prepared, since he who says it will come never lies. Beware of doubting what is true. This is what happened in the days of Noah: They ate, they drank, they took a husband, they took a wife, they bought, they sold, until Noah entered the ark and the flood came, which

He lost all those who put their hope in this world and wanted to live in peace, but not in the region of tranquility. Only those found in the ark were saved. 4. Many say to themselves: "We are commanded to wait for that day and that we may not be found such as those who were found outside the ark and perished in the flood were found. Truly, we are terrified by the trumpet of the Gospel, the word of God. What are we to do? Should we not take a wife then? This is how the young man and the adolescent speak. «Should we not eat or drink? "Do we have to fast continuously?" There are many who speak like this; and those who perhaps wanted to buy something will say to themselves: "There is nothing more to buy so as not to find ourselves among the number of those who perished in the flood." What are we to do, brothers? If things are like this, then we must cry, in the same way that the apostles were sad for the human race when they heard the Lord say: If you want to be perfect, sell all your things and give them to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven, and come and follow me. The one to whom he said this was filled with sadness and left. He called the one from whom he asked for advice regarding eternal life a good teacher; but this opinion lasted until he answered exactly what he had asked. The Lord answered him, and the rich man was filled with sadness. When he had gone away wrapped in his sadness, the Lord said to his disciples: How difficult it is for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven,1 as if the kingdom of heaven were closed to him.

8. Listen, my brothers: it was appropriate that times were difficult and hard. What would we have done if such a great comforter had not assisted us? From Adam to the end, the human race is seriously ill. Since we were born here, since we were expelled from paradise, the disease has been present, but in the end it had to be greater and perhaps close to health, although for others close to death. Having thus made the human race sick, that great doctor receives the sick in a kind of giant bed, that is, throughout the world; but, like a very skilled doctor, he waits for the right moment for the sick person; He sees and examines what is to happen, and in the most benign moments of the illness he sends his assistants ahead. Likewise, our doctor first sent the prophets to visit us. They spoke and preached; through them he cured and healed some. They predicted that there was going to be an extreme worsening of the disease and a major relapse of this patient that would require the presence of the doctor in person. This is what happened, since he said: “I will restore and heal the believer; "I will wound and I will heal." He came, became man and participated in our mortality so that we could become participants in his immortality. The patient is still agitated and, delirious from the fever and with the fever increasing, he says to himself: "Since this doctor arrived, I suffer from worse fevers, I agitate more violently and I endure terrible fevers. Why did you come to my house? I think it was not a good idea that he came to

her." So say all those who still suffer from the disease of vanity. How come they get sick with vanity? Because they don't want to receive the recipe for sobriety from him. God seeing that the miserable people were agitated in their worries and were involved in the various activities of this world that strangle their souls, He came as a doctor. And they are not afraid to say: «Since Christ came we have to endure these times; "Since Christians have existed, the world has gone down in everything." Oh sick fool! Your illness has not worsened because the doctor came; the good, pious, just and merciful doctor foresees it; He was not the cause. He came to comfort you, to truly heal you. What does it take away from you but the superfluous? You longed for harmful things and were content with them alone; what you were pining for was not good for your fever. Is the doctor cruel who removes harmful fruit from the sick person's hand? What did he take from you but the pernicious tranquility in which you were going to lie? Let out what damages your viscera; Also that which makes you moan and murmur is part of the medicine. If I didn't want to cure you, I wouldn't subject you to those unwanted torments. Times must be hard. Because? So that earthly happiness is not loved. It is appropriate, therefore, and it is medicinal that this life is mixed so that the other can be loved. If such great indolence still delights in earthly things and the amphitheater, what would happen if it did not see its works shaken? How many bitternesses does it have mixed inside it! And the world is still sweet!

Theme: The pilgrimage of life. Location: Unknown. Date: Around the year 405. 1. That this our life, dearly beloved brothers, is a certain pilgrimage far from the homeland of the saints, the heavenly Jerusalem, is taught very clearly by the apostle Paul when he says: While we are in the body we are pilgrims far from the Lord. And since every pilgrim has a homeland, since no one who lacks one is a pilgrim, we must know what ours is, where it is convenient for us to hasten to arrive, leaving aside all the pleasures and delights of this life; wherever we tend and the only place where it is lawful for us to rest. God wanted us to have true rest in no other place except in that homeland; Well, if I granted rest here too, I would not like to return. And call this homeland Jerusalem; not the earthly one, who is still a slave with all her children, according to the Apostle himself. She was given on earth as a dark symbol for carnal men, who, although they worship a single God, nevertheless expect earthly happiness from him. There is another Jerusalem, which claims to be in heaven: the Jerusalem above, the mother of us all. He calls her mother, as if SERMO

was the metropolis, since "metropolis" means mother city. To it, therefore, we must hasten; We must realize that we are pilgrims towards it and that we are on the way. 2. Every man who does not yet believe in Christ is not even on the path: he is lost, therefore. He too is looking for his homeland, but he does not know where he should go nor does he know where it is. What do I mean by saying that you are looking for your homeland? Every soul seeks rest and happiness; No one who is asked if they want to be happy hesitates to answer affirmatively; every man shouts that he wants to be one; but men do not know where that happiness is reached and where it is found; therefore, they are lost. No one who is not on the move is lost; The loss arises when the march begins and one does not know where to go. The Lord leads you back to the path; By becoming faithful, believers in Christ, we cannot say that we are already in the homeland, but we have already begun to walk the path. No one arrives except those who are on the path; but not everyone who is on the path arrives. What good thing did this life have, starting with the first man, since he deserved death and received the curse, a curse from which Christ freed us? Therefore, brothers, we must not murmur as some of them murmured, as the Apostle said, and perished because of the serpents. You meet men who murmur about the times in which they have lived, affirming that those of our fathers were good. What would they not murmur if they could return to the time of their fathers! omnes lecta perhorrescimus? Ut habeamus potius unde gratulemur, quam unde de nostris temporibus murmuremus. 2. When ergo bene fuet generi human? man who wants life? Every day we talk about life; but what to say about that other life? And loves to see good days.
