Topic: The fear of God. Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown. 1. Many are the precepts that have been given to us regarding the fear of God, brothers; Countless passages of Scripture proclaim how useful it is to fear God. Pay attention, because among so much abundance I am going to remember and comment on a few, as the brevity of time allows me. Who is not happy to be wise and, if he is not yet wise, does not wish to be? But what does the Scripture say? The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Who does not like to reign? Let us listen to what the Spirit warns us in the psalm: And now, kings, understand; Instruct you who judge the earth; Serve the Lord with fear and rejoice before him with trembling. Concerning which the Apostle also says: Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. We also read that it is written: You desired wisdom; Keep justice and the Lord will grant it to you. We have found many men most unconcerned with justice and most eager for wisdom. Divine Scripture teaches such that they cannot attain what they desire except by keeping what they despise. Keep, he said, justice, and SeSERMO

CAPUT I.—1. Timor Dei in Scripturis quam crebro commendatus.— Multa nobis, fratres, de Dei timore praecepta sunt, et quam sit utile timere Deum, innumerabiliter divina eloquia sonuerunt. Ex qua ubérrima copy pauca me commemorantem, et ad ea, quantum pro temporis brevitate potuero, disserentem libenter advertite. Quis non sapientem se esse laetetur, aut si nondum est, esse desideret? Sed quid clicit Scriptura? Initium sapientiae timor Domini (Ps 110,10). Quem non regnare delectet? Sed audiamus quid in Psalmo Spiritus moneat: Et nunc, reges, intellegite; erudimini, qui iudicatis terram; Servite Domino in timore, et exultate ei eum tremore (Ps 2,10.11). Unde et Apostolus dicit: Cum timore et tremore vestram ipsorum salutem operamini (Phil 2,12). Legimus etiam scriptum: Concupisti sapientiam, serva iustitiam, et Dominus praebebit illam tibi (Eccli 1,33). Multos enim reperimus neglegentissimos iustitiae, et avidissimos sapientiae. Hosdocet Scriptura divina pervenire non posse ad id quod appetunt, nisi servando quod neglegunt. Serva, inquit, iustitiam, et praebebit illam tibi Dominus, quam concupisti sa-

Lord will grant you the wisdom you desired. But who can keep justice if he does not fear God? For it says in another place: He who is not afraid cannot be justified. Therefore, if the Lord grants wisdom only to him who maintains justice, he who lacks fear cannot be justified; It is enough to resort to that sentence: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. 2. Also the prophet Isaiah, when extolling those seven well-known spiritual gifts, began with wisdom until he reached the fear of God, as if descending from the most sublime to us, to teach us how to ascend. It began with the gift we wish to reach and arrived at the gift where we must begin. The Spirit of God will rest upon him, he said; Spirit of wisdom and understanding, Spirit of counsel and strength, Spirit of knowledge and piety, Spirit of the fear of the Lord. Just as he descended from wisdom to fear not by failing but by teaching, so we too must ascend from fear to wisdom not by becoming proud but by progressing. For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Such, in fact, is that valley of weeping of which the psalm says: He prepared in his heart the steps in the valley of weeping. Humility is symbolized in the valley. And who is humble but he who fears God, crushing his heart with that fear, with the tears of confession and penitence? God does not despise a contrite and humiliated heart. But don't be afraid to stay in the valley. He himself arranged in the pientiam (ib., 33). Quis autem potest, nisi Deum timeat, servare iustitiam? Dicit enim alio loco: Nam qui sine titnore est, non poterit iustificari (ib., 28). Porro si Dominus non praebet sapientiam, nisi servanti iustitiam, qui autem sine timore est, non poterit iustificari: recurritur ad illam sententiam: Initium sapientiae titnor Domini (ib., 16). CAPUT II.—2. Gradus a timore ad sapientiam.—Isaiah etiam propheta cum septem illa notissima dona spiritualia commendaret, incipiens a sapientia pervenit ad timorem Dei, tanquam de sublimi descendens ad nos, ut nos divinoret ascenderé. Inde ergo coepit, quo volumus perveníre; et illuc pervenit, unde debenmus incipere. Requiescet in eo, inquit, Spiritus Dei, Spiritus sapientiae et intellectus, Spiritus consilii et fortitudinis, Spiritus scientiae et pietatis, Spiritus timoris "Domini (Is 11,2.3).

Sicut ergo ille, non deficindo, seddocendo a sapientia usque ad timorem descendit; sic nos, non superiendo, be professing to timore usque ad sapentiam oportet ascend. Initium enim sapientiae timor Domini (Eccli 1,16). Ipsa est enim convallis plorationis, from qua Psalmus dicit: Ascensions in corde eius disposuit in convalle plorationis (Ps 83,6-7). Per con[1525]vallem quippe humilitas significatur. Quis est autem humilis, nisi timens Deum, et eo timore conterens cor in lacrimis confessionis et paenitentiae? Quia cor contritum et humiliatum Deus non spernit (Ps 50,19). Sed non timeat ne in convalle reneat. In ipso enim

contrite and humiliated heart, which does not despise, the steps to ascend to it. This is what the psalm says: He prepared in his heart, in the valley of weeping, the steps to the place prepared by him. Where are the steps? In the heart, he said. But where do we have to ascend from? Without a doubt, from the valley of tears. And where do we have to ascend? To the place arranged by him. What place is this but that of rest and peace? There, indeed, is that resplendent wisdom that never withers. Therefore Isaiah, in order to exercise us in certain degrees of doctrine, descended from wisdom to fear, that is, from the place of eternal peace to the valley of temporal weeping, so that, grieving in the confession of penitence, groaning and weeping, we might not remain in pain, groaning and weeping, but, ascending from this valley to the spiritual mountain, on which the holy city, Jerusalem, our mother, is founded, we might enjoy unalterable joy. Therefore, having put wisdom first, that is, the indeficient light of the mind, he attached understanding to it, as if to answer those who asked from what step one passed to wisdom: “From understanding; and to the understanding, from the advice; to the council, from the fortress; to strength, from science; to science, from pity, and to pity, from fear. So to wisdom, from fear, since the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord: from the valley of weeping to the mountain of peace. corde contrito et humiliato, quod Deus non spernit, ascensiones per quas in illum assurgamus, ipse disposuit. Nam ita Psalmus dicit: Ascensions in corde eius disposuit in convalle plorationis, in locum quem disposuit (Ps 83,6.7). Ubi fiunt ascensions? In corde, inquit. Sed unde ascendendum est? Utique a convalle plorationis. Et quo ascendendum est? In locum, inquit, quem disposuit. Quis iste est locus, nisi quietis et pacis? Ibi enim est illa clear, et quae nunquam marcescit sapientia. Unde ad nos exercitandos quíbusdam doctrinae gradibus descendit Isaiah a sapientia usque ad timorem, a loco scilicet sempiternae pacis usque ad convallem temporalis plorationis: ut nos in confessione paenitentiae dolendo, gemendo, flendo, non remaneamus in dolore et gemitu et fletu; sed ascendants ab ista convalle in montem spiritualem, ubi civitas sancta Ierusalem mater nostra aeterna fundata est, imperturbabili laetitia perfruamur.

Ergo ille cum praeposuisset sapientiam, lumen scilicet mentís indeficiens, adiunxit intellectum: tanquam quaerentibus unde ad sapientiam vinoretur, responderet: Ab intellectu; unde ad intellectum: To council; unde ad consilium: A fortitudine; unde ad fortitudinem: A scientia; unde ad scientiam: A pietate; unde ad pietatem: A timore. Ergo ad sapientiam a timore; quia initium sapientiae timor Domini (Ps 110,10). A convalle plorationis usque ad montem pacis.

3. Blessed are the poor in spirit, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven. They are the humble ones found in the valley, the trembling ones who offer their contrite and humiliated hearts as a sacrifice to God; From there they ascend to piety so as not to resist his will, neither that expressed in his word—when they do not understand its meaning—nor that which is manifested in the very order and government of creation—when many things happen in a manner other than what the private will of man desires. There it must be said: But let it not be what I want, but what you want, Father. Blessed are the meek, for they will inherit the earth; not the land of those who die, but that of which it was said: You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living. From this piety they deserve the degree of science so that they know not only the evil of their own past sins, for which they already cried with pain in the first degree of penance, but also the evil in which they find themselves, the evil of this mortality and of this pilgrimage far from the Lord, even when temporal happiness smiles. That is why it is written: Whoever brings science, also brings pain. Blessed are those who cry, for they will be comforted. From this they ascend to the degree of strength, so that the world may be crucified for them, and they for the world, so that charity may not be cooled by the perversity of this life and by the abundance of iniquity, but rather the hunger and thirst for justice may be tolerated until the time of CAPUT III.—3. Gradus ex Isaia septem comparantur ad octo beatitudines Evangelü.—Beati enim pauperes spiritu, quoniam ipsorum est regnum caelorum (Mt 5:3). Ipsi sunt in convalle humiles, ipsi in tremente, cor contritum et humiliatum sacrificant Deo: unde ascendant ad pietatem, ut non resistant will eius, sive in sermonibus eius, ubi non capiunt sensum eius; sive in ordine ipso et gubernatione creaturae, cum pleraque aliter accidunt, quam privata hominis voluntas exposcit: ibi quippe digandum est: Verum non quod ego voló, sed quod tu vis, Pater (ib., 26,39). Beati enim mansueti, quoniam ipsi hereditate possidebunt terram (ib., 5,4): non terram mororientíum, sed terram de qua dictum est: Spes mea es tu, portio mea in terra vivostium (Ps 141,6).

Ab ista quippe pietate merebuntur scientiae gradum, ut noverint non solum mala praeteritorum peccatorum suorum, de quibus in primo gradu paenitentiae dolore fleverunt, sed etiam in quo malo sint huius mortalitatis et peregrinationis a Domino, etiam cum felicitas saecularis arridet. Nam ideo scriptum est: Qui apponit scientiam, apponit et dolorem (Eccli 1,18). Beati enim Ingentes, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur (Mt 5,5). Inde assurgunt ad fortitudinem, ut mundus eis crucifigatur, et ipsi mundo, ut in huius vitae perversitate et abundantia iniquitatis caritas non réfrigescat; thirst tolerate fames sitisque iustitiae, doñee ad eius saturita-

satisfy them in that immortality of the saints and company of the angels. Blessed then are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied. But, in response to the unrest caused by temptations and what was said: Woe to the world for scandals!, if perhaps some crimes that take hold of human fragility creep in little by little and stealthily, advice should not be lacking. Indeed, in this mortal life, the degree of strength does not have so much power as to ensure that one who finds himself in continuous struggle with such a cunning adversary will never be hurt, especially through the temptations of the tongue, where, if anyone says to his brother: "You fool," he will be subject to eternal fire. What then is advice but what the Lord says: Forgive, and you will be forgiven? And so, on the scale that we have learned in the prophet Isaiah, the counsel is in the fifth degree; In the same way, in the beatitudes of the Gospel it appears in fifth place: Blessed are the merciful, for they will obtain mercy. The sixth degree of Isaiah is understanding, where hearts are purified from all falsehood of carnal vanity to direct the purified intention toward the end. Therefore the Lord also said in the sixth place: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God. Once the end has been reached, one stops, rests and the triumph of assured peace is achieved. And what is the end but Christ God? The end of the law is Christ for the justification of every believer. And the Wisdom of God, what is it but Christ? And the Son of [1526] tem veniatur in illa immortalitate sanctorum, et societate Angelorum. Beati enim qui esuriunt et sitiunt iustitiam, quoniam ipsi saturabuntur (ib., 6). Verumtamen propter disturbinginem tentationum, et quod dictum est: Vae mundo ab scandalis (ib., 18,7); si qua forte delicta minutatim furtimque subrepunt, quibus humano praeoecupatur infirmitas, consilium deesse non debent. Ñeque enim tantum potest in ista mortali vita ille fortitudinis gradus, ut qui cum astutissimo adversary continua certatione conflict, non aliquando fairtur: máxime per tentationes linguae, ubi si dixerit quis fratri suo: Fatue; reus erit gehennae ignis (ib., 5,22). Quod est ergo consilium, nisi quod Dominus dicit: Dimittite, et dimittetur vobis? (Luke 6:37).

Et ideo sicut in gradibus quos per Isaiam discimus, quintum est consilium; sic in Gospel in illis beatitudeinis laudibus fifth loco ponitur: Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi mhericordiam consequentur (Mt 5,7). Sextas est apud Isaiam intellectus: ubi ab omni falsitate carnalis vanitatis corda mundantur, utpura intentio dirigatur in finem. Propterea sixth loco etiam Dominus dixit: Beati mundo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt (ib., 8). Cum vero ad finem perventum fuerit, iam consistitur, iam requiescitur, iam secura pace triumphatur. Et quis finis, nisi Deus Christus? Finís enim legis Christus, ad iustitiam omni credenti (Rom 10:4). Et sapientia Dei quis, nisi Christus? Et filius Dei quis, nisi Christus? In illo ergo sapientes, et in iÜo

God, who but Christ? Therefore, those who become wise and children of God become in him, and that is full and eternal peace. Consequently, as in Isaiah wisdom occupies the seventh stage in ascending order, from where he began to descend to teach us, the Lord, who raised us, also placed in seventh place: Blessed are the peaceful, for they will be called children of God. Having these promises and tending through these degrees towards the Lord, let us tolerate all the harshness and harshness of this world and do not let its cruelty break us, once defeated we will enjoy eternal peace. To this, once the end has been shown, the eighth beatitude exhorts us: Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven. SERMON
Topic: The fear of God. Location: Unknown. Date: Years 425 to 430.

1. I do not doubt, dearly beloved brothers, that the fear of God has taken root in your hearts and will lead you to true and solid strength. Although he who fears no one is called strong, he who does not want to fear, first of all, God, in order to fear Him, listen to Him is perverse strength; filii Dei fiunt, quicumque fiunt: et haec est pax plena atque perpetua. Ideo cum apud Isaiam sit seventh sapientia sursum versus ascendentibus, unde coepit ipse ad nos cenando I will descend; seventh etiam loco Dominus qui nos erigit, posit: Beati pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur (Mt 5,9). Has igitur promissiones habentes, et his gradibus tendentes ad Dominum, omnia mundi huius áspera et dura toleremus, nec nos eius frangat saevitia, qua victa in aeterna pace gaudebimus. Ad hoc nos enim iam demonstrate fine cohortatur octave sententia: Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter iustitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum caelorum (ib., 10).

CAPOT I.—1. Timore Dei fortitudo vera comparatur. Timor caritate pellendus non vanitate.—Non dubito, dilectissimi fratres, insitum esse cordibus vestris timorem Dei, quo ad veram et solidam fortitudinem perducamini. Cum enim fortis ille dicatur, qui neminem timet; perverse fortis est, qui primo Deum non vult timere, ut timendo audiat, audiendo

listening to it, loving it, and loving it, not fearing it. Then it will be very strong indeed, not with the harshness of pride, but with the security of justice. Thus it is written: The fear of the Lord is the hope of strength. When you fear the penalty that is threatened, you learn to love the reward that is promised. In this way, out of fear of punishment, a holy life is led; With holy life one acquires a good conscience, through which one fears no pain. Therefore, let him learn to fear who wants not to fear. Learn to live temporarily worried who wants to enjoy eternal security. As John says: Fear does not dwell in charity, but perfect charity casts out fear. He said it certainly and truly. Therefore, if you do not want to fear, first see if you already possess perfect charity, which casts out fear. If you exclude fear before achieving that perfection, pride puffs up and charity does not edify. Just as in good health hunger is driven away with food and not with boredom, so in the holy soul fear must be expelled not with vanity, but with charity. 2. You who want to no longer fear, examine your conscience. Don't stay on the surface; descend into yourself, penetrate into the interior of your heart. Search carefully and see if there is no poisoned vein that aspires and absorbs the poisonous love of the world, if you do not feel moved and captured by any carnal delight or pleasure, if you do not puff up and become arrogant with vain boasting, if no vain care has you in 11adiligat, et diligendo non timeat. Tune erit veré fortissimus, non superba duritia, sed secura iu[1527]stitia. Sic etiam scriptum est: Timor Domini, spes fortitudinis (Prov 14:26). Cum enim timetur poena quam minatur, discitur amari praemium quod pollicetur: ac sic per timorem poenae bona vita retinetur; per bonam vitam bona conscientia comparatur, ut per bonam conscientiam nulla poena timeatur. Quapropter discat timere, qui non vult timere. Discat ad tempus esse soílicitus, qui semper vult esse securus. Ut enim dicit Ioannes: Timor non est in caritate, be perfect caritas joras mittit timorem (1 lo 4,18). Dixit sane, et veraciter dixit. Si ergo habere non vis timorem, prius vide utrum iam perfection habeas caritatem, quae foras mittit timorem. Si vero ante istam perfectionem timor excluditur, superbia inflat, non caritas aedificat.

Nam sicut in bona valetudine fames non annoyance, sed cibo pellitur; ita in bona mente timor non vanitate, sed caritate pellendus est. CAPUT II.—2. Timore carere, qua dilectione contingat, discussiendum. Discute itaque conscientiam tuam, quisquís timere iam non vis. Noli superficialm compalpare, descends in te, penetrates interiora cordis tuí. Rimare diligenter, utrum nulla ibi vena venenata tabificum amorem saeculi sugat et sorbeat, utrum nulla camalis voluptatis movearis et capiaris ¡Ilécebra, nulla inani iactantia tumidus extollaris, nulla cura vanitatis exaestues:

further; dare to affirm that you see yourself pure and transparent, that you examine everything hidden in your conscience, whether in actions, sayings or perverse thoughts; If you are no longer tired by the concern of avoiding evil, see if any negligence in practicing equity does not creep in. If that is your real state, enjoy living without fear. The love of God will have excluded it, whom you love with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. It will also have been excluded by the love of your neighbor, whom you love as yourself, and that is why you strive so that he also loves God with you with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your mind, since you have no other way to love yourself rightly if it is not to love God in such a way that you do not love him less because you turn towards yourself. If, on the other hand, although no passion shakes you inwardly—who would dare to boast of this?—if you love yourself in yourself and take pleasure in yourself for your own sake, you should feel great fear precisely because you fear nothing. Fear is not to be cast out with any love, but with the right love by which we love God with all our mind 1 and, consequently, our neighbor, so that he also loves God. Loving oneself and pleasing oneself is not right love, but vain pride. Therefore, the Apostle rebuked with just rebuke those who love and please themselves. Perfect charity casts out fear. But what is cheapness should not be called charity 2. What

Is there more worthless than a man without God? See what he loves who loves himself; not in God, but in himself. It is rightly said to such a man: Do not be conceited, but rather fear. Since he is conceited, and therefore does not fear, it is certainly pernicious for him not to fear him, which is not solidly founded, but is carried by the wind of pride. Nor is he meek and pious who loves and praises himself; On the contrary, proud and fierce, he does not know how to say: My soul will be praised in the Lord; Let the humble listen to it and rejoice. What good does he love who perhaps loves not to fear for the sake of not fearing itself? You can convince yourself that this does not come from health, but from cruelty. For example, there is an extremely bold robber, all the more dangerously cruel as he is more perversely strong, who, out of his love for the one he loves not to fear, plots enormous atrocities to exercise what he loves, and by exercising it, strengthen it; The greater the atrocities committed, the greater the audacity of those who do not fear. Therefore, what can be found even in a terrible man should not be loved as a great good. 3. Therefore, we must mock the philosophers of this world - not only the Epicureans - who consider even justice to be venal, at the price of carnal pleasure. They say that the wise man must be just, either to acquire or to preserve the pleasure of the body. They also boast of being very strong and claim to fear absolutely nothing, since they think that God does not care in the least about human things and they do not believe

audeas nuntiare purum ac liquidum te videre, quidquid latebrarum in conscientia perscrutaris, a factis, a dictis, a cogitationibus pravis; si iam iniquitatis diligence non fatiguet, utrum aequitatis neglegentia nulla subrepat. Si haec ita sunt, recte gaudes, gaude esse te sine timore. Excluserit autem eum caritas Dei, quem diligis ex toto corde, et ex tota anima, et ex tota mente tua. Excluserit eum et caritas proximi, quem diligis tanquam te ipsum: et ideo pro illo satagis, ut etiam ipse tecum ex toto corde, ex tota anima, ex tota mente diligat Deum; quia non aliter recte diligis et te ipsum, nisi quia sic diligis Deum, ut non propterea minus eum diligas, quia converteris vel ad te ipsum. Si autem quamvis intra te ipsum nulla irritaris cupiditate (quod quidem de se quis audeat glorian?), tamen si te ipsum in te ipso diligis, et de te ipso tibi places, hoc ipsum vehementius timere deben, quia nihil times. Non enim quacumque dilectione foras mittendus est timor, sed recta dilectione qua tota diligimus Deum, et propterea proximum, ut sic et ipse diligat Deum. Se autem in se diligere, et sibi pleasureré, non est iustitiae caritas, sed superbiae vanitas. Ac per hoc Apostolus iusta reprehensione percussit se ipsos lovers et sibi pleasantes (cf. 2 Tim 3:1-5). Perfecta ergo caritas foras mittit timorem (1 lo 4.18). Sed ea dicenda est caritas, quae non est vilitas. May there be another life finished this one. And if something untoward happens to them in this, they consider themselves protected by the fact that, although they cannot have bodily pleasure in the same body, they can nevertheless think it in their mind and, delighting in that thought, preserve the joy of bodily pleasure even against the attack of bodily pain. Is it not the case in these that love casts out fear? But it is the love of the most sordid pleasure or, better, the love of the most clumsy vanity. In fact, when the presence of pain drives away pleasure from the members of the body, it will remain in the soul through its false and vain image. This vanity is so beloved that, when a vain man embraces it with all the strength of his heart, it even mitigates the harshness of pain. We must not only mock them, but also the Stoics 3, since these two sects, that of the Epicureans and that of the Stoics, dared to throw their smoke against the light of our Paul, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles. The Stoics also present themselves as very strong; but not for the pleasure of the body, but for the virtue of the soul, and they maintain not fear for the sake of not fearing, filled with pride; not healed by wisdom, but hardened by error. And they are so unhealthy that they thought they could heal the sick soul themselves. They consider that the health of the soul consists in the wise man becoming not even sorry. «Well, they say,

If you feel sorry, you feel pain, and where there is pain there is no health. This is how the body and soul of the saints will be in the resurrection of the dead, in which they do not believe, since they have incompetent teachers considering themselves such. The absence of pain due to health must be distinguished from that due to insensitivity. According to the health of this mortality, healthy flesh feels pain when pricked. The soul is also well endowed according to this life, which, stinged by the misery of those who tire, feels compassion out of mercy. However, the flesh made insensitive by a more serious illness or dead because the spirit has left it, does not experience pain even when pricked, just as the soul of those men who philosophize or, rather, drown without God. As the body lives animated by the soul, so the soul itself lives animated by God. Look, then, these ones, who neither feel pain nor fear, if instead of being healthy they are not dead. 4. Fear, then, the Christian before perfect love casts out fear; believe and understand that you are a pilgrim away from the Lord while you live in this body, which becomes corrupted and becomes attached to the soul. The less the fear the closer the homeland to which we tend is. Fear should be greater in those who are pilgrims, less in those who are already close, and none in those who have already arrived. Thus fear leads to charity, and perfect charity casts out fear. The Christian fears not those who kill the body and can do nothing else, but rather those who have the power to cast away body and soul.

Theme: The love and healing of a blind man as Jesus passes by (Luke 18:38-42). Location: Hippo. Date: In winter. Perhaps around the year 412.

1. Recently, when his letter was read, the Apostle spoke to us about love, and he urged it to us in such a way that we must understand that everything else, even if it is a great gift from God, is of no use without it. Love cannot be alone. I am also going to dedicate my sermon to love. There is a divine love and another human; Within the human, one is legal and the other illegal. I want to speak to you, as much as the Lord grants me, about these three forms of love or affection, a double way in which the only Greek term can be translated: agape. I distinguished first between human love and divine love; and then, within human love, between licit love and illicit love. I am going to deal first with licit, non-reprehensible human love, and then with illicit love, which is condemned; thirdly, of divine love, which leads us to the kingdom. 2. To put it briefly, the human love with which one loves one's wife is lawful; illicit is that with which one loves a prostitute or another's wife. In SERMO forums and public squares
DE CARITATE, ET DE CAECO ILLUMINATE, I

CAPUT I.—1. Caritas alia divine, alia human. Caritas humano, alia licita, alia illicita.—De caritate nobis paulo ante Apostolus loquebatur, cum eius Epístola legeretur: et eam nobis sic commendabat, ut intellegeremus cetera omnia, quamvis magna Dei dona, sine illa nihil prodesse. Ubi autem ipsa est, sola esse non potest. Et nos ergo vestrae Caritati sermonem de caritate reddamus. Caritas there is divine, there is human: there is human licit, there is illicit. De his ergo tribus caritatibus vel dilectionibus; duet enim nomina habet apud Latins, quae graece áyónrri dicitur; quod Dominus donaverit dicam. Haec ergo prima est distributio mea, quod dixi, aliam hu[1530]manam, aliam divinam esse caritatem: eamdemque humanom in duo distribuí, quod alia sit licita, alia illicita. Prius ergo loquor de humano licita, quae non reprehenditur: deinde de humano illicita, quae damnatur: tertio de divina, quae nos perducit ad regnum. CAPUT II.—2. De humano caritate licita.—Ut ergo breviter insiimem, licita est humano caritas, qua uxor diligitur; illicit, qua meretrix vel uxor aliena. In forum enim et plateis magis licita caritas diligitur quaro
The love and healing of a blind man

licit love is loved more than prostituted love; In the temple of God, in the house of God, in the body of Christ, the love of the prostitute leads even her lover to hell. Your love, then, be lawful; It is human, but, as I said, it is lawful. And it is not only lawful in the sense that it is permitted, but it is so lawful that its lack is reprehensible. It is lawful for you to love your spouses, your children, your friends and fellow citizens with human love. All of these names have a bond of need and, in a way, a binder of love. But you see that the wicked can also have this love, that is, the pagans, the Jews and the heretics. Who among them does not love his wife, his children, his brothers, neighbors, relatives, friends, etc.? This love is, therefore, human. Therefore, if someone feels carried away by such cruelty that makes him lose even the human affection of love and does not love his children or his wife, he does not even deserve to be counted among men. We should not lavish praise on those who love their children, but we should condemn those who do not love them. But look still with whom you have this love in common. Beasts also love their children: asps, tigers, and lions love them. There is no beast that does not tenderly make advances to its children. Well, although it terrifies men, it caresses its little ones. The lion roars in the jungle, and no one passes by; It enters its den, where it has its cubs, and lays down all its ferocity. Therefore, he who does not love his children is worse than a lion. It is a human love, but a lawful love.

^ 3. Beware of illicit love. You are members and body of Christ. Listen to the Apostle and be amazed. He could not have expressed it in a more energetic and vehement way; He could not have been harsher in separating Christians from fornicatory love than when he said: Shall I therefore take away my members from Christ to make them members of a prostitute? To get to this he had previously said: Don't you know that whoever unites himself with a prostitute becomes one body with her? And he adduced the testimony of the Scripture: They shall be two in one flesh. These are also divine words, but referring to husband and wife, where it is lawful, permitted and honest; No to the maximum union, illicit and condemnable from every point of view. Just as the lawful union of a husband and wife makes the two one flesh, so the union of a prostitute and her lover makes them one flesh. Becoming, therefore, one flesh, what he added must fill you with terror and fear: Shall I then take away my members from Christ? Consider, Christian, that they are members of Christ; See that they are members of Christ, not those of another, but your own, since you have been purchased with the blood of Christ. Shall I therefore take away the members of Christ to make them members of a harlot? Whoever is not horrified by that, causes horror to God. 4. I beseech you, my brothers, with all my heart: suppose—which is not true—that God had promised impunity to such people and had said: "I will have mercy."

meretrix: in domo Dei, in temple Dei, in civitate Christi, in corpore Christi, etíam meretricis amor ad gehennas amorm perducit. Licitam ergo caritatem habete: human est; sed, ut dixi, licita est. Non solum autem ita licita est, ut concedatur: sed ita licita, ut si defuerit, reprehendatur. Liceat vobis humano caritate diligere coniuges, diligere filios, diligere amicos vestros, diligere cives vestios. Omnia enim ista nomina habent necessitudinis vinculum, et gluten quodam moda caritatis. Sed videtis istam caritatem esse posse et impiorum, id est, Paganorum, Iudaeorum, haereticorum. Quis enim eorum non amat uxorem, filios, fratres, vicinos, affines, amicos, etc.? Haec ergo humano est. Si ergo tali quisque crudelitate effertur, ut perdat etiam humanum dilectionis affectum, et non amet filios suos, et non amet coniugem suam; nec inter homines numerandus est. Non enim laudandus est qui amat filios suos; sed damnandus est qui non amat filios. Adhuc enim videat cum quibus debent ei esse dilectio ist communis. Amant filios et ferae: amant filios asps, amant filios tigrides, amant filios lions. Nulla enim bestiaest, quae non filiis suis blande immurmuret. Nam cum terreat homines, fovet children. Fremit leo in silvis, ut nemo transeat: intrat in speluncam, ubi habet filios suos, omnem rabiem feritatis exponit. Foris eam ponit, cum ipsa non ingreditur. Ergo qui non amat filios suos etiam leone peior est. Humana sunt ista, et licita sunt.

CAPUT III.—3. Of illicit love. Membra Christi.—Illicitum amo rem cávete. Membra Christi estis, et corpus Christi estis. Audite Apostolum, et terreamini. Non potuit enim gravius ​​dicere, non potuit vehementius, non potuit acrius deterrere Christianos ab amore fomicationum, nisi ubi dixt: Tollens ergo membra Christi, faciam membra meretricis? (1 Cor 6:15). Ut autem hoc diceret, superius ait: Nescitis quia qui adhaeret meretrici, unum corpus efficitur? (ibid., 16). Et testimonium de Scriptura dedit quod scriptum est: Erunt duo in carne una (Gen 2,24). Dictum est enim hoc divinitus: sed de viro et uxore ubi licet, ubi concessum est, ubi honestum est; non ubi turpe, non ubi illicitum, non ubi omni ratione damnabile. Sicut autem una fit caro in permixtione licita viri et uxoris: sic una fit caro in permixtione illicita meretricis et amatoris. Cum ergo una fit caro, illud te terreat, illud exhorreat quod addidit: tollens ergo membra Christi (1 Cor 6,15). Membra Christi atiede, christiane: [1531] membra Christi noli in altero, in te atiede membra Christi, qui emptus es sanguine Christi. Tollens ergo membra Christi, faciam membra meretricis? (ib.). Hoc qui non horret, Deo horret. CAPUT IV.—4. Caritas divina amorem illicitum meretricis non compatitur.—Prorsus, prorsus obsecro vos, fratres meí: ecce ponamus, quod non est, promisisse Deum talibus impunitatem, et dixisse, Qui talia

kindness to those who do that; I will not condemn them. Suppose God said it. Even with impunity promised, will anyone take away the members of Christ to make them members of a prostitute? He will not do it if the third kind of love already dwells in him: divine love. I mentioned, in fact, three kinds of love; I promised to speak about the three that the Lord granted me: licit human love, illicit love, and excellent and divine love. Let us interrogate divine love, let us place before it the two human loves and let us say to that man: «Notice that there is a lawful human love, with which one loves one's own wife, and one's daughters, and other people to whom we are necessarily united; that there is another illicit act, with which one loves a prostitute, another's servant, another's daughter not yet asked in marriage, not promised, and another's wife. Before you are these two loves; Which of them do you want to stay with? Whoever chooses to keep licit human love does not keep illicit love. No one can say: "I'll take both." If you stay with both of them, admitting the love of the prostitute into your home, you do an insult to the divine love, which, like the owner of a house, dwells there. I think that, if you are married and love a prostitute, you do not bring her into your house to live with the housewife. You don't go that far. You seek darkness, darkness; You don't proclaim your clumsiness. But also those who do not have a wife and believe that it is more permissible for them to love prostitutes - I said "believe", since they are also condemned, if they are already baptized - I think that even the adolescent who has not yet fecerint, miserebor eorum, non eos damnabo. Faciamus hoc dixisse Deum. Etiam promissa impunitate tollit quisque membra Christi, et facit iam membra meretricis? Non facit, si est ibi tertia divina dilectio. Etenim tres dilectiones commemoravi: de tribus me, quod Dominus daret, dicturum esse promisi; of human licita, of human illicit, of illa excellenti atque divina. Interrogemus divinam caritatem, et ponamus ante illam duas humano caritates, et dicamus ei: Ecce licita caritas humano, qua uxor diligitur, et filiae aliaeque necessitudines saeculares: ecce alia illicita, qua diligitur meretrix, qua diligitur ancilla aliena, qua diligitur aliena fifia non petita, non promissa, qua diligitur uxor aliena. Duae ante te sunt caritates; cum qua istarum vis manere? Qui eligit manere cum illa humano licita, cum illa humano illicita non manet. Nemo sibi dicat: Both habeo.

Si both habes admittendo ad te dilectionem meretricis, iniuriam facis tanquam matronae, quae ibi habitat, divinae caritati. Puto enim, quia si homo coniugatus sis, et diligas meretricem, non mittis meretricem in domum tuam, ut habitet cum matrona tua. Do not usque adeo progressis. Tenebras quaeris, latebras quaeris, turpitudinem non profiteris. Sed et qui non habent uxores, et sunt meretricum quasi licentius amatores (ideo dixi: Quasi, quia et ipsi damnantur, si iam sunt fideles); puto quia et adolescens nondum habens uxorem, si düigat mere-

He has a wife, if he loves a prostitute, he does not make her live with his sister or his mother, so as not to offend human modesty and stain the fame of his blood. If you do not take the prostitute you love to live with your sister and your mother in order not to stain, as I said, the fame of your blood, do you allow the love of a prostitute and the love of God to cohabit in your heart, thus staining the honor of the blood of Christ? 5. Love God, since you find nothing better than him. You love silver because it is better than iron and bronze; you love gold even more, because it is better than silver; you love precious stones even more, because they surpass even the price of gold; Finally, you love this light that every man who fears death fears losing; You love, I repeat, this light just as the one who shouted after Jesus desired it with great love: Have mercy on me, Son of David. The blind man shouted when Jesus passed by. I was afraid it would pass and not cure him. How did he scream? To the point of not being silent, even though the crowd ordered him to. He conquered by opposing it, and obtained the Savior. When the crowd shouted and forbade him to shout, Jesus stood up, called him and said to him: "What do you want me to do to you?" —Sir, he said, let him see. —Look, your je has saved you. Love Christ; desire the light that is Christ. If he desired the light of the heart, how much more should you desire that of the heart! Let us shout before him not with our voice, but with our customs. Let us live holyly, destricem, non eam facit habitare cum sorore sua, non eam facit habitare cum matre sua, ne iniuriam faciat humanoe pudicitiae, ne offendat decus sanguinis sui. Si ergo non facis habitare meretricem, quam diligis, cum matre tua, cum sorore tua, ne, sicut dixi, offendas decus sanguinis tui; facis habitare in corde tuo dilectionem meretricis cum dilectione Dei, et offendis decus sanguinis Christi? CAPUT V.—5. LUCÍS internae amore exemplo caeci clamandum bene vivir. Contradictio mundi.—Amate Deum, nihil melius invenitis. Amatis argentum, quia melius est ferro et aeramento: amatis plus aurum, quia melius est argento: amatis plus lapides pretiosos, quia et auri pretium superant: amatis postremo istam luzem, quam dimitiere formidat omnis qui mortem timet; amatis, inquam, istam luzem, quomodo eam amore quodam ingenti desiderabat, qui post Iesum clamabat: Miserere mei, fili David (Luke 18:38). Clamabat caecus Christo passerby. Metuebat enim ne traniret, et non sanaret. Et how much clamabat? Ut prohibitive mob non taceret. Vicit contradictorem, tenuit Salvatorem.

Obstrepentibus turbis et clamare prohibentibus, stetit Iesus, vocavit eum, et dixit ei: Quid vis [1532] tibi fieri? Domine, inquit, ut videom. Réspice, fides tua te salvum fecit (ib., 41.42). Love Christum; desiderate lumen, quod est Christus. If you desideravit ille lumen corporis, how much more lumen cordis do you desiderare? Ad eum, non vocibus, sed moribus clamemus. Vivamus bene, mundum contemnamus: nihil nobis sit omne quod transit.

let us appreciate the world; Let us consider everything that happens as null. If we live like this, the worldly names, lovers of the earth, savorers of dust, who bring nothing from heaven, who have no more vital breath than what they breathe through their noses, without another in their hearts, will rebuke us, as if they did it for our love. Without a doubt, when they see us despising these human and earthly things, they will reproach us and say: "Why do you suffer? Have you gone crazy? There are Christians like that; but let us overcome them, let us live holyly; Let our lives be our cry to Christ. He will stop, since he is already stopped.' 6. A great mystery is also contained there. He was passing by when the blind man screamed; To heal him he stopped. The passing of Christ must keep us attentive to shout. What is the passing of Christ? Everything he suffered for us is his past. Born: passed; is it still born? It grew: it passed; Is it still growing? He took the breast; Do you still take it? Tired, he fell asleep; Is he still sleeping? He ate and drank; Do you still do it? Finally, he was captured, chained, scourged, crowned with thorns, slapped, covered in spittle, hung on the tree, killed, wounded with a spear, and buried, resurrected:

It still happens. He ascended into heaven, he is seated at the right hand of the Father: he stood. Scream as much as you can, which now grants you the vision. As far as he was the Word next to God, he was certainly standing, because he did not undergo any mutation. And the Word was God, and the Word became flesh. The flesh did many things in passing, and also suffered them; but the Word stood still. The Word itself is what illuminates the heart, since the flesh that received receives its honor from the Word. Eliminate the Word, what is your flesh? The same as yours. So that the flesh of Christ might be honored, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Let us shout, then, and live holyly. 7. Love your children, love your wives even according to the world. Such is that divine love. Well, what good is your fleeting and mortal love for them? However, love Christ more, even if you love them humanly. I'm not saying that you don't love your wife, but that you love Christ more; I'm not saying that you don't love your father or your children, but that you love Christ more. Do not think that these are my words; Listen to him say: He who loves his father or his mother more than me is not worthy of me. Do you not fear when you hear: He is not worthy of me? Theme: Love. Location: Unknown. Techa: Years 425 to 430. 1. He who has his heart full of love, my brothers, understands without error and maintains without effort the varied, abundant and vast doctrine of the Holy Scriptures, according to the words of the Apostle: The fullness of the law is love; and in another place: The end of the precept is the love that arises from a pure heart, from a right conscience and from a faith not finQuare time sine illo esse? If you don't love esse in regno, time esse in path ignis ardentis, inexstinguibilis, sempiterni. Vincat in te prius timor, et erit amor. Timor paedagogus sit, non ipse in te remaneat, sed te ad caritatem, quasi ad magistrum perducat.

1. Carylatis laus. Per eam divina doctrina sine errore comprehendi' tur, sine labore custoditur. Mandatum novum faciens hominem novum.— Divinarum Scripturarum multiplicem abundantiam, latissimamque doctrinam, fratres mei, sine ullo errore comprehendit, et sine ullo labore custodit, cuius cor plenum est caritate: dicente Apostolo: Plenitudo autem legis caritas (Rom 13:10); et alio loco: Finís autem praecepti est caritas de corde puro, et conscientia bona, et fide non ficta (1 Tim 1,5). Quis

gida. What is the purpose of the precept if not its fulfillment? And what is the fulfillment of the precept if not the fullness of the law? What he said in one place: The fullness of the law is love, is the same as what he said in the other: The end of the precept is love. There can be no doubt that the man in whom love dwells is the temple of God, since John also says: God is love. When the apostles tell us this and entrust us with the excellence of love, they are indicating that they did not eat anything other than what those belches manifest. The same Lord who fed them with the word of truth and love, which is the same living bread that came down from heaven, said: I give you a new commandment: that you love one another. And also: By this everyone will know that you are my disciples: if you love one another. He who came to put to death the corruption of the flesh through the ignominy of the cross and to loosen with the newness of his death the ancient chain of ours, created a new man with the new commandment. That man died was, indeed, something very old; So that it was not always a reality in man, something new happened: that God died. But since he died in the flesh, but not in divinity, through the everlasting life of his divinity he did not allow the perdition of the flesh to be eternal. And so, as the Apostle says, he died for our sins and rose again for our justification. Therefore, he who argued the newness of life against the oldness of death, himself opposes to the old sin the commandment nueest autem finis praecepti, nisi praecepti adimpletio? et quid est praecepti adimpletio, nisi legis plenitudo? Quod ergo ibi dixit: Plenitudo legis est caritas (Rom 13:10); hoc etiam hic dixit: Finis praecepti est caritas (1 Tim 1,5). Nec dubitari ullo moda potest, quod templum Dei sit homo, in quo habitat caritas. Dicit enim et Ioannes: Deus caritas est (1 lo 4,8). Haec autem dicentes Apostoli et nobis caritatis excellentiam commendantes, non utique aliud, nisi quod comederant, ructuare potuerunt.

Ipse quippe Dominus pascens eos verbo veritatis, verbo caritatis, quod est ipse pañis vivus, qui de cáelo descendit, Mandatum, inquit, novum do vobis, ut diligatis invicem: Et iterum: In hoc scient omnes quia discipuli mei estis, si vos invicem dilexeritis (lo 13,34.35). lile enim qui come per crucis irrisionem carnis perimere corruptionem, et vetustatem vinculi mortis nostrae suae mortis novitate dissolvere, manda novo fecit hominem novum. Res enim vetus erat, ut homo moreretur. Quod ne semper valeret in homine, res nova facta est, ut Deus moreretur. Sed quia in carne mortuus est, non in divinitate, per sempiternam vitam divinitatis non permisit esse sempiternum interitum carnis. Itaque, sicut dicit Apostolus: Mortuus est propter de[l534]licta nostra, et resurrexit propter iustificationem nostram (Rom 4,25). Qui ergo contra mortis vetustatem attulit vitae novitatem, ipse contra vetus peccatum opponit novum mandatum. Quapropter quisquis vetus pee

vo. Therefore, whoever you are who wants to extinguish the old sin, quench lust with the new commandment and embrace love. As lust is the root of all evil, so love is the root of all good. 2. The love by which we love God and our neighbor confidently possesses all the magnitude and latitude of the divine words. The only teacher, the heavenly one, teaches us and says: You will love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and you will love your neighbor as yourself. All the law and the prophets hang on these two precepts. If, then, you do not have time to scrutinize all the holy pages, to remove all the veils from their words and penetrate all the secrets of the Scriptures, remain in love, on which everything hangs; This way you will have what you learned there and even what you have not yet learned. In fact, if you know love, you know something that also depends on what you perhaps don't know; In what you understand from the Scriptures love is evident, in what you do not understand it is hidden. He who has love in his customs, therefore, possesses both what is visible and what is hidden in the divine word. 3. Therefore, brothers, pursue love, the sweet and healthy bond of minds, without which the rich is poor and with which the poor is rich. Love gives resistance in ad-

versities and moderation in prosperity; He is strong in hard trials, joyful in good works; confident in temptation, generous in hospitality; joyful among true brothers, very patient among false ones. Pleasant in Abel for his sacrifice, safe in Noah because of the flood, full of faithfulness in the pilgrimages of Abraham, most gentle in the midst of insults in Moses, most gentle in the face of tribulations in David. In the three children he waits innocently for the soft flames, in the Maccabees he tolerates the atrocious fires with strength; It is chaste in Susanna with respect to her husband, in Anna after her husband died, in Mary without a husband. It is free in Paul to argue, humble in Peter to obey, human in Christians to confess, divine in Christ to forgive. But can I say anything better and more abundant about love than the praises that the Lord lavishes on it through the mouth of the Apostle? He shows a super-excellent way and says: Although I speak in the tongues of men and angels, if I do not have love, I am like a ringing brass or a clanging cymbal; and although I have the gift of prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and although I have so much faith that I even move mountains, if I do not have love, I am nothing. And even if I give all my possessions and distribute everything I have to the poor, and even if I give my body to the flames, if I do not have charity, it is of no use to me. Theme: Love. Location: Unknown. Date: Year 399 or before.

1. I am not unaware that your hearts are fed daily with the exhortations of divine readings and with the nourishment of the word of God. But, in response to the desire for love with which we inflame each other, I am going to say something to your charity. What can I talk to you about but love? Love is such that, if someone wants to talk about it, they do not have to look for an appropriate reading for it, because any page, no matter where it is opened, does not say anything else. The Lord himself is a witness to this and the Gospel itself shows it to us; So, when they asked him what the greatest commandments of the law were, he answered: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. And so that you would no longer search in the sacred pages, he added and said: On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. If all the law and the prophets hang on these two commandments, how much more so does the Gospel! Love, in fact, renews man, for as concupiscence makes a man old, so love makes him new. by SERMO

That is why someone, groaning in the midst of the battle with concupiscence, says: I have grown old in the midst of all my enemies. That love belongs to the new man, the Lord indicates in the following way: I give you a new commandment: that you love one another. Therefore, if the law and the prophets depend on love, despite the fact that in the law and the prophets the Old Testament seems to be entrusted to us, how much more will the Gospel, clearly called the New Testament, belong only to love, since the Lord presented no other commandment than mutual love as his commandment! Not only did he call the commandment itself new, but he also came to renew us, made us new men and promised us a new and eternal inheritance. 2. If perhaps you are thinking how the law is called the Old Testament and yet it depends on love, whereas love renews man and belongs to the new man, here is the reason. There it is announced as the Old Testament because the promise is earthly, and the Lord promises, to those who worship him, the earthly kingdom. But even then there were lovers of God who loved him freely and purified their hearts by chastely sighing for him. They, having removed the veil that covered the old promises, came to perceive the prefiguration of the future New Testament and understood that all those things commanded or promised in the Old, according to the old man, were figures of the New, which the Lord was going to make a reality in the end times. He openly says it

the Apostle: All this happened to them in figures; but they were written for us, in whom the end of the centuries has become present. Thus, in a hidden way, the New Testament was announced in advance precisely through those ancient figures. But, with the arrival of the time of the New Testament, it began to be preached openly, and those figures began to be exposed and explained so that the new could be perceived where the old was promised. Moses announced the Old Testament, but whoever announced the Old Testament saw the New in it; The Old announced to the carnal people, but he, spiritual, warned of the New there. The apostles, on the other hand, were announcers and ministers of the New; not because what would later be manifested through the apostles was not already there. Love is in both the Old and New Testaments; but in the first love is more hidden and fear more visible; In the New, however, love is more manifest, and fear less. For the more love grows, the more fear diminishes. As love grows, the soul acquires security, and when security is total, fear is null, according to the words of the apostle John: Perfect love expels fear. 3. The Holy Spirit foreseeing this temptation of ours and changing our love so that it does not seem to us that the happier we see them to be, according to the world, those impious and criminal men, the more they must be imitated in the love of those things with whose abundance they were filled, he said to those men: Do not be envious of the wicked - this is how the psalm begins - nor be jealous of those who work iniquity, for they will quickly wither like hay and, like the grass of the field, they will instantly fall. Does hay never bloom? Yes, but it blooms for a short time; soon its flower will wither; flowering is the work of cold air. Now, the groans of your pain will be profitable for your salvation, but also for everlasting glory. They have nothing big that they can show us. They are happy now, we will be happy in the future, but we are more correct in saying that theirs is neither present nor will it be future, since those who love the false present happiness will not reach the true future. If, on the other hand, they do not worry about the false happiness of the present, they will know what to do with what they have and what to buy with it. Listen to the advice that the blessed Apostle commands Timothy to convey to the rich. Pharisee, confident in the counting of his merits. Although he also gave thanks to God, saying: I thank you, O God, because I am not like other men: unjust, adulterers, thieves; like that publican. Fasting twice on the Sabbath and paying tenths of everything I possess, the one who was standing far away, not daring to raise his eyes to heaven, took the lead and beat his chest, saying: "Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner." That Pharisee did not find so much joy in his health as in comparing it with the illnesses of others. Since he had come to the doctor, it would have been more useful for him to show, by confessing them, the illnesses that had made him sick than to hide his wounds and dare to boast about the scars of others. It is not strange, then, that the publican came out more healed, who had no qualms about showing what hurt him. In visible things, to reach what is on high one must stand up; God, however, although he is the highest of all, is reached not by exalting himself, but by humbling himself. That is why the prophet says: The Lord is close to those with a contrite heart. And also: The Lord is exalted and sets his sights on humble things; He knows the elevated ones from afar. High things are placed here to point out the proud. He sets his sights on those to lift them up; He knows these to bring them down. By saying that he knows high things from afar, he sufficiently showed that he looks closely at lowly things, despite having previously said that the Lord is exalted. Only

God does not sin from arrogance no matter how much he praises himself. Do not think about the pride that is hidden from the eyes of God, for God knows high things. Nor consider yourself united to God, since you know high things from afar. Therefore, he who refuses the humility of penance does not think of approaching God. Indeed, it is one thing to rise towards God and another to rise against him. Whoever prostrates himself before him, he lifts him up; Whoever rises up against him, he knocks down. One thing is the solidity that comes from magnitude and another is the emptiness of inflation. Whoever is swollen on the outside is rotten on the inside. Whoever chooses to be despised in the house of God rather than dwell in the tent of sinners, God chooses him to dwell in his courts and welcomes to the throne of blessedness the one who took nothing for himself. Which is why it is sung in the psalm with softness and truth: Blessed is the man whom you welcome, Lord. Do not think that he who humbles himself will always remain prostrate, since it has been said: He will be exalted. But lest you think that his exaltation will take place before the eyes of men by bodily means, after having said: Blessed is the man whom you welcome, Lord, he then added something still, showing that the exaltation that this welcome entails is spiritual: He prepared, he said, in his heart, in the valley of tears, steps towards the place that he has prepared for him. Where, then, did he arrange the steps? In the heart, that is, in the valley of tears. This is what it means: He who humbles himself will be exalted. As the steps allude to an exaltation, so the valley to humiliation and tears.

The other penance, the exercise of which lasts the entire life we ​​spend in this mortal flesh, must be submitted to the permanent humility of supplication. In the first place, because no one desires eternal, incorruptible and immortal life, if he is not grieved by this temporary, corruptible and mortal life. In fact, no one is born to new life through the sanctification of baptism and lays down all past sins in such a way as to lay aside, at the same time, the mortality and corruption of the flesh. If this does not happen, what is written remains standing, and that each person still feels in himself while he is in this life: The corruptible body aggravates the soul and the earthly abode oppresses the mind, dispersed in many thoughts. Since it will not then exist in that blessedness, when death is absorbed in victory, who doubts that, whatever happiness we may live in, we must nevertheless grieve for this life, to rush with all eagerness towards that incorruption? This is what the Apostle also says refers to: While we are in this body we are pilgrims far from the Lord, since we walk in faith, not in vision. Who but the one who regrets being a pilgrim hurries and desires to reach the homeland and participate in that vision that is face to face? Penitential voice also arises and resounds that voice of an unfortunate man: Woe is me! My pilgrimage has become long. They are not only words of a believing man, but also of a very firm evangelizer and a very courageous martyr. From there also come these words of the Apostle: For we know that, although our earthly house in this mansion collapses, we have another building, a gift from God, an eternal house in heaven; not made by the hands of men. Behold, we live among groans, desiring to be clothed with our habitation from heaven, in case we are found clothed and not naked. In fact, those of us who are in this abode groan under the weight of that of which we do not want to be stripped, but to be clothed, so that what is mortal is absorbed by life. What do we want, then, but to stop being as we are now? Why do we moan if not because it hurts us to be the way we are? But when will we stop being like this except once the earthly house has collapsed and the heavenly habitation falls to us through the transformation of the entire man, soul and body? That is why even the holy Job did not say that there were temptations in this life, but that life itself is a temptation, with these words: Is not the life of man on earth a temptation? In that same place he also touched in a wonderful way the mystery of fallen man when he said: suae paenituerit? If you have the opportunity, give your alms with joy, whether you offer something for the bodily needs of the poor or, as a dispenser of heavenly bread, you raise impregnable camps in the hearts of the faithful against the devil. For God loves him who gives with joy. Let him not be broken by boredom in the difficulties that must necessarily exist, to remind man that he is a man. Do not let anger slide against those who attack you with hatred or who, forced by necessity, ask you at the wrong time; or who without consideration begs you to help him in a matter of his, when you are busy with another more important matter; or who resists evident justice with his word, either out of blind ambition or out of regrettable indolence. Do not give more or less than is appropriate; Do not speak more than necessary or when it is not necessary. For precious are the feet of those who announce peace, those who announce good. However, from the dry land they accumulate dust, which will certainly be

shaken to the condemnation of those who with perverse will despise what has been shown to them. Our penance must be daily not only because of the mortality and ignorance of this life and because of the malice of each day, which I wish were enough, as it is written about it: its malice is enough for each day; malice that we are commanded to endure and endure until it passes and endure the Lord acting manfully to bear fruit with our tolerance; We must also do penance because of the very dust of this world, which adheres to the feet that walk along the roads looking for others, and the losses caused even by ministerial action, which occupies so much time; losses that the Lord pleases to compensate with greater gains. 5. And if the dispensers of the word of God and ministers of his sacraments must do this, how much more so should the remaining tributary multitude and certain province of the great king! In order not to offend her even with the false suspicion of greed, the apostle Paul, a most faithful and courageous soldier, fought at his own expense, and when perhaps he lacked what was necessary, he said: I despoiled other churches, receiving from them my salary to serve you. How much more must the provincials (lay people) of the Church, involved in worldly affairs, do penance! Although they are immune from theft, from plunder, from fraud, from adultery and fornication and from all kinds of lust, from cruel hatred and stubborn enmity, from the ugliness of any idol,

dares pecuniam meam, et ego veniens cum usuris demanding: ne auferatur ab eo quod accepit, ne proiciatur in exterior darkness (cf. Mt 25:26-30). Quam vehementissimam poenam si timere debent illi, qui servare integrum possunt quod acceperunt; quae spes illorum est, qui hoc impie scelerateque disperdunt? Versabitur ergo iste in rebus humanis, non carnalis, sed spiritualis acquisitionis devinctus officio; non quidem negotiis saecularibus obligatus, sed tamen quia militat Deo, non otio desidiae torpidus et abiectus. Det ergo, si potest, suas eleemosynas omnes cum hilaritate, sive cum carnalibus necessitatibus pauperum aliquid erogat, sive cum pañis caelestis dispensator invicta adversus diabolum castra in credentium cordibus construit. Hilarem enim datorem diligit Deus (2 Cor 9:7). Non itaque taedio frangatur in difficultatibus rerum, quae ne[1540]cesse est existant, ut ostendatur homini quod homo est. Non ira subrepat in eum qui aut odióse irruit, aut inopportune inopia coactus petit; aut business suo, cum tu maiore occupatus es, indifferent flagitat subveniri; aut in verbo manifestae iustitiae resistit caeca cupiditate, aut miserabili tarditate. Non det quidquam amplius vel minus quam oportet: non loquatur amplius quam opus est, aut cum etiam non opus est. Speciosi enim pedes evangelizantium pacem, evangelizantium bona (Rom 10:15). Sed tamen de terra sicca pulverem contrahunt, qui sane in

iudicium eorum excutitur, qui sibi banc exhibitionem perversa voluntate contemnunt. Non solum ergo propter ipsam vitae huius mortalitatem et ignorantiam, et propter diei malitiam, quae utinam sufficeret, sicut de illa dictum est: Sufficit diei malitia sua (Mt 6,34); quam iubemur ferré atque portare, doñee transeat, et sustinere Deum viriliter agendo, ut fructum afferamus cum tolerantia; sed etiam propter ipsum pulverem mundi huius, qui per itinera consulendi consulentium pedibus adhaerescit, et damna quae in ipsa negotiosissima dispensationis actione contingunt, quae Dominus praestet ut cum lucris maioribus compensentur, quotidianam debenmus habere paenitentiam. 5. Laicorum peccata quotidiana. Coniugü mus quandonam inculpabilis.—Sed si hoc dispensatores verbi Dei et ministri Sacramentorum eius, milites Christi; quanto magis cetera stipendiaria multitudo, et quaedam province magni regis? Quam ne forte vel false suspicione avaritiae miles ille fidelissimus atque fortissimus apostolus Paulus offenderet, suis stipendiis militavit: et ubi forte defuit sumptus necessarius: Alias, inquit, Ecclesias exspoliavi, accipiens ab eis stipendium ad vestram ministrationem (2 Cor 11,8). Quanto ergo magis Ecclesiae provinciales saecularibus negotiis obligad, quotidianam debent agere paenitentiam? Qui quamvis a furtis, a rapinis, a fraudibus, ab adulteriis et fornicationibus omnique luxuria, a crudelitate odiorum et inimicitiarum pertinacia,

latria, of the vanity of spectacles, of the impious heretical or schismatic vanity and of all crimes and clumsiness of the same style, must be pure and integrity; However, due to the administration of family affairs and the very close ties of marriage, they sin so much that they seem no longer sprinkled with the dust of this world, but covered with mud. This is what the Apostle tells them: Indeed, it is already a crime for you to go from court to court. Why do you not prefer to suffer iniquity? Why not be defrauded? In fact, what he added for the sake of some is an execrable thing: But you work iniquity and defraud, brothers! Disregarding iniquity and fraud, he affirmed that the very act of going to court and litigating over temporal matters was a crime; which would be bearable, he warns, if such disputes were decided in a Church court. The words also refer to this: He who has no wife thinks about the things of God, how to please God; He who, on the other hand, is united in marriage, thinks about the things of the world, about how to please his wife. And he says the same about women. Also that other thing: And again return to the same thing, so that Satan does not tempt you because of your incontinence. To show that this was a sin, even though it was a concession to weakness, he immediately added: But I say this as a concession, not commanding it. Only for the purpose of procreation does the woman lack all guilt.

union of both sexes 3. How numerous are the remaining sins, both in talking about other people's things or matters, which do not concern you, and in vain laughter, as it is written: The fool, when he laughs, raises his voice; The wise man, on the other hand, will laugh quietly; or in the same foods, prepared as necessary sustenance for life, when the appetite reveals itself to be avid and without moderation, frequently exceeding the measure, which will have repercussions on indigestion the next day; or in the perverse desires to sell high and buy low! It causes hesitation to enumerate everything that each person notices and rebukes in himself with greater accuracy simply by looking carefully at the mirror of the Holy Scriptures. Although the wound of each of these sins is not felt to be mortal, as in the case of homicide and adultery and other things of the same nature, nevertheless, all together, like scabies, being many, they cause death, or they spoil our beauty, in such a way that they separate us from the most chaste embraces of that husband, the most beautiful of the children of men, if they are not cut with the medicine of daily penance. 5. If what was said is false, why do we beat our chests daily? We bishops also do it like the others when approaching the altar. That is why we also say when praying what is convenient for us to say throughout life: Forgive us our debts, just as we forgive our debtors.

ab omni denique idololatriae foeditate, spectaculorum nugacitate, haeresum atque schismatum impia vanitate, atque ab ómnibus huiuscemodi flagitiis et facinoribus immunes, puri atque integrai esse debenant: tamen propter administrationem rerum familiarium, et coniugiorum artissima liga, tammula peccant, ut non tam de istius Mundi pulvere aspergi, quam luto obliniri videantur. Hoc est quod Apostolus eis dicit: lam quidem omnino delictum est in vobis, quia indicia habetis vobiscum. Quare non magis iniquitatem patimini? Quare non potius fraudamini? Nam illud exsecrabile est, quod propter quosdam [1541] addit et dicit: Sed vos iniquitatem facitis, et fraudatis, et boc fratribus (1 Cor 6,7.8). Exceptis tamen iniquitatibus et fraudibus, hoc ipsum habere Inter se iudicia et lites de saecularibus rebus, delictum esse dicit: quod tamen ferendum esse admonet, si vel ecclesiastico iudicio lites huiuscemodi finiantur. Hinc est etiam illud: Qui sine uxore est, cogitat ea quae sunt Dei, quomodo placeat Deo: qui autem marriage coniunctus est, cogitat ea quae sunt mundi, quomodo placeat uxori (ib., 7,32-33). Quod etiam de femina similiter notat. Vel illud cum ait: Et iterum ad idipsum estofe, ne vos tentet satanás propter intemperantiam vestram (ib., 5). Quod ut peccatum esse demonstraret, sed infirmitati concessum; subiecit statim: Hoc autem dico secundum veniam, non secundum imperium (ib., 6). Sola enim generadi causa est inculpabilis sexus utriusque commíxtio!

Quam fines sunt allia peccata, sive in loquendo de rebus et negotiis alienis, quae non ad te pertinent; sive in vanis cachinnationibus, cum scriptum sit: Stultus in risu exaltat vocem suam, sapiens autem vix tacite ridébit (Eccli 21,23); sive in ipsis escis, quae ad necessitatem sustandae huius vitae praeparantur, avidior atque immoderatior_ appetitus, saepe excessum modum postridiana cruditate contestans: sive in vendedis et emendis rebus caritatis et vilitatis vote perversa. Piget cuneta colligere, quae quisque in se ipso certius comprehendit atque reprehendit, si divinarum Scripturarum speculum non neglegenter attendat. Quae quamvis singula non lethali vulnere ferire sentiantur, sicuti homicidium et adulterium, vel cetera huiusmodi: tamen omnia simul congregata velut scabies, quo plura sunt necant, aut nostrum decus ita exterminant, ut ab illius sponsi speciosi forma prae filiis hominum (cf. Ps 44,3) castissimis amplexibus separent, nisi medication quotidianae paenitentiae desiccentur. 6. Peccata quotidiana omnes ex carnis infirmitate contrahimus. Lucta ebristianae animae.—Quod si falsum est, unde quotidie tundimus pectora? Quod nos quoque antistites ad altare assistentes cum omnibus facimus. Unde etiam orantes dicimus, quod in tota ista ista vita oportet ut dicamus: Dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus 3 See additional note [26]: Ekuso del matrimonial vol.7 p.753.

dores. We do not ask to be forgiven the sins that we believe have already been forgiven in baptism, otherwise we would doubt the faith; Our supplication refers to daily sins, for which each one does not stop also offering, according to his strength, the sacrifice of alms, fasting and the same prayers and supplications. Therefore, he who diligently examines himself and is not deceived by any type of flattery, sufficiently understands how many dangers of eternal death and how much scarcity of perfect justice the pilgrimage away from the Lord is made, even if, already finding himself in Christ, that is, on the way, he tries to return. In fact, if we have no sins and, beating our chest, we say: Forgive us our debts, no one doubts that for this very fact we sin gravely, for lying even in the midst of the sacred mysteries. Therefore, to the extent that we are united to our God through faith, hope and love and, as far as we can, we imitate him, we do not sin, but are children of God; but to the extent that, because of the weakness of the flesh, not yet suppressed by death, reprehensible and reprehensible movements unexpectedly arise, we sin. It is better for us to confess this, lest due to hardness of neck we deserve not the healing of our evil, but the condemnation of pride. Precisely both things are written: He who is born of God does not sin; and what we read in the same letter of John: If we said that we had no sin in us, we would deceive ourselves.

we and the truth does not dwell in us. The first thing was said about the firstfruits of the new man; the second, from the remains of the old man, since we carry one thing and another in this life. But little by little the novelty grows and, giving way to old age, gradually takes its place. While both things are taking place, we are in the stadium, and we not only deal blows to the enemy with our good works, but we also suffer them by not being cautious in avoiding sins. Now we don't look at who among us wins, but at who hurts more frequently and who fights with more courage, until he who, after having fallen, was envious of the man who stood firm, drags some with him to eternal death and, in the end, others, the victors, say: Where, O death, is your strife? Where is your sting, O death? The enemy never overthrows us more easily than when we imitate him in pride, nor do we inflict more intense pain on him than when we heal the wounds of our sins through confession and penance. 7. The third act of penance is that which must be suffered for those sins contrary to the Decalogue of the Law, and of which the Apostle says: Those who do such works will not possess the kingdom of heaven. In this penance, each one must show greater severity towards himself, so that, becoming his own judge, he will not be judged by the Lord, as the Apostle himself said: If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord. So let the man go up to the court

nostris (Mt 6,12). Non enim ea dimitti precamur, quae iam in Baptism nisi dimissa credimus, de ipsa fide dubitamus: sed utique de quotidianos peccatis hoc dicimus, pro quibus etiam sacrificia eleemosynarum, ieiuniorum, et ipsarum orationum ac supplicationum quisque pro suis viribus offerre non cessat. Quisquís! taque se diligenter attendens, nulla se ipsum adulatione seducit, satis intellegit cum quanto periculo mortis aeternae, et cum quanta penuria perfectione iustitiae peregrinetur a Domino; quamvis iam in Christo, hoc est, in via constitutus I will rediré conetur. Nam si non habemus peccata, et tundentes pectora [1542] dicimus: Dimitte nobis debita nostra; ex hoc ipso certe et graviter nullo dubitante peccamus, cum Inter ipsa Sacramenta mentimur. Quamobrem, in quantum Deo nostro fide, spe et caritate conectimur, et eum in quantum possumus, imitatur, non peccamus, sed filii Dei sumus: in quantum autem ex occasione carnalis infirmitatis, quia nondum morte resoluta, nondum resurrectione mutata est, motus reprehensibiles improbique subrepunt, peccamus. Quod utique fateri suited us; ne dura cervice, non languoris nostri sanitatem, sed damnationem superbiae mereamur. Unde utrumque verissime scriptum est: et, Qui natus est ex Deo, non peccat (1 lo 3,9); et quod in eadem Ioannis Epistle legimus: Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nosmetipsos decipimus, et ventas in nobis

non est (ib., 1,8). Illud enim ex primitiis novi hominis, hoc ex reliquiis veteris dictum est: utrumque enim agimus in hac vita. Paulatim autem novitas accessit, et paulatim vetustate cedent succedit. Cum vero utrumque agitur, in stadio sumus; nec solum percutimus adversarium bonis operibus, sed etiam peccata serendipity avoiding percutimur. Ñeque nunc quis nostrum vicerit, sed quis crebrius fairat, quis fortius confligat attenditur; doñee alios secum in sempiternam mortem pertrahat, qui homini stanti lapsus invidit, et ab aliis triumphantibus in fine dicatur: Ubi est, mors, contentio tua? ubi est, mors, aculeus tuus? (1 Cor 15:55). Sed ñeque facilius ab inimico deicimur, quam cum eum superiendo imitamur; nec vehementius eum prosternimus, quam cum humilitate Dominum sequimur; nec acriores ei dolors inflictimus, quam cum pestas peccatorum nostrorum confitendo et paenitendo sanamus. CAPUT IV.—7. Tertia paenitentia severior pro peccatis mortiferis. Lacrimae sanguis paenitentis.—Tertia actio est paenitentiae, quae pro illis peccatis subeunda est. Quae Legis decalogus continet; et de quibus Apostolus ait: Quoniam qui talia agunt, regnum Dei non possidebunt (Gal 5,21). In hac ergo paenitentia, maiorem quisque in se severitatem debent exercere; ut a se ipso iudicatus, non iudicetur a Domino, sicut idem apostolus ait: Si enim nos iudicaremus, a Domino non iudicaremur (1 Cor 11:31).
