The resurrection of the dead

5. I fear, said the Apostle, that as the serpent seduced Eve with his cunning, so also your minds may depart from the chastity that exists in Christ Jesus. These minds are corrupted by words like those: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die. Those who love and seek this, those who think that there is nothing but this life, those who hope for nothing more, those who either do not pray to God or ask Him for what they have said, those for whom every word that invites vigilance is burdensome, listen to those who say this with great sadness. They want to eat and drink, because tomorrow they will die. I wish they really thought that tomorrow they were going to die! Who, in fact, is so insane and so lost, who is such an enemy of his soul that, having to die tomorrow, he does not think that all the things for which he works will come to an end? Thus it is written: On that day all his thoughts will perish. If men, faced with the imminence of their death, worry about their will, thinking about those they leave here, how much more should they worry about their soul! Man thinks of those he abandons and does not think of himself, who abandons everything! Your children will have what you leave; You, on the other hand, swim, and all your thoughts end up teaching the pilgrims who come after you where they should go, not where they should arrive. I wish they would think about death! When the dead are taken to bury, one thinks of her and says: "How unfortunate! So it was; yesterday he was still walking. Or: "I saw him seven days ago, he spoke

with me of this and that. "Man is nothing." They murmur all this. But perhaps, while mourning the dead, while preparing the funeral, while preparing the obsequies, while taking him out of the house, while going to the cemetery, while burying him, such words have value; But, once the dead is buried, such thoughts are also buried. The deadly worries return, they forget the one they have taken to the cemetery, and the one who also has to die thinks about who will be the successor of the other; one returns to fraud, to plunder, to perjury, to drunkenness, to the innumerable bodily pleasures that must disappear, I am not saying when they are exhausted, but rather that they perish while they are consumed. And what is even more harmful, from the grave of the dead they draw an argument to also bury the heart, and they say: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die. 6. They also laugh at the faith of those who affirm that the dead must rise again, and say to themselves: "This man is already lying in the tomb; let's hear his voice. But his voice cannot be heard; I hear the voice of my father, my grandparents or great-grandparents. Who has risen from there? Who has shown what is in hell? Let's have a good time while we live, because once we have died, even if our parents or loved ones or our relatives take gifts to our graves, they take them for themselves, who are alive, not for us, who are dead. It is clear that these meals are not for the dead and that it is a pagan custom, which does not come from the root and source of justice of our fathers the patriarchs, regarding whom we read that funerals were celebrated, but not that sacrifices were offered in their tombs. This can also be seen in the customs of the Jews. They did not maintain the fruit of their virtue, but they did preserve the old customs in certain solemnities. Some object with texts from Scripture: Break your bread, pour your wine on the tombs of the righteous and do not give it to the unrighteous. It is not necessary to talk about this; but, nevertheless, I affirm that the faithful can understand these words. The faithful know how Christians do this religiously in the memories of the saints and that it should not be shown to the unjust, that is, to the unbelievers, since the just live by faith. The faithful also know this. Let no one, therefore, seek to make medicine a wound, nor attempt to twist a rope with the Scriptures, to cast the snare of death on his soul. Let us see, then, what he had begun to say, thinking of the men who whisper these words in the ears of the weak: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die; I mean what they say: «No one has been resurrected;

I have not heard anyone's voice; "Since my grandfather, my great-great-grandfather, my father was placed there, I have not heard the voice of any of them." Answer, Christians, if you are; lest, desiring to get drunk among the people, you should be ashamed to respond to corrupters. You have to respond: but the desire for pleasure makes you fluctuate and you want to be swallowed and buried alive. The desire for wine arises and falls like a wave on the soul, moved by the breath of one who persuades evil. You are suffering a great storm, you do not want to respond to the corrupter, while at the same time you favor the one who gives you drink; but the wave of desire rises too high and wants to cover your heart as if it were a ship. Christian, Christ sleeps in your ship; wake him up; He will give order to the storms so that everything regains calm. At that time, the disciples, fluctuating in the boat while Christ slept, were a symbol of the fluctuating of Christians when their Christian faith is dormant. You see what the Apostle says: Christ dwells in our hearts through faith. According to his beautiful and divine presence, he is always with the Father; On the other hand, according to the presence of faith, it is in all Christians. That is why you fluctuate: because Christ is asleep, that is, you cannot overcome those desires that arise with the breath of those who persuade evil, because your faith is asleep. We work on earth, but our head in heaven no longer dies, nor suffers a decrease, nor suffers anything; but he suffered for us, since he was delivered for our crimes and rose again for our justification. We know this by faith; those to whom it was manifested learned it with their own eyes. We must not consider ourselves reprobate because, resurrected, we have not been able to see him with carnal eyes. We have as testimony in our favor what the Lord Himself said to the disciple who doubted and wanted to touch in order to believe. After having felt his scars, now convinced, he exclaimed and said: My Lord and my God!; to which the Lord replied: Because you have seen me you have believed; Blessed are those who do not see and believe. Awake therefore to your salvation; May no one with bad persuasion tear from your heart what Christ nailed to it. 14. Don't come to me with another question either. This is said by all those who, even against their will, have yielded to the authority of Christ. Almost no pagan, even those who do not want or defer to possess Christ by devotion, dare to deny him; Although they dare to deny it in Christians, they do not dare to do the same with Christ; they yield to the head, but still insult the body. The body, upon hearing the insults of those who already bow before the head, should not be considered mutilated from the head, but united with it. Well, if we were disconnected from it, then we should fear the voices of those who insult us; but that we are not attests

the same one who said to Paul, still Saul, persecutor of the Church: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? He had already passed through the impious hands of the Jews, he had already entered hell, he had already risen from the dead, he had already ascended to heaven, he had already enriched and established the hearts of the faithful with the gift of the Holy Spirit while sitting at the right hand of the Father and interceding for us; He was no longer going to give himself over to death for us, but he was going to free us from it. What could Saul's cruelty do to him? How could that hand touch him, although he, as it is written, longed for death? He could attack Christians who were weary on earth, but Christ, when and how? However, he shouts out for the remaining members; but he does not say: "Why do you persecute mine?"; Well, if he had said that, we would believe ourselves to be servants. But servants are not as united to their master as Christians are to Christ. It is a different kind of union, the order of the members is different and the unity of love is different. The head speaks in favor of its members, but it does not even say: "Why are you persecuting my members?", but: Why are you persecuting me? It did not touch the head, but it touched what is attached to the head. I have already said it many times; But since the similarity fits perfectly and clarifies the subject well, I am going to repeat it. Whoever steps on you in the middle of a crowd steps on your foot, but does nothing on your tongue. What does it mean then when the tongue shouts: "You are treading on me!" »? The stomp is received by the foot and not by the tongue.

Awaken, then, your faith, and to anyone who tells you: "Only Christ could rise, we cannot," respond and say: "Christ was able because he was God, he was resurrected because he was God. Because he was God, that is, because he was omnipotent; And if he is omnipotent, why should I lose hope that he can also do in me what he showed in himself for my sake? Then I ask where Christ was resurrected from. He will answer: "From the dead." I keep asking why he died. Can God die? Could that divinity die, that is, the Word equal to the Father, the art of the almighty craftsman by whom all things were made; the immutable wisdom, which remains in itself and renews everything, which extends powerfully from one end to the other and arranges everything gently? "No," he says. And yet Christ died. How could he die? For he did not consider it a plunder to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. But what did he say beforehand? Who existing in the form of God. Had he received that form of God or was it natural to him? The Apostle distinguishes well. When speaking of the form of God, he uses the verb to be; while, when referring to the servant form, he uses receive. Therefore, Christ was one thing and received another, to be one thing with the other. In the form of God he was equal to God, as the fisherman evangelist says: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; that is to say: Who, existing in the form of God, did not consider it a plunder to be

equal to God. Theft occurs when what is not natural to one is unlawfully usurped. The angel usurped equality with God: he fell and became a devil; man usurped equality with God: he fell and became mortal. Christ, however, who was born equal, since he was not born in time, but as the everlasting son of the everlasting Father, born from everlasting, he, by whom all things were made, existed in the form of God. But to be a mediator between God and men, between the just and the unjust, between the immortal and mortals, he assumed something from the unjust and mortals, preserving something in common with the just and immortal. In common with the just and immortal he preserved justice; of the unjust and mortals he assumed mortality, placing himself in the middle as a reconciler, breaking down the wall of our sins. That is why his people sing to him: And in my God I will cross the wall, returning to God what sins had alienated from him and redeeming with his blood what the devil possessed; He died for us and for us he rose again. He bore our sins, not adhering to them, but carrying them, in the same way that Jacob carried the goat skin to appear hirsute before the father, who was going to bless him. Esau, who was bad, had hair of his own; Good old Jacob, on the other hand, was burdened with those of others. He carried other people's sins and was not punished for his own. Mortality is the punishment of sin for all men; It comes from the sin of origin from which we all come; of the fall of Adam, not the descent of Christ. Indeed, it is one thing to fall and another to descend. That one fell because of evil and this one fell because of mercy. For as all die in Adam, so all are made alive in Christ. By bearing the sins of others, he then returned what he had not stolen, that is, he died without having sin. Behold, he said, the prince of this world will come and find nothing in me. What does nothing mean will find in me? You will find nothing in me that deserves death, because what makes me deserve death is sin. Why then do you die? He continues saying: So that everyone knows that I am fulfilling my Father's will, get up, let's get out of here. And getting up he headed towards passion. Because? Because he fulfilled his Father's will, not because he owed anything to the prince of sin, the one in whom there was no sin. Thus, our Lord Jesus Christ brought his divinity with him, but mortality took it from us. He received it in the womb of the Virgin Mary, uniting himself, the Word of God, to human nature, as a husband to the wife in the virginal bed, to emerge as a husband from her bed.

Illi enim dicunt: Manducemus et bibamus; eras enim morimur (Wis 2,6), qui resurrectionem non sperant: nos autem qui iam resurrectionem et loquentibus Prophetis, et praedicante Christo et Apostolis credimus et annuntiamus, qui speramus nos post ístam mortem victuros, non deficiamus, nec corda nostra oneremus crápula et ebrietatibus; sed solliciti expectantes, accincti lumbis et luzernis ardentibus, adventum Domini nostri, ieiunemus et oremus, non ideo quia eras moriemur, sed ut securi moriamur. Quod restat ergo, fratres, in nomine Domini alio tempore a nobis demande. Conversi ad Dominum, etc.
The resurrection of the dead
Topic: The resurrection of the dead. Location: Unknown. Date: Winter of the year 410 to 411.

1. Remembering my promise, I had the appropriate texts of the Gospel and the Apostle read. Those of you who attended the previous sermon remember that the topic of the resurrection was proposed, which was then divided into two different questions: first, in response to those who doubt or even deny it, the existence or not of the future resurrection of the dead would be discussed; Then, as far as possible, one would examine, in accordance with the Scriptures, what the life of the righteous would be like in the future resurrection. I spent so much time on the first part, in which I dealt with the fact of the resurrection of the dead - you well remember this - that there was no time to consider the second question, and I was forced to postpone it until the present day. Your attention is asking me to pay this debt, and I recognize that the time is right. Together and with the pious gaze of our hearts, let us beseech the Lord so that I may fulfill my debt in the most convenient way and that you may receive it for the benefit of your salvation. It must be recognized that this question is more difficult; but love is stronger than any difficult question; love SERMO
DE RESURRECTIONE MORTUORUM, II

CAPUT I.—1. Dicendum qualisfutura sit iustorum resurrectio.—In memoria retinentes pollicitationem nostram, congruas etiam ex Evangelio et Apostólo fecimus recitan lectiones. Quicumque enim vestrum praeterito sermoni adfuerunt, remembering nobiscum propositam de resurrectione quaestionem in geminam disputationem a nobis distributam: ut primo dissereremus, propter eos qui dubitant, vel etiam qui negant, utrumfutura sit resurrectio mortuorum; Postea vero, quantum possumus, secundum Scripturas quaereremus, qualis in resurrectionefutura sit vita iustorum. In prima ergo parte ubi tractavimus quod resurgant mortui, tam diu sumus immorati, sicut meminisse dignmini, ut secundae quaestioni tractandae [1612] tempus deficeret, atque ita eam in hunc diem differre cogeremur. Hoc ergo a nobis debitum vestra poscit intentio, et nos reddendi tempus agnoscimus. CAPUT II.—Parker ergo pia cordis intentione Dominum deprecemur, ut et nos opportune solvamus debitum, et vos salubriter recipiatis. Est enim haec, quod fatendum est, maior quaestio: sed omnibus quaestioni-

whom we must all serve, so that God, who commanded us, transforms all our difficulties into ease and joy. 2. You remember that the other day I responded to some who say: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die. The Apostle already argued with them, adding: They corrupt good customs with their evil words, and concluding thus: Be sober and just and do not sin, for some have ignorance of God; I say it for your interest. Judge the works, if all of us together and each one in particular have heard these words of the Apostle and have sent them to our hearts. Whoever listens to them is like a field that receives the sower's seed; The one who sends them to the heart is like the one who breaks the clods and covers the seed; Whoever fulfills what he heard and sent to his heart, that is the one who becomes a harvest and bears fruit with tolerance: one thirty, another sixty and another one hundred. To him is reserved not the fire, as if it were straw, but the granary, as if it were grain. In these hidden granaries the perpetual happiness of the just will be found hidden in the resurrection of the dead; barns into which the Scripture itself indicates that they are to be gathered. 3. In another place he mentioned them under the name of baskets, when Jesus Christ the Lord said that the kingdom of heaven bus difficilibus fortior est caritas, cui omnes serve debenmus, ut Deus qui hoc praecepit, omnes nostras difficultates in facilitatem gaudiumque convertat. 2. idem tractatur argumentum.—Meministis esse a nobis illo die responsum quibusdam dicetibus, sicut Apostolus eos arguit: Manducemus et bibamus; eras enim morimur: subiungens et dices: Corrumpunt bonds mores bad colloquia; atque ita concludens: Sobrii estofe, iusti, et nolite peccare: ignorantiam enim Dei quídam habent; ad reverentiam vobis loquor (1 Cor 15:32-34). Haec verba apostolica omnes audierimus, et cordi mandaverimus: et quisquís audierit, et cordi mandaverit, opera indicent. Qui audit enim, tanquam ager est semen excipiens seminantis: qui autem cordi mandat, similis est glebam frangenti, et quod seminatum est opeienti: qui autem secundum id quod audivit et cordi mandavit operatur, ipse est qui surgit in messem, et fructum affert cum tolerantia, aliud tricenum, aliud sexagenum, aliud centenum (cf. Mt 13,23, et Le 8,15). Huic non ignis velut paleae, sed horrea sicut frumento praeparantur.

CAPUT III.—In ipsis ergo abditis horrières, in resurrectione mortuorum beatitudo est illa perpetua etiam ipsa secreta iustorum, quo eos recipiendos Scriptura commendat. 3. Vasculorum nomine beatorum secretae sedes significatae. Absconditum vultus Dei.—Vasorum etiam nomine alio loco commemoravit, quando ait Dominus Iesus Christus, simile esse regnum caelorum sa-

It was like a trawl net': The kingdom of heaven is like a net thrown into the sea, which gathers fish of every kind; When it is full, they take it out, and, sitting on the shore, they select them, throwing the good ones into the baskets, and the bad ones outside. Our Lord meant that now the word of God is cast over the people and nations in the same way as a net over the sea. Through the Christian sacraments, it collects good and bad, but not all of those that the net pulls out are kept in the baskets. The baskets are the abode of the saints and the great hiding places of a happy life, where they cannot reach for the simple fact of calling themselves Christians, unless, in addition to being called, they are one. Even inside the net, both good and bad fish swim; but the good tolerate the bad until they are separated at the end. It was also said in a certain place: You will hide them in the hiding place of your face, speaking of the saints. You will hide them, he said, in the hiding place of your face, that is, where the eyes of men and the thoughts of mortals cannot follow. To signify some secret places, too hidden and hidden, he spoke of the hiding place of the face of God. Should we think, in a carnal way, that God has an enormous face and that in it there is some bodily hiding place in which the saints must hide? You see, brothers, how carnal this way of speaking is and how the hearts of all the faithful must reject it.

What should be understood under the hiding of the face of God but what is only known to his gaze? When granaries and, in another place, baskets are spoken of to signify secret things, it is neither the granaries nor the baskets that we know; Well, if it were one of the two things, it would no longer be said that it was the other. But since the unknown is made knowable to men, as far as possible, through similarities, consider that it has been named in two ways, so that by the name of barns and baskets you understand that it is something secret. And, if you want to find out what secret, listen to the prophet who says: You will hide them in the hiding place of your face. 4. Things being this way, brothers, we are still pilgrims in this life, we still sigh, through faith, for that I don't know what country. And why do I speak of I don't know what country, despite being citizens of it, but because, traveling far away, we have forgotten it, to the point of being able to speak as I have done? This forgetfulness is expelled from the heart by Christ the Lord, the king of the same country, coming to meet the pilgrims; taking the flesh, his divinity becomes for us a path so that we may walk through Christ the man and remain in Christ God. What to say, brothers? With what words should I explain to you or with what eye should we see that secret that neither eye has seen, nor ear has heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man? Sometimes we can know something, without, however, being able to express it; what I don't know

genae, id est, retibus; retía enim quaedam sagena appellantur. Simile ergo est, inquit, regnum caelorutn sagenae missae in mare, et ex omnl genere congregante: quae cum impleta esset, edúcenles, et secus littus sepantes, elegerunt bonds in vasa, malas autem joras miserunt (Mt 13, 47-48). Significare voluit Dominus noster moda sic mitti verbum Dei super populos et super gentes, quomodo sagena in mare iacitur. Colligit autem moda sacramentis christianis et bonds et malo-, sed non omnes quos sagena tollit, etiam vasculis reconduntur. Vascula enim sunt sanctorum sedes, et beatae vitae magna secreta, quo non potemnt omnes pervenire quicumque christiani appellantur, sed qui sic appellantur, ut sint. Sane autem boni et malí pisces intra sagenam natant, et boni tolerant mals, doñee in fine separentur. Dictum est etiam quodam loco: Abscondes eos in abscondito vultus tui (Ps 30,21); loquebatur enim de sanctis. Abscondes eos, inquit, in abscondito vultus tui: id est, quo non possunt sequi oculi hominum, ñeque cogitationes mortalium; secret quaedam significans nimis abscondita nimis oceulta, in abscondito vultus Dei [1613] dixit. Numquid carnaliter cogitandum est habere Deum quamdam faciem grandem, et in facie eius esse aliquod receptaculum corporale, ubi sancti abscondendi sunt? Haec videtis, fratres, quemadmodum carnalia sint, et ab omnium fidelium corde respuende. Absi Agustín uses two Latin terms: sagena and retís, which in Spanish do not need to be maintained.

Cum ergo dicuntur horrea, ut significantur secreta, et alio loco dicuntur vascula; ñeque horrea sunt quae novimus, ñeque vascula. Nam si aliquid unum tale esset, alterum aliquid non diceretur. Sed quia persimilarities hominibus notes, ut possunt, insinuantur incógnita, ad hoc utrumque nominatum accipite, ut secretum ¡ntellegatis, et horrei nomine et vasculorum. Ad patriam fide suspiramus.—Quae cum ita sint, fratres, in hac adhuc vita peregrinamur, adhuc in illam nescio quam patriam fide suspiramus. Et quare nescio quam, unde cives sumus, nisi quia in longinqua peregrinando obliti eam sumus, ut patriam nostram possimus dicere nescio quam? Hanc oblivionem expellit de corde Dominus Christus, rex ipsius patriae, veniens ad peregrinos; et susceptione carnis divinitas eius fit nobis via, ut per hominem Christum pergamus, et in Deo Christo maneamus. Quid ergo, brothers? secretum illud, quod nec oculus vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit (cf. 1 Cor 2:9), quo eloquio vobis explicaturi sumus, aut quo oculo nos visuri? Possumus aliquid aliquando nosse, quod eloqui tamen non possumus:

We know, sometimes we can't talk about it. If it is possible that, even though I know something, I am unable to explain it to you, how much more difficult will it be for me to speak, if I also, brothers, walk with you in faith and not in vision! This is for me. What to say about the Apostle? He consoles our ignorance and builds our faith by stating: Brothers, I do not think I have achieved it. But I pursue only one thing: forgetting what is behind and in tension towards what is ahead, I pursue the palm of the supreme vocation; words with which he shows that he is still on the path. And in another place it says: While we live in this body we are pilgrims far from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by vision. And also: In hope we have been saved. The hope that is seen is not hope, because what one sees, how do you expect it? But, if we wait for what we do not see, through patience we wait for it. 5. Therefore, brothers, hear from my mouth the cry that is already in the psalms; pious, humble, meek cry; not conceited, nor boisterous, nor hasty, nor rash. The psalm says in a certain place: I believed, and therefore I spoke. And the Apostle, after having mentioned this testimony, added: We also believe, and that is why we speak. So do you want me to tell you what I know personally? I am not deceiving you; listen to what I have believed. Do not think it is despicable because you are going to hear what I have believed, because you are hearing a confession

truthful On the other hand, if I said: "Listen to what I know," you would hear a reckless presumption. Therefore, brothers, although all of us, and, since we give faith to the sacred Scriptures, also all those who lived in the flesh before us, through whom the Holy Spirit spoke and distributed to men what they needed as pilgrims; Although we all speak about what we believe, the Lord, on the other hand, spoke about what he knew. What can I say if only the Lord could know what he said regarding eternal life, and all those who followed him spoke because they believed? But we still find that Jesus Christ our Lord himself had something to say, but he said nothing about it. In a certain place he said to his disciples: I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. He deferred telling them what he knew because of his weakness, not because he personally had difficulty. We, on the other hand, due to our common weakness, do not try to explain with sufficient dignity what we know, but rather we explain as we can what we worthily believe; You, understand if you can. And if any of you can understand anything more than what I can say, do not focus on the smallness of the stream, but run to the abundant fountain, because in it is the fountain of life, in whose light we will see the light. 6. That there is a resurrection of the dead, I have already treated; This is how we believe it, this is how we should believe it, and this is how we speak, because this is how we have believed, if we are Christians, by con-

quod autem non novimus, aliquando eloqui non valemus. Cum ergo fieri possit ut si ego illa nossem, eloqui ea vobis non possem; quanto difficilius eloquium meum erit, quando et ego, fratres, vobiscum per fidem ambulo, nondum per speciem? Sed hoc ego, an et ipse Apostolus? Nam consolatur ignorantiam nostram, et aedificat fidem, they say: Fratres, ego me non arbitror apprehendisse. Unum autem, quae retro oblitus, in ea quae ante sunt extentus, secundum intentionem sequor ad palmam supernae vocationis (Phil 3:13-14); where it was demonstrated in via esse. Et alio loco: Quamdiu sumus, inquit, in corpore, peregrinamur a Domino: per fidem enim ambulamus, non per speciem (2 Cor 5,6-7). Et iterum: Spe enim, inquit, salvi facti sumus. Spes autem quae videtur, non est spes: quod enim videt quis, quid sperat? Si autem quod non videmus speramus, per patientiam exspectamus (Rom #,24-25). CAPOT V.—5. Ecclesia docet quod credidit, non quod novit.—Sic ergo, fratres, audite a me vocem quae est in Psalmis, piam, humilem, mansuetam, non elatam, non turbulentam, non praecipitem, non recklessm. Ait enim quodam in loco Psalmus: Credidi, propter quod locutus sum (Ps 115,10). Et interposuit hoc testimonium Apostolus, atque subiecit: Et nos credimus, propter quod et loquimur (2 Cor 4,13). Vultis ergo ea tell me what new life? Non vos falla, au [1614] díte quod credidi. Non vobis vilescat, quia quod credidi auditis: auditis efim veracem con-

fessionem. Si autem dicerem: Audite quod novi; audiretis recklessm praesumptionem. Si ergo, fratres, omnes nos, et, ut credimus sanctorum litteris, omnes etiam qui ante nos in carne vixerunt, et per quos loquens Spiritus Dei distribuit hominibus tantum quantum satis esset significan peregrinantibus, omnes quod credimus loquimur: Dominus autem ipse, quae noverat. Quid igitur, si solus Dominus de vita in aeternumfutura nosse poterat quod dicebat; there I see sequences Dominum, ideo quia crediderunt? Invenimus ipsum Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, scientem quid loqueretur, non dicentem tamen. Ait enim quodam in loco discipulis suis: Adhuc plana drooling vobis dicere; sed non potestis illa portare moda (lo 16,12). lile propter illorum infirmitatem, non propter suam difficultatem, quod noverat dicere differebat. Nos autem propter communem omnium nostrum infirmitatem, non quod novimus satis digne eloqui conamur, sed quae digne credimus, ut possumus, explicamus; et vos capite ut potestis. Et si amplius forte capere aliquis vestrum potest, quam ego dicere; non attendat ad exiguum rivum, sed currat ad uberrimum fontem: quoniam apud eum est fons vitae, in cuius lumine videbimus lumen (cf. Ps 35,10). CAPUT VI.—6. Cbristiano de resurrectione dubitare non licet.— Quia ergo est resurrectio disputavimus, sic credimus, sic credere debenmus, sic loquimur, quia sic credidimus, si christiani sumus, intuentes

temper the power of the arm of the Lord, which humiliates the pride of people everywhere and builds this faith throughout the world as widely as it had been promised before it became a reality. Seeing this, we are encouraged to believe what we have not yet seen in order to receive the vision itself as the reward of faith. Since it is, therefore, evident to our faith that the resurrection of the dead exists, and so evident that anyone who doubts it commits great imprudence by calling himself a Christian, the question concerns the body that the saints will have and what their future life will be like. Indeed, it seemed to many that the resurrection would exist, yes, but only for souls. 7. That bodies will also be resurrected, there is no need to discuss it again after the sermon the other day. But the following question is asked as an objection: «If bodies are going to exist in the future, what will they be like? Like the current ones or different? If different, how? If they are the same as the current ones, will they be assigned to the same functions? That they will not have the same functions, the Lord indicates; that neither will they be alike, the Apostle. They will not be destined for the same life or for the same mortal, corruptible, perishable and passing deeds, nor for carnal joys, nor for the consolations of the flesh. And, if they are not intended for the same things, neither for other similar things. And, if neither to other similar ones, how then is the flesh resurrected? We find the resurrection of the body in the rule of faith and we confess it when we are baptized. Everything we profess in it, we profess from the truth

and in the truth in which we live, move and exist. Through temporary gestures and some transitory and passing events, we are indoctrinated about eternal life. Everything that took place so that we could hear something that was healthy for us, so that miracles were performed, so that our Lord was born, suffered hunger and thirst, was captured, mocked, scourged, crucified; for him to die, be buried, rise again and ascend to heaven, all that happened. When all these facts are preached, certain temporal and transitory facts of our faith are preached. Because they pass, is what built through them going to pass in the same way? Pay attention, your holiness, to see it through an example. An architect uses temporary scaffolding to build a house that must remain. Also to build this large and spacious building that we are seeing, scaffolding was needed that now no longer exists, since what was built thanks to them is already firm. Likewise, brothers, when the Christian faith was being built it was necessary to build some temporary scaffolding. Referring to our Lord Jesus Christ, his resurrection was a temporary action, since he is not yet resurrecting; His ascension to heaven was also fleeting, since he is not yet ascending. On the other hand, what exists in that life in which he no longer dies and in which death no longer has dominion over him; the same living forever even in the human nature that he deigned to take, and in which he wanted to be born, die and be buried, is the building that has been

potentiam brachii Domini sternentis usquequaque superbiam gentium, et aedificantis hanc fidem tam late per orbem terrarum, quam promissum est multo antequam ièret: haec intuentes, aedificamur ad credendum ea quae nondum videmus, ut ipsam visionem mercedem fidei recipiamus. Cum ergo manífestum sit fidei nostrae future resurrectionem mortuorum, et ita manifestum, ut hinc quisquís dubitaverit, impudentissime se dicat christianum; quaeritur qualia corpora habebunt sancti, et quae vita eorumfutura sit. Multis enim visum est resurrectionem quidem fieri, sed per solas animas. CAPUT VII.—7. Quaestio, qualiafutura sintcorpora. Regula fidei, symbolum. Apta úmilitudo.—Quia vero resurgunt et corpora, non opus est diu disserere post sermonem praeteritum. Sed obicitur huiusmodi quaestio: Si corpora Futura sunt, qualia Futura sunt? Talia qualia nunc sunt, an alterius modi? Si alterius modi, quis ille modus? If talia, ergo ad eadem opera? Quia ergo non ad eadem praescribit Dominus, quia non ad talia docet Apostolus. Nam non ad eamdem vitam, non ad eadem facta mortalia et corruptibilia et peritura atque transeuntia, non ad carnalia gaudia, non ad carnales consolationes. Si ergo non ad eadem, nec talia. If not, how does expensive resurface? Carnis autem resurrectionem habemus in regula fidei, et eam confitentes baptizamur. Et quidquid ibi confitemur, ex veritate et in veritate confitemur, in qua vivimus

et movemur et sumus. Temporalibus enim [1615] gestis et transeuntibus quibusdam ac praetereuntibus factis instruimur ad vitam aeternam. Omnia quae gesta sunt, ut salubre aliquid audiremus, ut miracula ieront, ut Dominus noster nasceretur, esuriret et sitiret, comprehenderetur, contumeliis afficeretur, vapularet, crucifigeretur, moreretur, sepeliretur, resurgeret, in caelum ascenderet, omnia transierunt; et cum praedicantur, fidei nostrae actions quaedam temporal et transitoriae praedicantur. Numquid quia ipsae transeunt, quod per eas aedificatur similiter transit? Intendant enim Sanctitas vestra, ut videatis hoc per similarityinem. Architectus aedificat per machinas transituras domum mansuram. Nam in isto tam magno et ampio, quod videmus, aedificio, cum instrueretur, machinae fuerunt, quae hicmo non sunt; quia quod per eas aedificabatur, iam perfectum stat. Sic ergo, fratres, aedificabatur aliquid in fide christiana, et perfection sunt quaedam machinamenta temporalia. Dominus enim noster Iesus Christus quod resurrexit, transactum est; ñeque enim adhuc resurgit: et quod ascendit in caelum, transactum est; ñeque enim adhuc ascendit. Quod autem in illa vita est, ubi iam non moritur et mors ei ultra non dominabitur (cf. Rom 6,9); quod vivit in aeternum etiam ipsa in illo natura humano, quam suscipere, et in qua nasci, et in qua mori et sepeliri dignitatus est, hoc aedificatum est, hoc semper manet.

risen and remains forever. The scaffolding by which it was raised disappeared, since it is not always being conceived in the womb of a virgin or it is always being captured, judged, scourged, crucified and buried. All this is considered as if they were scaffolding, to build with them what remains forever. The resurrection, however, of our Lord Jesus Christ is placed in heaven. 8. Consider your charity this admirable building. The earthly buildings press down on the earth with their weight, and all the gravitational force of this gigantic structure falls on it, and, if it is not supported, it tends lower, where its own weight takes it. And since it is built on the earth, the foundations are first laid on it, to raise the building on a sure foundation. For this purpose, very solid masses capable of supporting the weight placed on top of them are placed at the bottom and the solidity of the foundations is adjusted to the magnitude of the building; but always on the earth, as I said, because what is built is also built on the earth. That 'our pilgrim Jerusalem is built in heaven. For that reason Christ preceded us there, to be the foundation of it; There is our foundation and the head of the Church, since the foundation is also called the head, and that is how it is in reality. The foundation of the building is also its head, since the head is not that in which something ends, but rather that from which it rises upward. In terrestrial buildings, the summit goes up, while they have

his head in the solidity of the earth. Likewise, the head of the Church preceded us to heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father. When making the foundations, men try to put something that gives solidity below, for security of the future mass as the building is built; Likewise, through the things that happened in Christ—being born, growing up, being captured, being mocked, being scourged, crucified, dying, and being buried—it was as if the mass was dragged to form the heavenly foundation. 9. Therefore, since our foundation is on high, let us build on it. Listen to the Apostle: No one can lay another foundation than the one that is laid, which is Christ Jesus. But how does it continue? Let each one see what he builds on that foundation: gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw. Christ is certainly in heaven, but also in the hearts of believers. If Christ occupies the first place, he is undoubtedly placed as the foundation. Therefore, he who builds can build in peace if, in accordance with the dignity of the foundation, he raises gold, silver or precious stones. But, if you do not build what deserves such a foundation, that is, if you raise wood, hay or straw, at least preserve the foundation, and, because of those arid and fragile things that you raised, prepare for the fire. If the foundation is maintained, that is, if Christ obtained the first place in the heart, the goods

Aedificium caelestis Ierusalem habet fundamentum sursum. Christus et fundamentum nostrum, et caput.—Attendat Caritas vestra aedificium mirabíle. Aedificia quippe ista terrena pondere suo terram premuní, totusque nutus ponderum in this structura magnitudeine ad terram nititur, et nisi contineatur, ad inferiora contendit, quo pondus adducit. Quia ergo in terra aedificatur, in terra fundamentum praemittitur; ut supra fundamentum securus instruat qui aedificat. Ergo ponit in imo firmissimas moles, ut idonee possint portare desuper quod imponitur, et pro magnitudeine aedificii magnitudeo fundamenti praeparatur: in terra tamen, ut dixi, quia et illud quod aedificatur supra, utique in terra collocatur. Ierusalem illa nostra peregrina in cáelo aedificatur. Ideo praecessit fundamentum Christus in caelum. Ibi enim fundamentum nostrum est et caput Ecclesiae: nam et fundamentum dicitur et caput, et revera ita est. Quia et caput aedificii fundamentum est: non enim caput est quod finitur, sed unde incipit sursum versus. Terrenorum aedificio-

rum culminates subriguntur, caput tamen in terrae soliditate constituunt. Sic et caput Ecclesiae praecessit in caelum, et sedet ad dexteram Patris. Quomodo operantur homines, ut ad [1616] constituendum fundamentum aliquid trahant quod in imo stabiliant, propter securitatem superventurae molis in constructionibus fabricae futuree: sic per omnia illa quae contigerunt in Christo, nasci, crescere, comprehendi, contumeliam pati, flagellari, crucifigi, occidi, mori, sepeliri, velut attracta est moles ad fundamentum caeleste. 9. Agendum ut in Christo aedificemur. Christus fundamentum est, si primum in corde locum obtineat. Ignis gehennae quam timendus.— Pósito ergo in summis fundamental nostro, aedificemur in eo. Audi Apostolum: Fundamentum, inquit, aliud nemo potest seguiré, praeter id quod positum est, quod est Christus Iesus (1 Cor 3:11). CAPUT IX.—Sed quid sequitur? Unusquisque autem videat quid superaedificet super fundamentum, aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos, ligna, fenum, stipulam (ib., 10.12). In cáelo quidem Christus est, sed etiam in corde credentium. Si primum locum habet Christus, recte positum est fundamentum. Ergo qui aedificat, securus aedificet, si pro dignitate fundamenti aedificat aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos. Si autem non pro dignitate fundamenti aedificat, lignum, fenum, stipulam, saltem teneat fundamentum, et propter illa quae exstruxit arida et fragilia, ad ignem se praeparet. Be si fundamentalum est, id est, si primum locum in corde Christus obtinuit, saecularia vero sic amantur, ut non Christo

worldly people love each other without putting them before Christ; On the contrary, putting them before Christ so that he continues to be the foundation of the building of the heart, that is, occupying the first place, he will suffer damage, he said, but he will be saved, as by fire. Now is not the time to exhort you to build on such a great and solid foundation gold, silver and precious stones instead of wood, hay and straw; but, although said briefly, receive it as if it had been explained for a long time and with an abundance of words. I know, in fact, brothers, that all of you, if any judge threatens to send you to prison and suffer only the torment of smoke because of the goods that you love here, you would rather lose them than suffer that place. I don't know why, when it is indicated that there will be smoke on the day of judgment, everyone despises it and, despite fearing the flames of fire, they do not give importance to the flames of hell. How hard is this? Where does such great perversity of heart come from? If men at least feared what the Apostle says: by fire, as everyone fears being burned alive, which lasts for a few brief moments, until sensitivity abandons the members and makes all flames superfluous, they would fear and would not do anything prohibited by law so as not to come to the torment of a brief moment. 10. But, as I said, brothers, now is not the time to talk about this matter. What I am saying is that we must expect in the resurrection of the dead what was manifested in our head, what was manifested in the body of praeponantur, sed eis Dominus Christus, ut sit in aedificio cordis tenens fundamentum, id est, primum locum: detrimentum, inquit, patietur; ipse autem salvus erit, sic tamen quasi per ignem (ib., 15). Non est nunc tempus hortari vos, ut potius aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos aedificetis, quam lignum, fenum, stipulam, super tam magnum et validum fundamentum: sed tamen breviter dictum sic accipite, quasi diu et multis verbis dictum. Novimus enim, fratres, quia quisquís vestrum propter illa quae moda diligit, per comminationes alicuius iudicis in carcerem mitteretur, ut solum fumum pateretur, illa omnia mallet amittere, quam locum illum pati. Nescio quo autem moda cum ignis nominatur in die iudicii futurus, omnes contemnunt, et flammas foci timentes, flammam gehennae pro nihilo ducunt. What is this hard time? What are so many perversitas cordis?

Si vel sic timerent nomines quod ait Apostolus, per ignem, quomodo timet quisque ne vivus ardeat, quod illi uno momento contingit, doñee sensus membra desetens omnes illas flammas superfluas facit; timeret tamen, et non facetet aliquid quod iure prohibetur, ne ad illum cruciatum momenti unius perveniret. CAPUT X.—10. Resurrectio talis speranda qualis in Christo praecessit. Angelí apud Abraham veré manducarunt.—Sed, ut dixi, fratres, nunc de hac re spatium non est disserendi: illud dico, hoc nos sperare debené in resurrectione mortuorum, quod expressum est in capite nostro, quod
The resurrection of the dead

our Lord Jesus Christ. Whoever expects anything else no longer builds on the foundation; I'm not saying gold, silver or precious stones; not even straw. He builds everything outside, because he builds it outside of Christ. Our Lord Jesus Christ was resurrected in the same body in which he was buried. Christians are promised the resurrection. We await the resurrection as it preceded in our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the faith of all of us. That's why he came ahead: to build our faith on him. What to say then? Why should we not be such as we are now? The flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ was resurrected, but ascended to heaven. On earth he maintained his human functions as a means of persuasion that he had resurrected the previously buried body. Is there also such food in heaven? We also read that angels have fulfilled human functions on earth. They went to Abraham's house and ate; An angel also accompanied Tobias, who ate. What should we say? That eating was a simulation and not a real event? Is it not evident that Abraham killed a calf, kneaded bread and put it on the table, served the angels, and they ate? All these things have been evidently done and very clearly written. 11. And what does the angel say in the book of Tobias? You saw me eat, but you saw me with your eyes. Did he say this because he was not eating, but pretending to eat? On the contrary, he really ate. What does it mean then: You saw me with your eyes? expressum is in corpore Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Quisquís alíud sperat, iam non aedificat super fundamentum, non solum aurum, argentum et lapides pretiosos, sed nec ipsam [1617] stipulam. Extra enim ponit totum, quia non in Christo ponit. Resurrexit ergo Dominus noster in eo corpore, in quo sepultos est. Resurrectio promittitur Christianis. Talem resurrectionem speremus, qualis in Domino nostro praecessit omnium nostrum fidem. Ad hoc enim praevenit, ut fides nostra superedificetur. Quid igitur? What non such, what never sumus? Caro enim Domini nostri Iesu Christi resurrexit, sed ascendit in caelum. In terra officia humano servavit, ut persuaderet hoc resurrexisse quod sepultum erat. Numquid autem et in cáelo talis cibus est? Nam et Angelos oficia humano in terra legimus exsecutos. Venerunt ad Abraham, et manducaverunt; et cum Tobia angelus Fuit, et manducavit. Quid dicimus, quia phantasma erat illa manducatio, et non erat vera?

Nonne manifestum est, quod vitulum occidit Abraham, panes fecit, et ad mensam posuit; ministravit angelis, et manducaverunt? (cf. Gen 18:1-9). Omnia is manifestissime face et manifestissime expressa sunt. CAPUT XI.—11. Homo ex necessitate manducat, angelus ex potestate.—Quid ergo dicit in libro Tobiae angelus? Vidistis me manducare, sed visu vestro videbatis (Tob 12,19). Numquid quia non manducabat, sed manducare videbatur? Immo vero manducabat. Quid est ergo, visu vestro videbatis? Intendat Sanctitas vestra quod dico: intendat in oratio-

Your holiness pay attention to what I say; Pay more attention to the prayer than to me, so that you understand what I am going to say and so that I can say it in the way that is convenient for you to hear and understand what you hear. Our body, while it is corruptible and subject to death, suffers the need to replenish itself, which is why hunger exists; That is why we feel hunger and thirst, and if we delay satisfying them for longer than the body can endure, it leads to skeletal weakness and a certain sickly thinness, which causes our strength to disappear and not be recovered; and if it continues further, even death ensues. In fact, something always flows from our body, as if it were a river that carries things with it, but we do not feel our strength diminishing, because we recover it through refection. What comes at once, goes away little by little; That is why our refreshment lasts a brief moment, while the forces that we have recovered with food require a longer period of time to leave us. The same thing happens with the lamp: the oil is poured in an instant, but it is consumed little by little; But, when it is almost completely consumed, the weakness of the flame, as if it were the hunger of the lamp, is a warning to us, and we immediately replace the oil, its food, so that that beauty is restored and there is light in the lamp. Identical is the case of our forces; By eating we replenish them, and they go away and abandon us in a slow but continuous flow. The same thing happens now in us: in all our actions, nem plus quam in me; ut intellegatis quod dicimus, ut et nos ita dicamus quemadmodum vos oportet audire et intellegere quod auditis. Corpus nostrum quandiu corruptibile est et moriturum, indigentiam patitur refectionis, inde et fames existit: propterea esurimus et sitimus; et si esuriem sitimque nostram distulerimus diutius quam potest corpus sustinere, perducitur ad tabificam maciem, et ad quamdam morbidam exilitatem, discedentibus viribus et non succedentibus: et si amplius fiat, mors etiam consequetur. Nam semper de corpore nostro discedit aliquid quasi quodam fluvio discessionis, sed inde non sentimus vires discedentes, quia per refectionem assumimus succedentes. Quod enim copióse accessit, paulatim discedit: propterea parvo tempore reficimus, productiore autem tempore deserunt nos vires, quae acceptae sunt cum reficeremus.

Sicut oleum in luzern, quod parvo tempore mittitur, diutius paulatimque consumitur. Cum autem prope consumptum fuerit, iam languor flammulae illius quasi fames luzernæ, admonet nos, et continuo subvenimus, ut instauretur illa species, et maneat lux in luzern, cibo suo refecta cum adicimus oleum. Sic vires nostrae, quas accipimus manducando, eunt et deserunt nos perpetua discessione, sed paulatim. Nam et idipsum nunc agitur in nobis, et in omnibus actionibus nostris, in omni etiam quiete
The resurrection of the dead

and even in our rest, what we previously received never ceases to abandon us; and, if it is completely exhausted, the man dies just as the lamp goes out. But so that it does not die, that is, so that it does not go out -—and not because the soul dies, but so that our bodily life does not go out and continue as a kind of being awake in this body—, we run and replace what has left, and that is what we call replenishing strength. Whoever talks about regaining strength, how can he restore it if he did not lose it? Therefore, because of this poverty and corruption, we all have to die, because this body is such that the death it deserves is reserved for it. This mortality is signified by the skins that Adam and Eve wore when they were expelled from paradise. The skins mean death, since they are usually stripped from dead beasts. Therefore, while we drag this weakness that is prone to fainting, although it never lacks food and replenishes its strength with it, death will not cease to be a reality. Any state of the body, according to the succession of ages, no matter how long one lives, will eventually reach the end of old age, beyond which it will find nowhere to go, except death. The lamp itself, even if you always replenish the oil, will not be able to burn indefinitely, because, if it is not extinguished due to other circumstances, the tow will run out, consuming itself in a kind of senescence. Therefore, I repeat, as long as we drag such bodies, their deficiency leads us to destitution; indigence, al nostra non cessat iré quod acceptum est: et si fuerit omnino consumptum, ita homo et moritur quomodo luzern exstinguitur. Ut autem non moriatur, id est, ut non exstinguatur, non quia moritur animo, sed ut corporalis haec vita nostra non exstinguatur, et quaedam quasi vigilatio in isto corpore succedat, currimus [1618] et subicimus quod reccesit, et reficere dicimur. Quid reficit, quid reficit, yes nihil deficit? Per indigentiam ergo hanc et corruptionem etiam morituri sumus omnes, quia tale est hoc corpus, ut ei mors debita reservatur. Hanc enim mortalitatem significant pelles, quibus induti sunt Adam et Eva, et dimissi de paradiso (cf. Gen 3,21-24). Pelles enim mortem indicat, quae a mortuis pecudibus detrahi solent.

Cum ergo portamus istam defectibilem infirmitatem, cui etsi cibus nunquam desit, sed subinde reparet vires, non tamen efficit ut mors non sit future (totus enim ille status corporis per succedentes aetates, etiamsi diutius hic vivatur, veniet aliquando ad terminum senectutis, et ultra quo porrigatur non inveniet nisi mortem. Nam et luzern ipsa, etiamsi subinde semper mittas oleum, non valet semper arderé; quamdiu ergo talia corpora gerimus, ex defectu indigemus, ex indigentia esurimus, ex esurie mandu-
The resurrection of the dead

hunger, and hunger, to food. The angel, on the other hand, does not eat out of necessity. It is one thing to do something of one's own free will and another out of necessity. Man eats not to die; The angel eats to conform to mortals. In fact, if the angel does not fear death, it is not his deficiency that leads him to recovery; and if the refection is not caused by the deficiency, he does not eat out of necessity. Those who saw the angel eat believed that he ate because he was hungry. This is what it means: You saw Me with your eyes. He did not say: "You saw me eat, but I didn't really eat," but: You saw me eat, but you saw me with your eyes; That is to say, I ate to conform to you, not because I was suffering from hunger or any need, in the face of which urgency you usually eat, so when you see someone eating, you suspect that they do it out of necessity, since you measure what you see according to the meter of your custom. That means: You saw me with your eyes. 12. What should I say, my brothers? According to the Apostle, we know that Christ, risen from the dead, no longer dies and that death no longer has dominion over him. For what has died to sin has died once and for all; but what lives, lives for God. If he no longer dies and death no longer has dominion over him, let us hope to be resurrected in such a way that we always remain in that state in which we will be transformed at the moment of resurrection. There will no longer be a need to eat and drink, even if it can be done. The Lord then had a reason for it, because

Those to whom he wanted to conform and to whom he also wanted to show his scars still lived in the flesh. He who gave the blind man the eyes that he had not received in his mother's womb, did not lack the power to resurrect without the scars. If he had wanted to change the mortal need of his flesh before death so that he would not have suffered any need, he could have done so, he had it in his power, since he was God in the flesh and omnipotent Son, just as the Father is omnipotent. Indeed, even before his death he changed his flesh into whatever he wanted: while he was on the mountain with his disciples, his face shone like the sun. He did this by his power, wanting to show that he could have transformed his flesh, freeing it from all destitution, in such a way as not to die if he did not want to. I have power, he said, to give up my soul and power to take it back. Nobody takes it away from me. This great power is to be able not to die; but greater is the mercy for which he wanted to die. He did by mercy what he could not have done by his power, to lay the foundation for our resurrection; so that what he carried for us might die, since we must die, and resurrect it to immortality, so that we may hope for immortality. Therefore, it is not only written that before his death he ate and drank, but also that he felt hungry and thirsty; On the other hand, after the resurrection it is only said that he ate and drank, but not that he felt hunger or thirst, because a body that will no longer die lacks indigence, which produces corruption and causes the need for refection; yes I had,

camus. Angelus vero non ex indigentia manducat. Aliud est enim ex potestate aliquid faceré, aliud ex necessitate. Manducat homo, ne moriatur: manducat angelus, ut mortalibus congruat. Si enim mortem non timet angelus, non ex defectu reficitur: si non ex defectu reficitur, non ex indigentia manducat. Qui autem videbant angelum manducare, tanquam esurientem putabant. Hoc est quod ait: Visu vestro videbatis. Non enim dixit: Videbatis me manducare, sed non manducavi: Videbatis, inquit, me manducare, sed visu vestro videbatis (Tob 12,19); id est, ego manducabam ut vobis congruerem, non quia famem ullam aut indigentiam patiebar, qua cogente vos manducare consuevistis, et ideo quos manducare videritis, ex indigentia id fieri suspicamini, qui ex vestra consuetudine metimini quod videtis: hoc est, visu vestro videbatis. CAPUT XII.—12. Manducandi potestas post resurrectionem erit, sicut in Christo, non necessitas.—Quid ergo, fratres mei? Scimus, sicut dicit Apostolus, quia Christus resurgens ex mortuis iam non moritur, et mors ei ultra non dominabitur. Quod enim mortuus est peccato, mortuus est semel: quod autem vivit, vivit Deo (Rom 6,9-10). Si ergo ille iam non moritur, et mors ei ultra non dominabitur; sic nos resurrecturos speremus.ut in eo statu semper simus, in quem resurgendo mutabimur. Manducati autem et bibendi etiamsi potestas erit, necessitas non erit. Erat autem tune cur hoc faceret Dominus, quia erant adhuc in carne

quibus vellet congruere, quibus etiam scars ostendere voluit. Non enim qui fecit oculos caeci, quos in matris uterus non acceperat, sine cicatricibus resurgere non valebat. Qui si vellet ipsius carnis suae mortalem indigentiam ante mortem ita commutare, ut non haberet aliquam necessitatis inopiam, posset utique: in manu enim habebat, quia Deus erat in carne, et omnipotens Filius, sicut omnipotens Pater. Nam et ipsam carnem suam ante mortem mutavit in quod voluit. In monte quippe cum discipulis cum esset, sicut sol splenduit vultus eius (cf. Mt 17,2). Hoc autem potestate fecit, ostendere volens quia et [1619] ipsam carnem suam posset ab omni indigentia commutare, ut non moreretur si nollet. Potestatem, inquit, drooling ponendi animam meam, et potestatem drooling iterum sumendi eam. Nemo eam tollit a me (lo 10,18). Potestas haec magna, qua posset et non mori: sed maior mercy, qua voluit morí. Ad hoc enim fecit per misericordion, quod posset et non faceré per potestatem, ut nobis constitueret fundamentum resurrectionis: ut illud quod propter nos mortale portabat, et moreretur, quia morituri sumus; et ad immortalitatem resurgeret, ut immortalitatem speremus. Ideoque ante mortem non solum scriptum est quia manducavit et bibit, sed etiam quia esuvirit et sitivit (cf. Mt 4:22, et lo 19:28); post resurrectionem tantum quia et manducavit et bibit, non autem quia esurivit et sitivit; quia in corpore non amplius morituro non erat illa indigentia corruptioS.Ag. 26
The resurrection of the dead

instead, the power to eat. Jesus ate to accommodate others; not to relieve the need of the flesh, but to persuade them of the truth of their body. 13. Against such great evidence, some propose a question that they take from the Apostle. Note what they object to that way of presenting the issue. «The flesh, they say, will not rise again; Well, if he is resurrected, he will possess the kingdom of God; but the Apostle says very clearly: Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God. You heard it when the Apostle was read. We say that the flesh is resurrected, but the Apostle cries: Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God. So, did we preach against the Apostle or did he preach against the Gospel? The Gospel testifies with divine voice: The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. If he became flesh, he became true flesh; Well, if it is not true meat, it is not meat either. As the flesh of Mary was true, so was the flesh of Christ who took from her true. This true flesh was seized, scourged, slapped, and hanged; This true flesh died and was buried; This true flesh also rose from the dead. The testimony of the scars returns again: the eyes of the disciples see them, and the admiration still fluctuates; The hands touch it so that the soul does not doubt. It is so evident, brothers, that our Lord Jesus Christ wanted to persuade his disciples in this way who were to preach it throughout the world; to this evidence, I repeat,

The Apostle seems to oppose it when he says: Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God. 14. We could resolve this issue by covering the mouths of vain slanderers; but it will be resolved by showing how it can be answered instantly, and we will carefully consider the Apostle's words to see what they refer to. I'm going to tell you how you can answer it very easily. What does the Gospel say? That Christ was resurrected with the same body in which he was buried; that he was seen, that he was touched, that he said to the disciples, who believed that he was a spirit: Feel and see, that a spirit has neither flesh nor bones, as you see that I have. What does the Apostle say, on the contrary? Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God. I accept both things and do not consider them contrary, so as not to fight the sting myself. How can I accept both at the same time? I could answer briefly, as I said. The Apostle states: Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God. Very well said, since it is not characteristic of the flesh to possess, but to be possessed; In fact, your body does not possess anything, but it is your soul that possesses through your body, which possesses the body itself. If the flesh is resurrected in this way: to be had, not to have; to be possessed, not to possess, what is strange that flesh and blood do not possess the kingdom of God, if both will be possessed? Indeed, the flesh possesses those who are not the kingdom of God, but the kingdom of the devil, and that is why they are slaves to the pleasures of the flesh. That's why

nis, ut esset necessitas refectionis, sed erat potestas edendi. Factum est causa congruendi, non ut subveniretur inopiae carnis, sed ut suaderetur veritas corporis. CAPUT XIII.—13. Quaestio, quomodo caro et sanguis non possidebit regnum Dei.—Adversus hanc tantam evidentiam, nonnulli nobis ex Apostólo faciunt quaestionem: contra istam quippe disputationem, vide quid obiciunt. Non, inquiunt, resurget caro: si enim resurget, possidebit regnum Dei; aperte autem dicit Apostolus: Caro et sanguis regnum Dei non possidebit (1 Cor 15,50). Audistis, cum Apostolus legeretur. Dicimus carnem resurgere, et clamat Apostolus: Caro et sanguis regnum Dei non possidebit. Ergo against Apostolum praedicamus, aut ipse against Evangelium praedicavit? Evangelium divina voce testatur: Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis (lo 1,14). If caro factum est, vera caro factum est. Nam si non vera expensive, nec expensive. Sicut vera caro Mariae, vera caro Christí, quae inde suscepta est. Haec vera caro comprehensa, flagellata, colaphizata, suspensa; haec vera caro mortua, haec vera caro is buried; haec vera caro a morte etiam resurrexit. Reddunt testifies scars: vident oculi discipulorum, et adhuc fluctuat admiratio; compalpat manus, ne dubitet animus. Contra tantam evidentiam, fratres, quam hoc modo voluit Dominus noster Iesus Christus persuadere discipulis eam per orbem terrarum praedicaturis; contra hanc evidentiam pugnare vi-

detur Apostolus, you say: Caro el sanguis regnum Dei non possidebit? (1 Cor 15:50). 14. Solvitur quaestio. Frima expositio Apostoli.—Possemus hanc quaestionem ita solvere, et resistere vanis calumniatoribus: verumtamen et sic solvetur, quomodo potest cita responder, et diligentius, quod ait Apostolus, considerabimus unde sit dictum. I say ergo quomodo possimus facillime I will respond. What is Evangelium? Quod resurrexit Christus in eo corpore, quo sepultus est: quia visus, quia contrectatus est, quia discipulis ait putantibus quod spiritus est: Pálpate, et videte, quia spiritus carnem et ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere (Luke 24:39). Quid against Apostolus? Caro et sanguis, in[1620]quit, regnum Dei non possidebunt. Amplector utrumque, nec dico ista pugnantia, ne ego ipse contra stimulum pugnem. What ergo amplector utrumque? I quote, ut dixi, possem sic I will answer: Apostolus ait: Caro et sanguis regnum Dei hereditóle possidere non possunt. Recte dixit; non est enim carnis possidere, sed possideri. Non enim corpus tuum aliquid possidet, sed anima tua per corpus possidet, quae ipsum etiam corpus possidet. Si ergo sic resurgit caro, ut habeatur, non habeat; ut possideatur, non possideat: quid mirum si caro et sanguis regnum Dei non possidebit, quia utique possidebitur? Nam eos possidet caro, qui non sunt regnum Dei, sed regnum diaboli, et ideo subditi sunt voluptatibus carnis. Unde et ille
The resurrection of the dead

They carried that paralytic on his stretcher; but, after having healed him, the Lord said to him: Take up your mat and go home. Thus, once the paralysis is cured, it is he who governs his flesh and takes it wherever he wants; the flesh does not take him where he does not want; It is he who carries the body and not the body that carries him. It is evident that in the resurrection the flesh will not feel the attraction of pleasures, to lead the soul by certain softness and softness where it does not want to and is often defeated, saying: I notice another law in my members that opposes the law of my mind, and takes me captive in the law of sin that resides in my members. The paralytic is still carried on the stretcher, he is not carrying it yet. I exclaimed, then: Unhappy one! Who will free me from the body of this death? Listen to the answer: there is grace from God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Therefore, when we have risen, it will not be the flesh that carries us, but we who carry it; and, if we carry it, we will possess it, instead of being possessed by it, because, freed from the devil, we are the kingdom of God, and thus flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God. Be silent, then, those slanderers who are truly flesh and blood and cannot think anything if it is not carnal. Also of those who persevere in the same prudence of the flesh, which is why they are rightly called flesh and blood, it could be rightly said: Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God. Let the question be resolved in this way: those men who are flesh and blood - of which he also says -

Well the Apostle: Your fight is not against flesh and blood—if you do not convert to the spiritual life and do not mortify the acts of the flesh with the spirit, you will not be able to possess the kingdom of God. 15. "But what did the Apostle really say?" someone will ask. The most accurate meaning is that which is extracted from the context of the reading. So, let's listen to him, and from the broad scriptural context see what he wanted to be understood under those words. It goes like this: The first man, born from the earth, is earthly; the second man comes from heaven; As is the terrain, so are the terrestrials, and as is the celestial, so are the celestials. As we bear the image of the earthly man, so we must also bear that of the man who comes from heaven. This I say to you, brothers: flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, nor corruption incorruption. Let's look at each point in particular. The first man, he says, born of the earth, is earthly; the second man, from heaven. As is the land, so are the lands; that is, everyone must die; and as the celestial is, so are the celestials also; that is, everyone must be resurrected. If someone asks why, with regard to the second man, it was not said that he was in heaven, but that he came from heaven, even though the Lord himself took the body from the earth, since Mary certainly came from the lineage of Adam and Eve, he must understand that the earthly man was so called in attention to his earthly concupiscence and because that affection is earthly thanks to which, through the union of man and woman, men are born, who also contract original sin; The body of the Lord, on the other hand, was created from the virginal womb without such effect, although Christ took flesh from the earth, which the Holy Spirit wants to symbolize by saying: truth has sprung from the earth; and yet he is not called earthly man, but celestial, and is said to come from heaven. If this was granted by grace to his faithful until the Apostle could rightly say: Our life is in heaven, how much more reason should it be affirmed that the heavenly man himself, in whom there was never any sin, comes from heaven! Because of sin it was said to man: You are earth, and to earth you will return. Quite rightly, then,

He says that the celestial man is from heaven, whose life never left heaven, although the Son of God, also made son of man, took the body from earth, that is, the form of a servant. Indeed, nothing ascended but what descended. Although the others to whom it has been granted ascend or, rather, are elevated to heaven by his grace, he also ascends, inasmuch as they become his body, and in this sense only one ascends, since the Apostle expounds, referring to Christ and the Church, the great sacrament contained in these words: And the two will become one flesh. Therefore it is also said: Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore, no one ascends to heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the son of man who is in heaven. And he added that he is in heaven so that no one would judge that his life had departed from there when he manifested himself to men on earth through his earthly body. Therefore, as we bear the image of the earthly man, we must also bear the image of him who comes from heaven; for now, through faith, by which we have also been raised with him, so that we may also have our hearts on high, where Christ is seated at the right hand of the Father, and, consequently, we may seek and taste the things above, not those of the earth.

had said: The first man, born of the earth, is earthly; the second, from heaven. As is the earth, so are the earthly, and as the heavenly, so are the heavenly, so that we may hope that what has already taken place before in that of Christ will take place in our body. Although we do not yet have it in reality, we must retain it through faith. That is why he had added: As we bear the image of the earthly man, so we must also bear that of the one who comes from heaven. So that we would not believe that we were going to be resurrected for the same things that we did corruptibly according to the first man, he immediately added: This I say to you, brothers, that flesh and blood will not inherit the kingdom of God. He also wanted to show that he calls flesh and blood not these corporeal realities, but that under those names he means corruption, a corruption that will not exist there. The body without corruption should not properly be called flesh and blood, but rather body, without further ado. For if it is flesh, it is corruptible and mortal; If, on the contrary, it no longer dies, it is no longer corruptible; Therefore, the same reality remaining, but incorruptible, it is no longer called flesh, but body. And, if it is called flesh, it is not spoken properly, but on the basis of an external similarity. Based on that same similarity, perhaps we could speak of flesh in the angels, since they appeared to men in the form of a man, despite being a body; but not meat, since they lack corruption. Thus, since by a certain similarity, we can also call flesh the body that is no longer corrupted, the Apostle prexerat: Primus homo de terra terrenus, secundus homo, de cáelo. Qualis terrenus, tales et terreni; et qualis caelestis, tales et caeles tes (1 Cor 15,35.47.48); ut hoc speremus in nostro corpore futurum, quod in Christi corpore praecessit; atque hoc quanquam nondum reipsa percepimus, interim fide teneamus. Ideo subiunxerat: Sicut portavimus imaginem terreni, portemus et imaginem eius qui de cáelo est (ib., 49). Ne ad talia nos resurrecturos crederemus, qualia secundum primum hominem corruptibiliter agebamus, subiecit statim: Hoc autem dico, fratres, quia caro et sanguis regnum Dei hereditate possidere non possunt (ib., 50). Atque ostendere volens quid dixerit carnem et sanguinem, quia non ipsam speciem corporis, sed corruptionem significat nomine carnis et sanguinis, quae corruptio tune non erit. Corpus enim sine corruptione, non proprie dicitur caro et sanguis, sed corpus.

Si enim caro est, corruptibilis atque mortalis est: si autem iam non moritur, iam non corruptibilis; et ideo sine corruptione manente specie, non iam caro, sed corpus dicitur: et si dicitur caro, non iam proprie dicitur, sed propter quamdam speciei similarityinem. Sicut possumus forte propter eamdem similarityinem, etiam Angelorum carnem dicere, cum sicut homines apparuerunt hominibus; cum essent corpus, non caro: quia corruptionis indigentia non inerat. taking a husband, taking a wife and begetting children 2. These are works of the corruption of the flesh, not the reality of the flesh. That we must not be resurrected for such things, as I have already mentioned before, the Lord made it clear in the Gospel reading that we read recently. The Jews certainly believed in the resurrection of the body, but they thought it would be such that life then would be the same as the one they led here. Thinking in this carnal way, they could not respond to the Sadducees, who, regarding the resurrection, proposed the following question: "Whose wife will be the woman who was successively had by seven brothers, each of them wanting to raise offspring for his brother?" The Sadducees were a sect within Judaism that did not believe in the resurrection. The Jews, fluctuating and doubting, could not answer the Sadducees who proposed such a question to them, because they thought that flesh and blood could possess the kingdom of God, that is, that corruption could possess incorruption. The Truth has arrived, and the Sadducees, deceived and deceivers, question the Lord by proposing the same question. The Lord, who knew what he was saying and wanted us to believe what we did not know, answers, with the authority of his majesty, what we must believe. The Apostle expounded it to the extent that it was granted to him; We have to understand it as much as possible. What then did the Lord say to the Sadducees? You err by not knowing the Scripture or the power of

utes. In the resurrection they do not marry or take wives, nor do they begin to die, but they will be equal to the angels of God. Great is the power of God. Why don't they marry or take wives? Because they won't start dying. Every successor succeeds someone. There will be no such corruption there. And the Lord passed through all ages, from infancy to youth, because he still bore the mortality of the flesh; After being resurrected at the same age as when he was buried, are we to believe that he ages in heaven? They will be, he said, similar to the angels of God. He put to rest what the Jews suspected and refuted the slander of the Sadducees, since the Jews believed, yes, that the dead were to be resurrected, but they thought carnally regarding the works for which they were to be resurrected. They will be, he said, similar to the angels of God. You have heard what refers to the power of God; listen to it in the Scriptures too. Have you not read, concerning the resurrection, how the Lord spoke to Moses from the bush, saying: "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob"? He is not a God of the dead, but of the living. 19.
