learned, but that the same only Son of God, equal to the Father, who sits at his right as your advisor, your own judge, will teach you the few words that any person, however ignorant, can retain and repeat; In them, by their will, lies your cause; He taught you the heavenly right, how you should pray. But perhaps you will answer: "For whom should I ask: for myself or for others?" The one who taught you to pray is the one who prays for you, since you were guilty. Jump for joy, because then it will be your judge who is now your lawyer. Since you will have to pray and plead your cause with few words, you must arrive at those: Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. God tells you: «What do you give me in exchange for me forgiving you all your sins? What gift do you offer me, what sacrifice of your conscience do you place on my altar? Next he has taught you what you have to ask for and what you have to offer him. You ask: Forgive us our debts; but what do you offer him? Just as we forgive our debtors. You are indebted to him who cannot be deceived; but you are also a creditor. God tells you: «You are my debtor; so-and-so is yours; I will do to you, my debtor, what you do to yours. This is the gift you have to offer me: forgiving your debtor. You ask me for mercy; do not be lazy in granting it. Pay attention to what the Scripture says: I want mercy before sacrifice. Do not offer a sacrifice that is not accompanied by mercy, because your sins will not be forgiven if you do not accompany it with mercy. You may say, "I lack

sins." Even if you move carefully, brother, as long as you live bodily in this world, you find yourself in the midst of tribulations and hardships and you have to go through innumerable temptations: you will not be able to live without sin. It is true that God tells you: “Do not be troubled by your sin; do not forgive if I have nothing to forgive you; If you owe nothing, be tougher in demanding; But if you are a debtor, rather congratulate yourself that you have a debtor to whom you can do what will be done to you. Listen to me and examine yourself whether you are one of those few righteous 2 who can truly recite the Lord's Prayer and say with sincerity: "Lord, forgive me, as I forgive." Do it without deception, without pretense, with a noble heart, so that it is truly fulfilled in you. If he asks you for forgiveness and you grant it to the one who hurt you, to the one who sinned against you, you can now confidently say: Forgive us our debts, just as we forgive our debtors. Well, if you deny forgiveness to those who beg you for it, you will find yourself ignored when you beg for it. You closed the door to whoever knocked, you will find it closed when you knock. And if you open the bowels of mercy to those who ask you for forgiveness, God will open them to you when you ask him. And now I am going to address those who beg forgiveness from their Christian brothers and do not receive it. If you grant it, you will be able to pray confidently. But if he begs you and you do not grant it, how can you be calm? Whoever you are who has sinned and has not been granted forgiveness, do not fear; question God, his God and yours. he; Notice that he said it while on the cross, not in heaven. He is always, in effect, God with the Father in heaven; but on the cross he was a man for you, offering himself as an example for all. That voice spoke for you, so that everyone could hear it. He could have prayed for them silently, but you would not have his example. If the Lord is too much for you, let the servant not be too much. Are you unable to imitate your Lord when He hung on the cross? Look at his servant Stephen when he was stoned to death. First he says as a servant to his Lord: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit; and then, on his knees: Lord, do not impute this sin to them. Having said these words, he fell asleep in the rest of love. He was met with exuberant peace because he wished peace to his enemies. Did he then also pray for those who asked him for forgiveness and not, rather, for those who were stoning him and killing him? There you have the example; learn and notice how, while praying for himself, he stood, and to pray for them he knelt down. Are we to think, brothers, that he loved them more than himself? He prayed standing up, because, being just, it was easy for them to listen to him; but for the wicked we had to pray on our knees. He showed, therefore, a love that reached even his enemies, who did not beg him for forgiveness 5. Therefore, brothers, forgive from the bottom of your heart those who beg you, so that you can recite without problems the Lord's prayer and so that the Lord may forgive you your sins in this mortal body, but which will last forever and ever, etc.

1. This evangelical reading is for me an exhortation from the Lord to speak to you about how to obtain heavenly bread. There is this earthly bread, necessary to the earth, since our flesh is earth. It could not be that our flesh had its bread and our soul did not have it. Our soul is also in this world in certain need, and needs its bread, as the flesh needs its bread. Who does not need bread? He is, in fact, the bread of our soul, who does not need any other bread, but being sufficient for himself, he also feeds us. He is manifestly the heavenly bread on which our soul feeds. 2. We need advice on how to get to him to be satisfied with the one of whom we now barely get a few crumbs, so as not to perish from hunger in this desert; about how to reach the fullness of that bread of which the Lord says: Whoever eats this bread will no longer be hungry and whoever drinks the drink that I will give him will never be thirsty again, promising us a certain fullness and satiety without discomfort. We need, therefore, advice on how to achieve that satiety of bread so different from the satiety of those who suffer from hunger here below. If we despise the advice, we will uselessly knock on the doors of that bread. Furthermore, if anyone despises this advice that I am going to give you or, better yet, that I am going to remind you, since what I have learned with you is not from me, I am not saying that they call uselessly, but that they do not even call. Calling consists of nothing more than following and acting on this advice. Do you think, my brothers, that God has a hard, material door that closes against men, and that is why he told us: Knock, so that we can reach and press on it until by pressing we make ourselves feel like the father of the family, hidden in a certain place, and he orders it to be opened for us, asking: "Who is knocking?" Exhorting the people to give alms, the Apostle said: I give you some advice in this regard. It is to your advantage that you not only did it, but that you began to love it from the previous year. Daniel also said to King Nebuchadnezzar: Receive my advice, O king, and redeem your sins with alms. Consequently, if, when we are commanded or exhorted to give something of our possessions to those in need, what we receive is advice, we should not be arrogant when we give. If what you received is advice, following it is more useful to you than to the person to whom you gave it. Let us not be proud because of our works or take pleasure in ourselves because we do a favor to the one to whom we do it. Whoever wants to receive advice, wants to receive

something that is beneficial to him, and whoever gives the advice looks out for the good of the other. And if he looks for the good of the other, it is profitable for the one for whose good he looks. Any poor beggar receives something from you with humility; Well, if it is not decent for you to give with pride, with much more reason should he also receive without pride; receive something from you with thanksgiving. You, on the other hand, have to know and remember not only what you give, but also what you receive. If that poor man had the freedom to respond to you, if he had noticed that you were proud of him, he would say to you: "Why are you proud? What are you proud of? What have you given me something about? What have you given me? Bread. If you put that bread in your house and neglect it, it will become moldy, and, once moldy, it will rot and end up on the ground; It will be land that returns to earth. You who stretched out your hand to give to mine stretched out to receive, remember where your hand was made and where mine was made. With earth you have put earth on the earth. Also, what do I do with your bread? I eat it and calm the discomfort of hunger. I receive a favor; I don't want to be ungrateful. You, however, think about what the Lord and Savior himself has warned you: Everything that enters the mouth goes to the belly and is expelled in the latrine. And what did the Apostle tell you, in turn? The delicacy, for the belly, and the belly, for the delicacy, but God will destroy both. So, like I said, bread is land that goes from one land to another land to sustain and replenish land. You think about what you gave and not about what you will receive. Sed quomodo solet fieri civibus peregre constitutis, fac traiectitium. Multi sane hoc faciunt, cum ideales inveniunt, dant impigre. Fecit Dominus tuus Christus, sursum dives, hic pauper. Esurit hic: traiectitium a te petit, aequum restituet. Quid ergo doubts, quare differs will I give? aut is not gone-
Address to the spouses

return? Give to the poor, do not fear losing anything; When you give to one of His little ones, it is Christ to whom you give. Listen to the Gospel. When those on his right, after having enumerated some of their needs, ask him in astonishment: When did we see you in them?, the Lord will answer them: "When you did it to one of these little ones of mine, you did it to me. I, he says, was the one who received it when a poor man received it; In him I suffered hunger and in him I was satisfied. Give calmly: the Lord is the one who receives, the Lord is the one who asks. You would have nothing to give him if you had not received it from him. By lending with interest to a man, you increase his burden; but Christ is not such as to be overwhelmed by interests. «If you want to lend with interest, make the loan to me, says the Lord; give me I will restore it to you with them. Get up now; widen your greed. For a single solid, perhaps you will receive not ten, nor a hundred, nor a thousand, nor the earth, but the sky. If you gave a pound of bronze and received it in silver, or gave it in silver and received it in gold, you would consider yourself happy. What you give is truly transformed; It will become for you not gold or silver, but eternal life. It will transform, because you will transform. The giver will become an angel; what is given will become an angel's throne. Outside of alms there is no other remedy that can free you from death. It is difficult for any man to live this life without sin. Give then, my brothers; distribute your goods. Provide yourselves with bags of money that do not age, the treasure that endures in heaven. Listen to the psalm: Although the man
He walks in image, his confusion is useless; He hoards, and does not know for whom he accumulates. Give, and it will be given to you.

Neus reddere? Da paperibus, non perdes, noli timere: ipsi das, cuín uni ex minimis eius das. Audi Evangelium. Cum illi ad dexteram positi expavescerent, emitnetatis quibusdam necessitatibus, dicentes: Quando te vidimus in bis? responds Dominus: Cum uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis (Mt 25,37-40). Ego, inquam, accepi, quando pauper accepit: in illo esuriebam, in illo satiabar. Da securus: Dominus accipit, Dominus petit. Non haberes quod ei dares, nisi prius ab illo acciperes. Si nomines fenerares, tumbares: non est hic talis qui fenore gravetur. Si vis fenerator esse, apud me esto, dicit tibi Deus, mihi da: ego cum usuris restituo. Iam never erect you; dilate avaritiam tuam. Pro uno forte solido, non decem, non centum, non mille, non terram, sed caelum accepturus es. Si dares libram aeramenti et acciperes argenti, aut libram argenti et acciperes auri, felicem te gauderes. Mutabitur revera quod das; non aurum, non argentum, sed vita aeterna tibi fiet. Mutabitur, quia tu mutaberis. Qui dedit, fiet angelus. Quod dedit, fiet sedes angelica. Remedium is not quod liberet a morte, nisi eleemosyna. 1 (2). Concubines habere non licet; nec maritatas uxores ducere; nec a marito repudiatas.—Audite, carissimi, membra Christi et matris Catholicae filii. Quod dico competentibus, audiant fideles; quod dico fidelibus, competent audiant; quod dico competentibus et fidelibus, audiant paenitentes; quod dico fidelibus et competentibus et paenitentibus, audiant catechumeni, audiant omnes: omnes timeant, nemo contemnat. Sit mihi in consolationem vester auditus, ne sit vobis in testimonium dolor Some author has considered its authenticity doubtful, although referring to the sermon in the form it appears in MIGNE, which in the present edition appears divided into two sermons, 162 B and the present one. 2 The numbering in parentheses is what appears in MIGNE,

child against you. I say to those competent: “You are not permitted to commit fornication. Your wives must be enough for you or no one; "Nor are you allowed to have concubines." Hear me God, if you are deaf; Let the angels listen to me, if you despise what I say. You are not allowed to have concubines. Even if you do not have a wife, you are not allowed to have concubines that you later abandon to take a wife. How much greater will be your condemnation if you want to have both concubines and a wife! You are not permitted to have as wives those whose previous husbands are still alive; Nor are you women allowed to have as husbands those whose previous wives are still alive. These marriages are adulterous; not in civil law, but in celestial law 3. Nor can you marry the woman who divorced her husband while he lives. Only on the grounds of fornication is it permissible to dismiss an adulterous woman; but while she lives it is not permitted to take another. Nor are you women allowed to have as husbands those who divorced their wives; it is not permitted to you; More than marriage, that is adultery. If you despise Augustine, at least fear Christ. Do not imitate the mob of the wicked and the infidels, my children; do not follow the broad path that leads to destruction. Whoever is baptized, either consecrates his chastity to God or stays with his wife, or, if he does not have one, gets married. 23). Listen to me, faithful; that is, the baptized. Why meus? Competentibus dico: Fornican vobis non licet. Sufficiant vobis aut uxores aut nec uxores: concubines vobis habere non licet. Audiat Deus, if you surdi estis; audiant Angelí eius, si vos contemnitis. Concubines vobis habere non licet. Et si non habetis uxores, non licet vobis habere concubinas, quas postea dimittatis, ut ducatis uxores; quanto magis damnatio vobis erit, si habere volueritis et concubinas et uxores? Non vobis licet habere uxores, quarum priores mariti vivunt: nec vobis, feminae, habere viros licet, quorum priores uxores vivunt. Adulterina sunt ista coniugia, non iure fori, sed iure caeli. Nec eam feminam quae per repudium discessit a marito, licet vobis ducere vivo marito. Solius fornicationis causa licet uxorem adulteram dimitiere: sed illa vívente non licet alteram ducere. Et vobis, feminae, nec illos viros a quibus per repudium discesserunt uxores eorum, maritos habere concedítur; non licet: sunt adultery, non coniugia.

Contemnitur Augustinus, tímeatur vel Christus. Nolite imitarí turbam malorum, infidelium; filii mei: nolite sequi vias latas, quarum finís ad interitum ducit. Qui baptízatus fuerit, aut continentiam Deo voveat, aut permaneat cum uxore sua, aut si non habet, ducat uxorem. 23). Paenitentia iis qui a castitatis proposito lapsi sunt amplectenda. Address to the spouses

do you die after being reborn? Why do you go, once baptized, along tortuous, slippery and unclean paths? Do you not know that they lead you to perdition? You are going to perdition, my children; believe me Don't you want to believe it? What do I have to do? Those of you who are baptized and listen to me, if perhaps you have committed such actions, do not add more and pray that God forgives you. If you could not or did not want to maintain marital fidelity or chastity and you deviated from what was promised, whether in the marital bond or in consecrated chastity, let the pain and humility of penance be found in you. I am going to say it more clearly: let no one say that they have not understood. Those of you who stained yourselves with any illicit intercourse outside of your wives, if you slept with any other woman outside of yours, do penance, as is usually done in the Church, so that she may pray for you. Let no one say: «I will do it secretly; I will do it before God. God, who must forgive me, knows that I do it in my heart. So, was it said in vain: What you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven? Have the keys been given to the Church for no reason? Do we declare the Gospel and the words of Christ null and void? Should we promise you what he denies you? Have we deceived you? Job says: If I have been ashamed to confess my sins in the presence of the people. Whoever says this is a righteous man, fine gold from the divine treasure and tested in his crucible, and does the son of pestilence resist me and is he ashamed to bend the knee, under the blessing of God, the proud neck and the tortuous mind? Perhaps, or, better, without perhaps, since he is baptized. Quare moriemini iam renati? When baptized by tortuous routes and lubricates and immundas itis, nescitis quia peritis? Peritis, filii mei, credite. Non vultis credere? Quid vobis fació? Qui fideles estis, et [1711] auditis me, si forte talia commisistis, nolite addere; et ut vobis Deus ignoscat, orate. Si non potuistis habere, vel noluistis, pudicitiam coniugalem seu continentiam, et deviastis a proposito vel vinculi coniugalis vel devotae continentiae, sit in vobis dolor et humilitas paenitentiae. Apertius dico: nemo dicat: Non intellexi. Qui post uxores vestras vos illicito concubitu maculastis, si praeter uxores vestras cum aliqua concubuistis; agitate paenitentiam, qualis agitur in Ecclesia, ut oret pro vobis Ecclesia. Nemo sibi dicat: Occulte ago, apud Deum ago: novit Deus qui mihi ignoscat, quia in corde meo ago.

Ergo sine causa dictum est: Quae solveritis in terra, soluta erunt in cáelo? (Mt 18,18). Ergo sine causa sunt keys datae Ecclesiae Dei? frustrationus Evangelium, frustrationus verba Christi? Promittimus vobis quod ille negat? Nonne vos decipimus? Iob dicit: Si erubui in conspectu populi confiteri peccata mea (Iob 31,33). Talis iustus, thesauri divini obryzum, tali path probatas ista dicit; et resistit mihi filius pestilentiae, et erubescit genu figere sub benedictione Dei superba cervix, mens tortuosa? Fortassis,

There is no doubt, God therefore wanted the emperor Theodosius to undergo public penance in the presence of the people, especially taking into account that his sin could not be hidden 4. And is the senator ashamed of what the emperor was not ashamed of? Is he, not the senator, but the simple courtier, ashamed of what the emperor was not ashamed of? Is the commoner or the businessman ashamed of what the emperor was not ashamed of? What arrogance is this? Wouldn't she alone be enough to send to hell, even if there was no adultery? 3 (4). Finally, my brothers and sisters, men and women who listen to me, why are you angry against me? If only you would do what is written: Be angry and sin not! Should I fear that what happened to the apostle Paul might happen to me? If you were attentive, you heard it when it was read, namely: So, have I become your enemy by telling you the truth? If it is for that reason, be it so. If it is necessary to become your enemy, I prefer to be your enemy than to be an enemy of justice. I place you in the custody of your wives. They are my daughters, as you are also my sons. Listen to me; be jealous of your husbands; do not reserve vain glory with immo quod non dubitatur, propterea Deus voluit ut Theodosius imperator ageret paenitentiam publicam in conspectu populi, máxime quia peccatum eius celari non potuit; et erubescit senator, quod non erubuit impetator? Erubescit, nec senator, sed tantum curialis, quod non erubuit imperator? Erubescit plebeius sive negotiator, quod non erubuit imperator? What is this superbia? Nonne sola sufficeret gehennae, etiamsi adulterium nullum esset? 3 (4). Christianae mulleres quomodo zelare debenant viros suos.— Postremo, fratres mei, audiunt me viri, audiunt me feminae, quid ad me irascimini? Utinam faciatis quod scriptum est: lrasámini, et nolite peccare (Ps 4,5). Timere debeno, ne contingat mihi quod contigit apostólo Paulo, quod moda cum legeretur, si attempti Fuistis, audistis: Ergo inimicus factus sum vobis verum praedicans? (Gal 4:16). And if ita est, fiat. Si necesse est ut inimicus sim vobis, melius vobis opto esse, quam iustitiae. Commendo vos custodiendos etiam uxoribus vestris. Filiae meae sunt, sicut et vos filii mei estis. Audiant me: zelent viros suos; non sibi servent vanam gloriam, qua solent a maritis impudicis matronae It refers to the famous Thessaloniki episode. To punish a rebellion in the city, Theodosius decides to carry out a massacre.

Ambrosio gets the law repealed, but then applies it. The troops cause numerous inhabitants to perish by sword in the circus grounds. Ambrose invites him to submit to public penance; Otherwise, you will be deprived of the sacraments and denied entry into the church. At first he opposed, but ended up accepting Ambrose's conditions, remaining for some time excluded from the church, until he was acquitted on Christmas 390. See Saint Ambrose's letter 51 and the funeral eulogy on the death of Theodosius; from Saint Augustine, The City of God V 26,1 ("the people, in prayer for him, wept more for the prostrate imperial celsitude than for fearing it in its angry sin").
Address to the spouses

the one that impudent husbands usually praise their matron, that is, they endure their infidelity with a calm spirit. I don't want Christian women to have that kind of patience; Be jealous of your husbands, not for your own flesh, but for their souls. I admonish, order and command absolutely; The bishop commands it, and Christ commands it in me. He knows it well in whose presence my heart is burning. I command it, I repeat. Do not allow your husbands to engage in fornication. Challenge the Church against them. I do not say that you accuse them before worldly judges, before the proconsul or his vicar, the count or the emperor, but before Christ. In everything else, be servants of your husbands, subject to their obedience. Let there be no arrogance, nor pride, nor shameful attitude, nor any disobedience in you; Serve them in everything as servants. But as regards that aspect in which the blessed apostle made you equal to them when he said: Let the husband grant what he owes to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband, he added: The woman has no power over her body, but the man. What are you proud of? Listen to what follows: In the same way, the man does not have power over his body, but the woman does. When it comes to this matter, shout for what is yours. If the husband sells your gold according to his needs, bear with him, wife; endure it, servant; do not litigate, do not contradict him. Despising your gold is equivalent to loving your husband. If he sells your property for his needs, which are also yours—well, there can be no need that is only his and not yours, if there is laudari, quia impudicitiam virorum suorum aequo animo ferunt. Nolo talem patientiam habeant christianae mulieres: prorsus zelent viros suos; non propter carnem suam, sed propter animas illorum. Omnino ego moneo, ego praecipio, ego iubeo: episcopus iubet, Christus in me iubet. Novit ille in cuius conspectu ardet cor meum. Ego, inquam, iubeo. Nolite viros vestros permitiere fornican. Interpellate yourself against the Ecclesiam. Non dico, public judices, non proconsulem, non vicarium, non comitem, non imperatorem; thirst Christum. In ceteris omnibus ancillae estote virorum vestrorum, subditae ad obsequium. Nulla sit in vobis proptervitas, [1712] nulla superbia, non contumeliosa cervix, non aliqua inoboedientia: prorsus tanquam ancillae servite.

Sed ubi ventum fuerit ad illud negotium, ubi vos beatus Apostolus aequavit, they say: Uxori vir debitum reddat, similiter et uxor viro; subintulit: Uxor non habet potestatem corporis sui, sed vir. What are you extolliing? Audi quod sequitur: Similiter et vir non habet corporis sui potestatem, sed mulier (1 Cor 7,3.4). Ubi ad hoc ventum fuerit, clámate pro re vestra. Aurum tuum vendit maritus pro necessitate sua: ferto, femina; ferto, ancilla; noli litigare, noli contradicere. Contemptus auri tui, dilectio est viri tui. Si villam tuam pro necessitate sua vendet, quae est et tua (non enim potest esse ipsius, quae non sit tua, si est caritas in te, quae debent esse in

in you the love that every wife should have—bear it with patience; and, if he doubts, offer it to him; despise everything for the love of your husband. But you want him to be chaste, you fight for his chastity. Bear with patience the perishment of your property, as long as its soul does not perish because of your patience. 4 (5). I don't tell men to be jealous about their women, because I know they are. Who can stand their wife being an adulteress? And the woman is asked to tolerate her husband's adulteries! What justice! —Why?, I beg you. Because? —Because I am a man. —Are you male? You have to show with your strength that you are. Are you male? Passion conquers. How can you be a man if your wife is stronger than you? You, man, are, in truth, the head of the woman. If it is the head, let the woman be the guide and follow. In a well-ordered house, the man is the head of the woman. If you are the head, be the guide; follow the woman at his head. But look where you're going. Don't go where you don't want her to follow you; Do not go where you do not want to have her as a companion, so as not to fall together into the pit of adultery, lest, by doing so, you teach her to do it. Your soul will hurt if you both fall together into the pit of adultery; but it must hurt you even if only you fall. You feel jealous, you don't want her to fall; fear, do not fall. But you, most chaste women, do not imitate your impudent husbands. Far be it from you! May they live with you or may they perish alone! The woman does not owe her chastity to the impudent husband, but to God, to Christ. Stay faithful not for your husband, who does not deserve it, but for Christ. Consider the uxore), ferto patienter; et si doubtat, tu offer: contemne omnia propter amorem viri tui. Sed castum opta, pro castitate litigate. Patienter pereat villa tua, non anima ipsius te pariente pereat. 4 (5). Caput mulieris vir. Ducat hic in bonum, illa sequatur.— Non dico vitis, ut in hac causa zelent uxores suas. Scio quia faciunt, novi. Quis ferat uxorem adulteram? Et imperatur feminae ut ferat adulterum virum! O iustitia! Quare, do I ask you? Quare? Quia ego sum vir. Vir is it? in fortitudine tua probemus, quia vir es. Vir is it? vince libidinem. Quomodo vir, quo uxor est fortior? Tu es caput mulieris, vir, verum est. Si caput est, ducat, uxor sequatur. Sed ubi recta est domus, caput mulieris vir. Si caput es, duc: sequatur illa caput suum. Be vide quo eas.

Noli iré quo non vis ut sequatur: noli iré quo times pedissequam, ne in toyeam adulterii simul ruatis: ne cum tu facis, twelves quod facis. Dolet tibí anima, si in foveam adulterii ambo simul ruatis: doleat tibi, si tu solus ruatis. Zelas, non vis ut ruat illa: time, tu noli ruere. Nolite autem,. pudicissimae feminae, imitari impudicos viros vestros. Absit a vobis. Aut vobiscum vivant, aut soli pereant. Immodest marito non debent mulier pudicitiam, sed Deo illam debent, Christo illam debent. Non propter íllum faciat, qui non meretur; sed propter Christum faciat. Premium

own price, read your tables. Finally, let those who perhaps feel indignant because I speak of these things think what they like, because I know that those who judge rightly love me for it, since it is not without reason that it is written: Correct the wise man, and he will love you; correct the fool, and his hatred towards you will increase. He did not say that he will begin to hate you, but that he will increase his hatred, since he already had it. Therefore, I know that the wise love me for this point. Those who know that I know their sins deprive themselves of communion, so as not to be expelled from inside the gates. Those whose sins I ignore, I summon before the presence of God. Let them also do penance and abstain henceforth from the filthiness of their fornications. 5 (6). To the penitents I say: «What are you doing? Know it well: you do nothing. "What good is it to humble yourself if you don't change your life?" To the catechumens I say: “Be inflamed with the desire to receive grace. But choose who to imitate in the Church of God. If you find no one, woe is me, my God! What do I say: 'If you find no one'? So you won't find anyone among the faithful people? If in it there are not those who preserve what they received, those who keep what they heard, I have wasted my time in baptizing so many men for so many years. Far be it from me to believe this! If that were the reality, it would be better for me not to be your bishop. But I hope to be and I believe I am. But my unfortunate condition is that I am often forced to cosuum attendat, tabulas suas legat. Postremo quod libet sentiat, qui forte indignatur, quia talia dispute: nam scio, qui sapiunt, amant inde me; quia non sine causa scriptum est: Corrípe sapientem, et amabit te; Corripe insipientem, et adiciet odisse te (Prov 9,8). Non dixit, Incipiet; thirst, addiet: quia iam oderat. Ergo scio quia sapientes amant me in hoc. A communione se cohibeant, qui sciunt quia novi peccata ipsorum; ne de cancellis proiciantur. Quorum autem nescio, hos coram Deo Covenant. Agant etiam ipsi paenitentiam, et deinceps ab immunditia abstineant fornicationum suarum. 5 (6). Paenitentes mutentur. Catechumeni imitentur bonds of Ecclesid.—Paenitentibus dico: quid est quod agitis? Scitote, nihil agitis. Quid prodest quia humiliamini, si non mutamini? Catechumenis dico: exardescite volúntate ad percipiendam gratiam. Sed eligite vobis in Ec-; clesia Dei quos imitemini. Si [1713] non inveneritis: heu mihi, Deus meus! What is the meaning: If not inveneritis?

Ergo in populo fidelium non est quem inveniatis? Per tot annos, tot homines sine causa baptizavimus, si non ibi sunt qui servent quod acceperunt, qui custodiant quod audierunt. Absit a me ut hoc credam. Melius non vobis essem episcopus, si hoc ita est. Be rough esse, credo esse. Inde est autem misera condicio mea, quia plerumque cogor adultereros nosse, castos nosse non possum.

Address to the penitents

I know the adulterers, but I cannot know the chaste. In secret I do not lack reasons for joy, nor for torment in public. Therefore, desire the grace of God; Choose who to imitate, who to live with and with whom to maintain the sweet conversations of love. Do not admit bad gossip. Bad conversations corrupt good customs. Live like the ears of corn among the tares; suffer the tribulations of this world like grains on the threshing floor. The fan will arrive; no one constitutes a permanent divider at this time.

and do you laugh and mock the patience of God? If you are penitent, repent; If you do not repent, you are not penitent. And, if you repent, why do you continue doing the evil you did before? If you regret doing it, don't do it. If you're still doing it, you certainly haven't regretted it yet. It is true, dearly beloved, that when a man falls ill, they send him or bring him to the Church, where he is baptized, renewed and where he will be happy. But that is not the reason for penance. He who has not yet received baptism has not yet profaned the sacrament; but whoever has profaned it with his evil and dissipated life, which is why he was kept away from the altar so that he does not eat and drink his own condemnation, must change his life, correct himself and be reconciled while he lives, while he enjoys health. Does he wait to reconcile when he begins to die? 2 I am a witness that many died before they were reconciled. Furthermore, in the presence of God, I expose my fear to you for your fear. He who does not fear, despises me for fearing, but to his harm. Listen, then. I am certain that a baptized man, if he leads a life—I dare not say without sin, for who is without sin?—if he leads a life without serious sins, even if he has those others that are forgiven daily by saying in prayer: Forgive us our debts, just as we forgive our debtors, when his days are over, his life will not end, but will pass from one life to another, from the life of work to the life of rest, from the miserable to the happy; whether he runs of his own free will to the baptism

Topic: Address to the penitents. Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown. Penitents, penitents, penitents, if you are penitents and not mockers: change your life and be reconciled to God. You also go out to the grass tied with a chain. "With what chain?" you ask. What you bind on earth will be bound in heaven. You hear about a bondage, and do you think God is deceiving? You are doing penance, you bend your knee, In occulto est unde gaudeam, in publico est unde tequear. Ergo desiderate gratiam Dei, eligite quos imitemini, cum quibus vivatis, et cum quibus colloquia dulcía caritatis habeatis. Nolite admits bad whispers. Corrumpunt mores bonds bad colloquia (1 Cor 15:33). Vivite sicut spicae inter zizania: ferte tribulationes huius saeculi, sicut grana inarea. Veniet fan: nemo sit passim isto tempore separator.

Paenitentia non vera, si non vita mutatur. "Paenitentia in extremis quam incerta.—Paenitentes, paenitentes, paenitentes (si tamen estis paenitentes, et non estis irridentes), mutate vitam, reconcilíamini Deo. Et vos enim cum catena pascitis. Qua, inquis, catena? Quae ligaveritis in terra, erunt ligata et in cáelo (Mt 18,18). Audis ligaturam, et Deo putas faceré imposturam? Paenitentiam agis, genu figis, et rides, et subsannas Allusion to the Donatists, who sought to establish here a clear division between the just and sinners. There are many authors who doubt the Augustinian authenticity of this sermon.

patientiam Dei? Si paenitens es, paeniteat te: si non paenitet, paenitens non es. Si ergo paenitet, cur facis quod male fecisti? Si fecisse paenitet, noli faceré. SUPPLEMENTARY NOTES [1] The synod of Diospolis.—The synod of Diospolis was one of several convened to examine the doctrine of Pelagius and his followers. The first of them was held in Carthage in the year 411, presided over by the city's primate, Aurelius. The accused was not Pelagius, but his disciple Celestius, who, by not retracting certain propositions, was excommunicated and retired to the East. A second took place in Jerusalem, in 414 or 415, where Pelagius was, who at that time enjoyed the esteem of Bishop John for his life as an ascetic. Saint Jerome and Orosius, a Spanish priest sent there by Saint Augustine, intervened in it, each in their own way. As it was difficult to understand each other due to the mutual incomprehension of the language, Bishop John limited himself to sending the documentation to Pope Innocent I so that he could rule and then act according to his opinion. Meanwhile, Pelagius would cease his propaganda and his accusers would stop treating him as a heretic. Very shortly afterwards, still in 415, the synod of Diospolis was held. The Gallic bishops Heros and Lazarus had drawn up a report listing the errors taught by Pelagius and Celestius, which they sent to Eulogius, bishop of Caesarea. Fourteen bishops of Palestine attended the synod convened to examine the cause of Pelagius. The defendant defended himself by presenting laudatory letters addressed to him by notable people in the Christian world, among them one from Augustine, whose reading he asked to be done, and was successful, at least in part. The accusations, written in Latin, were translated directly into Greek, and Pelagius also responded in Greek. The examination was based on the Líber testimonyrum. The central point was impecance, or man's possibility of living this life without committing sin. Pelagius knew how to emerge victorious. More difficulty, however, was caused by the demand that he condemn some other statements; for example, that grace is free will. He endorsed the condemnation pronounced against Celestius in Carthage, in the synod of 411, and also condemned, with a generic formula, everything that was opposed to the Catholic faith. In view of his answers, the synod declares him innocent and in communion with the Church. "In view of the satisfactory explanations of Pelagius here present, who professes sound doctrine and condemns and anathematizes the doctrine contrary to the faith of the Church, we declare that he is worthy of the communion of the Catholic Church" (The minutes of the trial of Pelagius 20,44).

To achieve victory, Pelagius had used somewhat ambiguous language, which the eastern bishops, unaware of the problem as it was seen in Africa, failed to detect. Since none of the accusers had attended, nor had Orosius, who was present at the Jerusalem assembly, there was no one who could force him to make the language more precise. In fact, although Pelagius was acquitted, the "Pelagian" doctrine was condemned. Hence the words of sermon 348 A,5: «Let no one say that he has already been absolved by the bishops. She was acquitted, yes, but the confession was corrected, since what she said before the bishops seemed to be Catholic. The bishops who absolved him were unaware of what he had said in his books... In any case, it was not the heresy that was absolved, but the man who denied it. As is easy to understand, Pelagius proclaimed his triumph to all the winds, sending it to Rome, but without the minutes of the synod. Augustine then warned of the naivety of the judges. As soon as the minutes of the aforementioned synod came into his hands, he began to write

the work The minutes of the trial against Pelagius to confront the heresiarch's propaganda. As already said, the Saint recognizes that he was personally absolved, but remembers that heresy was condemned. Pelagius, therefore, could no longer continue to rely on that sentence to defend doctrines that he never renounced. At the same time, the African bishops, gathered in Carthage and Milevi and led by Augustine, once again condemned the Pelagian errors, along with the heretics, as long as they did not deny the heresy. Condemnation confirmed by Pope Innocent I in 417. [2] The mediation of the Church in the granting of forgiveness.—The Church, from its beginnings, was clearly aware of the power to forgive that Jesus conferred on it, as the evangelical texts attest (Mt 16,19: 18,18; Jn 20,22). But there were no shortage of heretics who limited this power either by taking it away from the institutional Church, leaving it to the spiritual (Tertullian the Montanist), or by excluding from it certain categories of sins (Tertullian also, Novatian, etc. See the complementary note [ 5 ]: Heresies contrary to penance), leaving exclusively to God directly the forgiveness of them. Thus the Church ceases to be a conditio sine qua non for forgiveness. Evidently, Augustine, rooted in the great current of ecclesial tradition, could not participate in these opinions. On the one hand, he affirms that there is no sin that cannot be remitted by the Church (in the famous sin against the Holy Spirit of Mt 12:32, the Saint sees final impenitence; cf. sermon 71); On the other hand, he defends that only in the Church and through the Church can forgiveness be obtained. In sermon 71,37 he indicates it clearly: "We must believe that penance is only beneficial when it is accepted in the Church, in which the remission of sins is given and the society of the spirit is maintained in the bond of peace." But Augustine is convinced that forgiveness, as it is life, can only be granted by God, who truly gives life through the Spirit of life. In this context, the question arises about the specific function of the Church in granting this forgiveness. His theological method of interpreting Scripture has allowed him to find the solution or the way to combine the action of God and that of the Church in the text of the resurrection of Lazarus, which he always interprets in the same way.

Lazarus, symbol of the sinner already buried under the slab of the habit of sin, comes to life before the voice of Jesus. Augustine, who interprets the text in a penitential key, expressly raises the objection: "Perhaps someone will say: 'What good is the Church, if he who confesses his sin is already resurrected by the voice of the Lord?' What does the Church profit to him who confesses his sin, to which the Lord said: Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven? (Mt 18,18)'” (sermon 67,3). Attentive to all the details of the Gospel text, the Saint warns that in the resurrection of Lazarus there are two moments: one is his return to life and the other is being unleashed and able to walk. Full liberation only occurs after these two moments, the first of which is the work of the Lord, and the second is the work of the apostles (disciples, ministers of the Church) commissioned by the Lord. In fact, Augustine constantly associates Jn 11:44: Loose him and let him go, with Mt 18:18: Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. In the same sermon 67 cited above, Augustine continues: «Look at Lazarus when he comes out with his bonds. "I already lived thanks to confession, but I still did not walk free, constrained by the same bonds." That is to say, focusing now on the sinner, there are two moments: the first is that of confessing one's own sin, recognizing oneself as a sinner; This is the work of Christ, who calls

inside; but it is not enough; Although he has returned to life, he must be loosed by the Church, by its ministers. Only then will you be free. "What then is the Church to do, to which it was said: Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven, except what the Lord said next: Loose it and let it go?" (ibid.). «Those who are loosed fear being bound; The bound pray to be loosed. Outside the Church nothing can be unleashed. To a four-day dead person it is said: Lazarus, come out, and he came out of the tomb, bound hand and foot with bandages. The Lord awakens the dead to come out of the tomb if he touches the heart so that the confession of sin comes out. But he's still kind of tied up. Consequently, after Lazarus came out of the tomb, the Lord commanded his disciples, to whom he had said: Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven, to loose it and let it go. He resurrected him personally and unleashed him through his disciples (sermon 295,2. See also sermons 98,6; 139 A,2 [r=MAl, 125]; 352,8; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 49,24). In the mentioned texts we must highlight the emphasis that the Saint places on the resurrection taking place through confession, that is, by recognizing oneself as a sinner, when others would rather put it in penitential practices. [3] Funeral banquets.—Banquets at the tombs of the dead were always characteristic of pagan piety. The sacred duty towards the deceased required not only burying and caring for it, but also visiting it, particularly on certain dates. The Parentalia are famous, which lasted from February 13 to 22, festivals dedicated to celebrating the memory of the deceased of a family. On that occasion, living relatives gathered at a funeral banquet in honor of dead relatives, who were somehow present there. The banquet provided them with relief, company and food, since they participated as invisible diners in it. Hence the name refrigerium. Christians maintained some aspects of this pagan piety, although radically transformed in its meaning. The new faith in eternal life now illuminated the atmosphere and the rites. The sacrificial banquet for the dead was replaced by the Eucharist, and, instead of feeding the spirits of the ancestors, the poor were fed.

But the mass conversions that followed Constantine's new policy markedly changed the situation. Less convinced Christians returned, more or less veiled, to their more deeply rooted ancient customs. In many cases, Christian names and appearances hide pagan customs. Banquets are recovering their popularity, and their distinctive note is not exactly sobriety. Not only the carnal ancestors are celebrated, but also the notable figures of the Christian family: the bishops of the city and, above all, the martyrs. The "memories" of the latter become, on certain dates, places of celebration, where wine flows in abundance and leaves the marks of its presence. Many do not go there to pray, but to get drunk and dance, as is the case with the memory of Saint Cyprian in Carthage. The most attentive spirits notice the degradation that has been reached. The most vigilant pastors consider that measures must be taken, even if they are severe and encounter opposition from the masses. The first of them is Saint Ambrose, who categorically prohibits all kinds of banquets and meals at the tombs of the martyrs. It was the surprise that Saint Monica received when she tried to follow her African customs in Milan (Confessions VI 2,2). Other Italian Churches, such as Verona and Brescia,

They imitated the example of the Bishop of Milan. Later it was Africa's turn, where the abuses had reached exceptional dimensions, although there was no shortage of followers of the ancient traditions with an authentic Christian spirit. Monica is an example. The Donatist cult of the sect's martyrs had become veritable bacchanals. Augustine, still a simple presbyter from Hippo, reflects on how to put an end to these customs, which have more pagan than Christian flavor. He thinks that it is impossible to prohibit in a second-class city what is allowed in the capital, Carthage, and also that, once suppressed in the capital, it would be easier to do so in the remaining locations. That is why he wrote to the bishop of Carthage, Aurelius, inviting him to act in that direction, because he knew that it would not be difficult for him to convince him. When he was still a simple deacon he had publicly shown his disapproval. The letter that Augustine addressed to him, the 22nd in the Augustinian series, is a monument of wisdom and pastoral prudence and deserves to be read. Shortly after, the Council of Hippo in 393 was held, in which meals were prohibited in the memorials of the martyrs. Aurelius' energy achieved its purpose in Carthage. Augustine then took action in his diocese. In two tense days, in which he had to use all his oratory skills, he managed to overcome the habit. He left the narration of the events in letter 29 to Alypius, which also deserves to be read. You can see F. VAN DER MEER, Saint Augustine, shepherd of souls (Barcelona 1965) p.633-669: "The funeral banquets." [4] The usefulness of mystery.—Augustine sees Scripture as a jungle full of mysteries. In his capacity as a teacher and pastor, and before that as a man who feeds his own spirit with his reading, the holy bishop has encountered almost at every step dark words, enigmatic facts, almost impenetrable statements. The question arises spontaneously: Why did God want man to fatigue, when everything could be clearer, all that was needed was an adequate formulation, undoubtedly within the Lord's reach? Furthermore, fewer risks would be run, since there is no doubt that the swarming of so many heresies has its origin precisely in a misinterpretation of obscure passages of the Word of God. What then is the function of this mysterious presentation of truth, necessary for our salvation?

When it comes to God, one cannot think that this is the result of chance or any other kind of inability. We must assume, therefore, some precise and concrete intention. The Saint considers the existence of such mysteries, in any of their manifestations, as the fruit of God's wise pedagogy. Man must love, seek, value and enjoy the truth. This is what, paradoxically, its mysterious presentation leads to. Therefore, the fact that the truth is veiled to a certain extent does not have the purpose of denying access to it (sermon 51,5; 270,1), much less deceiving (sermon 352,6), nor does it mean that anyone who wants to discover it should be treated with suspicion (sermon 60 Á, l [ = M A I, 26]). Quite the opposite. What it aims to do is stimulate the desire for it, relying on that reality of the human spirit that makes it curious about the occult (sermon 51.5; 156.1). The truth is shown wrapped in mysteries to solicit investigators, to incite them to search (sermon 8,18; 32,1; 41,7; 60 A, l; 145,1; 156,1; 270,1). At the base of this darkness is not contempt for man, but the desire that he exercise himself with healthy exercise (sermon 71,38; 80,2). But exercise, like research and search, are not ends in themselves; The benefit they bring is not only that of the truth discovered, but also the joy of personal discovery of it.

This idea of ​​joy and pleasure is very dear to Augustine. "If the truth were not shrouded in mystery, we would never investigate it diligently, and if we did not investigate it diligently, it would not give us so much pleasure to find it" (sermon 8:18); "the veil of mystery incites the search and makes the discovery more pleasant" (sermon 41,7; 51,12). And, at the same time, the truth acquires greater value in the eyes of its investigator. When your achievement has been the result of personal effort, you will no longer be held in contempt. In fact, the danger of undervaluation always surrounds things that are easy to achieve. "Nor would it be sweet to understand them if ease had made them vile" (sermon 352,6; 71,10). In this way, his satiety will not cause boredom (sermon 2,6). Finally, remaining enclosed in mystery, the truth is given to those who are truly lovers of it, to those who in their love have sought it, and is denied to those who do not deserve it (sermon 60 A, l; 270,1). Obviously, not everything is a mystery nor can it be, because there would be another danger: discouragement and distance from the truth. For this reason, God's wise pedagogy has known how to combine darkness with light, so that the latter illuminate the former: «The depth of the word stimulates desire, but does not prevent understanding. If everything was closed, there would be no way to discover the dark. If everything were covered, the soul would have no place to receive the food that would give it the strength with which to call to understand the dark" (sermon 156,1). Thus, in Scripture, there is no lack of clear texts, so that no one has excuses for not having known the truth necessary for their salvation, nor the obscure ones, for the exercise and joy of the brave. The first, for the crowd; the seconds, for a few. See also Christian Doctrine I I 6,7-8 and Confessions VI 5,8, which expand the texts that we have collected here only from the sermons. [5] Heresies contrary to penance.—Other texts of the Saint indicate to us which heretics deny penitence, since it is referred to in sermon 359,2. They are, fundamentally, the Novatians and the Luciferians. Of the former he says in the work Heresies 38: «Full of pride and becoming extremely hateful, the Cathars, who give themselves this name in honor of their purity, do not admit remarriages and deny penance. They follow the heretic Novatus, from whom they receive the name of Novatians.

And in an even more controversial tone he says in The Christian Combat 31,33: «Let us not listen to those who deny that the Church of God can forgive all sins. Those wretches, by not understanding the stone in Peter and by refusing to believe that the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been given to the Church, have lost them in their hands... If those Cathars wanted to recognize his name, they would call themselves worldlings rather than worlds. If they sin, they do not admit repentance; Therefore, they have chosen nothing other than to be condemned with the world. They deny the sinner the forgiveness of his sin not to preserve him in health, but to deprive the sick person of medicine...» Novatian refused penance, even at the moment of death, to apostates of any category, not excepting libellatics, that is, those who, without having actually sacrificed to the pagan gods, procured a certificate of having done so to avoid subsequent persecution. Relying on Mt 10:33, he affirmed that the Church could not forgive sins committed directly against God, although God could forgive them; but this is unknown to man. In the Commentary on Psalm 54:22, recalling the usefulness of the heretics, Augustine also mentions the positive fruit for penitence that was derived from the challenge by the Novatians.

If the position of the Novatians was the result of pagan persecution, that of the Luciferians originated from the pressure of the Emperor Constantius, a Christian, but Arian, for the Catholic bishops to sign the Arian formula of Sirmium of 357. For different reasons, some succumbed to the pressures. Such a signature was considered by a group of radicals, led by Lucifer of Cagliari, as a true apostasy, to which penance had to be denied. Of them he says in the work, already mentioned, The Christian Combat 30,32: «Let us not listen to those who... departed from unity and preferred to call themselves Luciferians rather than Catholics... Because nowhere should the bowels of mercy reign as much as in the Catholic Church; As a true mother, she should not proudly insult sinful children or oppose difficulties to the forgiveness of the repentant. Not without reason does Peter stand in for the Catholic Church among all the apostles. This Church was given the keys to the kingdom of heaven when they were given to Peter... After the persecution that the Arian heretics promoted when the secular princes gave the Catholic Church the peace that it always has in the Lord, many bishops repented and requested to enter the Catholic Church. They anathematized what they had believed and pretended to believe. The Catholic Church received them into its maternal womb... The Luciferians looked with pride at this charity of the mother and impiously disapproved of it. For not having congratulated Peter when he recovered at the crowing of the cock, they deserved to fall with Lucifer, who came out into the dawn. Among the heretics who deny penance we must also count Tertullian. In his mountaineering stage he denied the Church the power to forgive sins; power which, however, it grants to the spiritual. But a limited power, because the three great crimina—adultery, homicide, apostasy—are excluded from any forgiveness that is not directly that of God (see De pudicitia V 4.14; IV 5; X; XXI 17). But Augustine, when talking about Tertullian, does not mention this aspect of his doctrine (see Heresies 86). Saint Cyprian himself mentions in letter 52 of some bishops who denied forgiveness to adulterers. Agustín knows her and quotes her (letter 93,10,41), but in passing and at the service of other interests. Finally, although they do not fall into the category of heretics, there are pagans.

On more than one occasion, Augustine alludes to the accusations leveled at Catholics of perverting the customs of the human race. According to them, the simple possibility of forgiveness is an open door to committing any kind of misdeed. Men increase their sins in the hope of forgiveness. Augustine strives to show them precisely the opposite: how forgiveness enables and facilitates the correction of customs (Commentary on Psalm 101,1,10; Sermon 359,2). [6] Women's monasteries.—Consecrated virginity is attested in Africa already in times before Saint Augustine. The data is provided by both Tertullian and Saint Cyprian, and, of course, abounds in Augustine himself. When she had to say goodbye to her lover, she returned to Africa, consecrating herself to God and vowing never to know a man again (Confessions VI 15,25). The council of Hippo in 393 recommends that virgins who live alone be entrusted to women of recognized probity, to defend their reputation. But admitting the existence of consecrated virgins is not the same as admitting the existence of monasteries. Precisely the canon of the Council of Hippo does not mention the monasteries of virgins, when its content is demanding such mention if they had existed. Female monasteries are mentioned for the first time at the Council of Carthage in 397,
Additional notes

and, without a reasonable doubt, its appearance is in connection with Augustine. Saint himself provides us with data, as does his friend and biographer Posidio. Speaking of what Augustine had left to the Church when he died, he mentions, among other things, the following: "He left the Church plenty of clergy and monasteries full of men and women who lived in perfect chastity, with their respective superiors" (Life of Saint Augustine 31). Del Santo also says that he only visited the nuns' monasteries out of urgent need (ibid., 27), which indicates their existence in an indeterminate number, but always plural. In a very generic way, Augustine alludes to its existence in a text from the work Holy Virginity 45,46: «There are many men and women who maintain marital chastity, without however achieving what the Lord says: If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven...(Mt 19,21), not daring to join the ranks of those who have nothing. own, but everything is common to all. Here we find not only the reference to female monasteries, but also to monasteries with Augustinian spirituality. Indeed, Augustine founded female monasteries. The statement is explicit in reference to Hippo: "Because I have not planted and watered that garden of the Lord in you to collect those thorns from you." The text corresponds to letter 211, addressed precisely to the residents of that monastery. It was written in the year 423, but its foundation must be lowered considerably in date. Together with 210, the letter is motivated by the divisions that arose in the community by not accepting the one who had been elected superior after the death of Augustine's sister, who had previously governed the monastery. It probably has to be put before 397, when, as has already been said, the Council of Carthage legislates on monasteries of virgins. And the fact that the council deals with them is an indication that there were already more than one at that time. It is difficult not to see Augustine's hand not only in the emergence, but also in the multiplication of this new way of living consecrated virginity, that is, life in common. Although the Saint stayed away in terms of his physical presence, he was concerned and followed the life of these female monasteries very closely. Proof of this are the letters already mentioned, 210 and 211. See A.

[7] The conference of Carthage.—The conference of Carthage means, without a doubt, the most important event in the long struggle between Catholics and Donatists. For the Donatist Church it meant its definitive legal defeat and the beginning of the process of disappearance. Its convocation was the work of the emperor Honorius, through an edict of October 14, 410, at the request of the Catholic council of Carthage, of June of the same 410, which had been preceded by another in the same sense from the Donatist side in January 406. The emperor entrusted the celebration of it to the tribune and notary Marcellinus, appointing him judge (cognitor). He convened it by an edict of January 19, 411. Although the conference began on June 1 of the same year, the activity prior to it was notable both on the part of the civil power and on the part of each of the Churches, the Catholic and the Donatist, that were present in Carthage around May 20. Already on the eve of the conference, around May 20 itself, Marcellin published a second edict that contained the regulations for the According to him, only a group of 18 people would attend.

sounds for each side. Of them, seven would actually be the spokespersons; Another seven would act as experts and advisors to the previous ones, but without public voice, and four in charge of reviewing the preparation of the complete minutes of everything that happened and said in each session. The rest should be left out, both the bishops and, of course, the laity. The same edict presented the procedure for the preparation with full guarantee of the minutes, which would be exposed to the public. Precisely the review of the works of notaries, both civil and ecclesiastical, was entrusted to the four bishops mentioned above. Catholics and Donatists had to give their assent to these provisions in a writing signed, at least, by the primates of each party. The Donatist response was made public on May 25. Although submitting, they state their opposition to the regulations, particularly to the point that it does not allow everyone to participate, in a conciliar plan. They also present the names of their spokespersons and other representatives of the Church. The Catholic response occurs in two moments. The first (1) also saw the light around May 25; It is full adherence and, in addition, the Catholic bishops present an offer to the Donatist bishops (see complementary note [ 9 ]: The offer of the Catholic bishops to the Donatist bishops). A second (2), later, perhaps around 30, in which they present their spokespersons, among whom is obviously Agustín, the first after the primate Aurelio, and other representatives. In the same letter they indicate what lines of action and discussion to follow. They did not miss the opportunity to show their rejection of the aforementioned Donatist response. Finally, the conference opened on June 1, at the Gargilio baths. On the Donatist side, the bishops present were 284, and on the Catholic side, 286. The first day was consumed by the reading of the convocation documents and the verification of the powers: recognition of the bishops of one party by those of the opposite party. To give time for the drafting of the minutes, the next session was announced for day 3. From the beginning, the Donatists They adopted a clearly obstructionist stance. On day 2 they asked for, and were granted, the Catholic brief (2) in which they named their own delegates to examine it. On day 3, the session resumed, with the same obstructionist tactic.

The Donatists demand that they be given the complete verbal report of the previous session, which, since it is not available, forces the resumption of the conference to be delayed until the 8th. On the 7th, always the Donatists, they delivered a second letter to Judge Marcellinus, a response to the refutation that the Catholics had made before (2) and demanded that it be read the next day, the 8th, the date of the final session. After new attempts at obstruction, based on prejudicial reasons, and the reading of official documents, the debates were fully entered, focused on two fundamental points: the cause of the Church and the cause of Caecilian, that is, a theoretical and a historical aspect. Once the debate is over and the members of both parties are called again, Marcellin dictates the sentence, which proclaims the Catholics the winners; sentence that later, on June 26, will be materialized in the legal provisions and subsequent coercive measures against the Donatists. The minutes, exposed in public, as had been announced, were given maximum publicity by the Catholic side. Augustine even exploits them in his sermons (see sermon 359). See P. MONCEAUX, Histoire littéraire de l'Ajrique chrétienne (Paris 1912) IV p.388-425. [8] Scripture as a testament of God.—Which is the authentic Church of Christ: the Catholic or the Donatist? This was, on a practical level,
Additional notes

what was discussed in the controversy between the two Churches. To arrive at the right answer, it was necessary to go one step further and know what the Church should be and is in its very reality. Catholics and Donatists agree that it is the fulfillment of God's promise, that it is the inheritance that the Father left to Christ. The Church will then be known by knowing that heritage. In turn, the inheritance is discovered by the will. This is a very common way for Augustine to talk about Scripture: Scripture as God's testament. Testament understood not in the usual sense, according to which we say Old or New Testament, that is, in the sense of a pact or alliance, but in the legal sense, that is, as the legal act by which heirs are established. Among others, we remember the following texts in which the bishop of Hippo resorts to this conception: Commentaries on Psalms 18 I I 5; 21 I I 30; 24,14; 36 I I I 18; 54.21; 88 I 28; Sermons 47,22; 358.2; Reply to the letters of Petiliano I 23,25; I I 8,20; The unity of the Church 6,11; Sermon to the people of the Church of Caesarea 1,5; letter 93.19; Reply to the grammarian Cresconio, Donatist I I I 63,70; IV 53.63; 60.72. Augustine therefore considers Scripture as God's testament in which the inheritance and, therefore, by identification, the Church is described. But try, however, to note the inevitable differences with respect to any human will, because they will serve your cause. They are the following: a) In the divine will it is the case that the testator is still living after the will has been opened, b) The inheritance bequeathed is something infinitely superior to what any man can leave, c) Contrary to human inheritance, the divine inheritance is indivisible: either one possesses it all or one does not possess it. Nor does each person's share decrease because the co-heirs increase. d) The behavior of the heirs is also different: they do not seek division, but rather possession in common, e) The divine will is always fulfilled. /) The judge who interprets the divine will is the testator himself. Having already entered into the will itself, after having been read and interpreted, it is clear that: a) The testator is God (the Father or Christ), b) The inheritance is the totality of the earth and peace, which is identified with it, because it exists where there are no parts, c) The heir is Christ, d) The co-heirs are Christians.

Ultimately, the most important thing about it is that the inheritance is the entirety of the land. And, therefore, the Donatists must recognize that it is the Catholics who possess the inheritance, and what it means, namely: that they have respected the will, because they possess the whole and the peace. The reading of the will has declared the Donatists defeated; But this neither humiliates them, the Saint will say, nor does it take anything away from them; On the contrary, it favors them, in that the will gives them more of what they fought for: they fought for a part (Africa) and they are offered the whole (the entire world). Hence the invitation to abandon his party and take possession of the authentic heritage, entering the Catholic Church. Nothing prevents him from doing so: neither the quality of the inheritance nor the remaining co-heirs, who, as stated above, do not seek to divide the inheritance, but rather to possess it in common. Thus, after reading the passages of Scripture that, for different reasons, can be considered as clauses that describe this inheritance, one discovers, as a characteristic note, universality, catholicity. Consequently, if the inheritance of God (the Church, by unanimous concession) has universality or catholicity as its characteristic note: where the latter exists, the former will exist. In a way, the dispute between Catholics and Donatists is resolved by simply resorting to geography. And not because

geography is in itself a theological criterion, but because no one can annul the promise of God. God's faithfulness is above human weakness. To renounce this catholicity in fact and in extension, as the Donatists do, would be to pretend that God's promise—his testament—has remained unfulfilled. In short, the Catholic Church, as the only truly universal one, with universality in fact, not just in law, is the authentic Church of Christ. Thus the center of the discussion has been reached, which has been resolved in favor of Augustine's thesis. The de fado is in accordance with the de jure. The Catholic Church is the authentic Church of Christ. See P. DE LUIS, The Holy Scripture as a "testament" of God in the anti-donatist work of Saint Augustine: Augustinian Study 15 (1980) 3-37. [9] The offer of the Catholic bishops to the Donatist bishops.—At the doors of the Carthage conference, the Catholic bishops, like the Donatists, had to give in writing their assent to the edict promulgated by Judge Marcellinus on the manner of proceeding therein (see complementary note [ 7 ]: The Carthage conference). The assembly of Catholic bishops, gathered for this purpose, took advantage of the occasion to present the offer to which Augustine alludes in sermon 358,4, and which tried to regulate the situation of the bishops in the eventual event that peace came, particularly in the cities where there were two, one Catholic and the other Donatist. In summary, the offer was that, if the judge ruled in favor of the Donatists, the Catholic bishops would resign en bloc; while, if the sentence favored them, they were willing to accept the Donatist bishops as brothers in the episcopate and co-episcopates in the same see according to practical modalities that they were responsible for suggesting. Nothing better than to bring here the very text of the letter that the assembly addressed to the imperial delegate, Marcellinus: «If the Donatists with whom we have to confer show that the Church of Christ suddenly disappeared due to contagion from I do not know what subjects whom they accuse, leaving only the party of Donato; If the Donatists can prove it, not only will we not violate the honors due to their episcopal ministry, but we will follow their advice for eternal salvation alone and we will remain grateful to their gracious benefit for having made the truth known to us.

On the other hand, if we could demonstrate that this Church of Christ, which already occupies with its numerous population the soil not only of the African provinces, but also of many transmarines and of many other towns, could not perish due to the sins of any men of its guild, which is fruitful throughout the world... and continues to grow; if we demonstrate that the cause of those whom they preferred to accuse, but were unable to convince, is finished and dismissed, although the cause of the Church is independent of that other personal cause; if we demonstrate the innocence of Cecilian and the violence and slander of the Donatists...; Finally, if with human or divine documents we prove... that these are innocent people persecuted with false accusations or that the Church of Christ, to which we are united, has not been destroyed with such crimes, in that case let them accept unity with us, so that they not only succeed in the path of salvation, but also retain their episcopal honor... "Each of us may take an honorary partner, both occupying the seat, like a pilgrim bishop with his colleague. This privilege is granted to some basilicas and both bishops honor each other with mutual honor... In this way, when one of them dies, the other will rule alone, according to the ancient custom. This is nothing new. The

Catholic charity has been observing it since the very beginning of the schism with those who, after seeing the criminal error of division condemned, came to taste, albeit late, the sweetness of unity. In any case, if the Christian populations prefer a single bishop and do not know how to tolerate the consortium of two because of that appearance of novelty, we will both leave the ministry. Let us eliminate the schism in the churches and build them in peaceful unity. Then, the bishops who do not have a rival in their diocese will establish bishops for the places they deem necessary once peace is settled. How would we hesitate to offer our Redeemer this sacrifice of humility? He descended from heaven to human members so that we might be his members, and will we refuse to descend from our seats lest his members be torn to pieces in cruel division? Personally, our greatest honor is to be faithful and obedient Christians; let's always be it. They only consecrate us bishops for the benefit of the Christian population. Let us contribute with our position to the Christian peace that the Christian population needs. If we are useful servants, how can we prefer our temporal dignities to the eternal reward of the Lord? If leaving the episcopate contributes to gathering the flock of Christ, will not our dignity be more profitable to us than if we retain it to divide that flock? "With what face will we dare to hope in the future century for the honor promised by Christ, if our honor prevents Christian unity in this century?" (letter 128,2-3). The letter bears the name of the entire assembly of Catholic bishops, but there is no doubt that its editor was Augustine. The expressions and ideas declare it openly. [10] Reconciliation at the time of death.—Christ had left to his Church the power to forgive all sins. Therefore, any faithful who had seriously stained baptismal purity could approach the bishop and request penance. The maternal wombs of the Church welcomed the repentant sinner and granted him forgiveness after having submitted to penitential practices that showed the sincerity of repentance. But this public and solemn forgiveness was only granted once in a lifetime. There was no possibility for a second public penance. Anyone who fell again had no other recourse but to entrust themselves exclusively to the mercy of God.

The Church did not ignore these subjects, but its work was reduced to the private sphere, inviting them to prayer and private penance as means to reconcile God's forgiveness. The doors of forgiveness were not closed, but it was left exclusively in the hands of God. To deprive a man of all hope of forgiveness would mean sinking him deeper and deeper into sin. That is why the Saint writes: «Sometimes the iniquity of men increases so much that, after having done their penance and after being reconciled with the altar, they return to commit similar or greater crimes. And yet, God also makes his sun rise upon them and continues to grant them, as before, the generous gifts of life and health. And, although in the Church there is no place for humiliation and penance for them, God does not forget his endurance with them... Cautiously and healthily, it has been prescribed that the place of humiliation and penance be granted only once, lest medicine become debased and prove less useful for the sick, since it is healthier the less it is despised. But who will dare to say to God: 'Why do you forgive again that man who, after his first penance, once again becomes entangled in the bonds of evil?'” (letter 153,3,7). But the faithful felt safer with the forgiveness granted by the Church; on the other they had no sensible evidence. On the other hand, the lady

The rigid model of single penance had its consequences for the lives of the faithful. Faced with the fear of falling again, many who had already joined the group of penitents indefinitely deferred asking for reconciliation and continued in their life of sin. Hence Augustine's persistent exhortation to penitents to change their lives (sermon 232,8; 393). Others did not even dare to ask for penance, which carried very heavy burdens. Both hoped to be able to reconcile quickly at the time of death, since then the Church was much less demanding in its conditions. It was certainly a shorter and less annoying possibility. But the bishop's pastoral care could not be satisfied with that. God's mercy should never be a reason to live apart from him. And, on the other hand, who can have the time of his death? Who has been assured that he will be able to do penance at that time? There is no other alternative, therefore, for anyone who wants to obtain God's forgiveness, than to do penance while he is in health, when he still has time. As the Bishop of Hippo says so many times, God has assured you forgiveness for when you repent tomorrow; but no one has assured you of tomorrow. Furthermore, Augustine in sermon 393 confronts the excessive confidence of some in the forgiveness obtained by this quick penance, without the expiatory exercises for sins: the purification obtained by such penance is not identical to that of baptism. Baptism certainly erases everything, without the slightest doubt; But does the same happen with that penance? Augustine neither affirms nor denies; He limits himself to expressing his doubt.
